The meaning should be understood everywhere by this method.

mula_pali: 34. ‘‘‘Dinnādānaṃ nissāya adinnādānaṃ pahātabba’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu adinnādāyī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana adinnādāyī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya adinnādānapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ adinnādānapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā adinnādānapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ adinnādānaṃ. Ye ca adinnādānapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā adinnādānā paṭiviratassa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Dinnādānaṃ nissāya adinnādānaṃ pahātabba’nti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.
mula_english:
34. “'With the support of taking what is given (*dinnādānaṃ*), taking what is not given (*adinnādānaṃ*) is to be abandoned (*pahātabba*)'—so it was said. What is the reference for what was said? Here, householder (*gahapati*), a noble disciple (*ariyasāvako*) reflects thus: 'Those fetters (*saṃyojanānaṃ*) because of which I might be one who takes what is not given (*adinnādāyī*), for the abandonment (*pahānāya*) and complete destruction (*samucchedāya*) of those fetters (*saṃyojanānaṃ*) I have undertaken the practice (*paṭipanno*).

"If I were one who takes what is not given (*adinnādāyī*), I would blame myself for this; the wise (*viññū*), having investigated (*anuviccāpi*), would censure me for this; and on the dissolution (*bhedā*) of the body (*kāyassa*), after death (*maraṇā*), an unhappy destination (*duggati*) would be expected because of taking what is not given (*adinnādānapaccayā*).

"But this taking what is not given (*adinnādānaṃ*) is itself a fetter (*saṃyojanaṃ*) and a hindrance (*nīvaraṇaṃ*).

"And while taints (*āsavā*), vexation (*vighāta*), and fever (*pariḷāhā*) might arise through taking what is not given (*adinnādānapaccayā*), there are no taints (*āsavā*), vexation (*vighāta*), and fever (*pariḷāhā*) in one who abstains (*paṭiviratassa*) from taking what is not given (*adinnādānā*.'

'With the support of taking what is given (*dinnādānaṃ*), taking what is not given (*adinnādānaṃ*) is to be abandoned (*pahātabba*)'—so it was said. So it is with reference to this that it was said.

mula_pali: 35. ‘‘‘Saccavācaṃ nissāya musāvādo pahātabbo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu musāvādī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana musāvādī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya musāvādapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ musāvādapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā musāvādapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ musāvādo . Ye ca musāvādapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, musāvādā paṭiviratassa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Saccavācaṃ nissāya musāvādo pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.
mula_english:
35.
“‘With the support of truthful speech ( *saccavācaṃ*), false speech ( *musāvādo* ) is to be abandoned ( *pahātabbo* ).’ So it was said. But with reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Those fetters ( *saṃyojanānaṃ* ) on account of which I might be a liar ( *musāvādī assaṃ*), for the abandonment ( *pahānāya* ) and complete destruction ( *samucchedāya* ) of those fetters ( *saṃyojanānaṃ* ) I have undertaken the practice ( *paṭipanno* ).
If I were a liar ( *musāvādī assaṃ*), I myself would blame ( *upavadeyya* ) myself on account of false speech ( *musāvādapaccayā* ); the wise ( *viññū* ), having investigated, would censure ( *garaheyyuṃ* ) me on account of false speech ( *musāvādapaccayā* ); and on the dissolution ( *bhedā* ) of the body ( *kāyassa* ), after death ( *maraṇā* ), an unhappy destination ( *duggati* ) would be expected ( *pāṭikaṅkhā* ) on account of false speech ( *musāvādapaccayā* ).
Indeed, this is a fetter ( *saṃyojanaṃ* ), this is a hindrance ( *nīvaraṇaṃ* ), namely, false speech ( *musāvādo* ).
And while taints ( *āsavā* ), vexation ( *vighāta* ), and fever ( *pariḷāhā* ) might arise through false speech ( *musāvādapaccayā* ), there are no taints ( *āsavā* ), vexation ( *vighāta* ), and fever ( *pariḷāhā* ) in one who abstains ( *paṭiviratassa* ) from false speech ( *musāvādā* ).’
‘With the support of truthful speech ( *saccavācaṃ*), false speech ( *musāvādo* ) is to be abandoned ( *pahātabbo* ).’ So it was said with reference to this."

mula_pali: 36. ‘‘‘Apisuṇaṃ vācaṃ nissāya pisuṇā vācā pahātabbā’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu pisuṇavāco assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana pisuṇavāco assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya pisuṇavācāpaccayā , anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ pisuṇavācāpaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā pisuṇavācāpaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ pisuṇā vācā. Ye ca pisuṇavācāpaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, pisuṇāya vācāya paṭiviratassa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Apisuṇaṃ vācaṃ nissāya pisuṇā vācā pahātabbā’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.
mula_english:
36. "'With the support of unmalicious speech, malicious speech is to be abandoned.' Thus, it was said. Now, what was said with reference to what? Here, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'Indeed, because of which fetters I might be of malicious speech, I have undertaken the path for the abandoning and complete destruction of those fetters.'

If I were of malicious speech, I would blame myself for this; the wise, having investigated, would censure me for this; and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination ( *durgati*) would be expected because of malicious speech.

But this malicious speech is itself a fetter (*saṃyojanaṃ*) and a hindrance (*nīvaraṇaṃ*).

And while taints (*āsavā*), vexation (*vighāta*), and fever (*pariḷāhā*) might arise because of malicious speech, there are no taints (*āsavā*), vexation (*vighāta*), and fever (*pariḷāhā*) in one who abstains from malicious speech.’

‘With the support of unmalicious speech, malicious speech is to be abandoned’ – thus, whatever was said, this was said with reference to this.

mula_pali: 37. ‘‘‘Agiddhilobhaṃ nissāya giddhilobho pahātabbo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu giddhilobhī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana giddhilobhī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya giddhilobhapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ giddhilobhapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā giddhilobhapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ giddhilobho. Ye ca giddhilobhapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, giddhilobhā paṭiviratassa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Agiddhilobhaṃ nissāya giddhilobho pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.
mula_english:
37. ‘“With the support of refraining from rapacious greed (*agiddhilobha*), rapacious greed (*giddhilobha*) is to be abandoned." So it was said… But with reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: "Those fetters because of which I might be rapaciously greedy, I have undertaken the practice for the abandoning and complete destruction of those fetters."

If I were to be rapaciously greedy, I would blame myself for this; the wise, having investigated, would censure me for this; and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination would be expected because of rapacious greed.

But this rapacious greed is itself a fetter (*saṃyojana*) and a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).

And while taints (*āsava*), vexation (*vighāta*), and fever (*pariḷāha*) might arise through rapacious greed, there are no taints, vexation, and fever for one who abstains from rapacious greed."

‘“With the support of refraining from rapacious greed, rapacious greed is to be abandoned.” So it is with reference to this that it was said.

mula_pali: 38. ‘‘‘Anindārosaṃ nissāya nindāroso pahātabbo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu nindārosī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana nindārosī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya nindārosapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ nindārosapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā nindārosapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ nindāroso. Ye ca nindārosapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, anindārosissa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Anindārosaṃ nissāya nindāroso pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.
mula_english: 38. ‘With the support of refraining from spiteful scolding, spiteful scolding is to be abandoned.’ So it was said. But what was said with reference to what? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Because of whatever fetters I might be spitefully scolding, I have undertaken the path for the abandoning, for the complete destruction of those fetters.’ If I were to be spitefully scolding, I would blame myself for this; the wise, having investigated, would censure me for this; and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination would be expected because of spiteful scolding. But this spiteful scolding is itself a fetter and a hindrance. And while taints, vexation, and fever might arise through spiteful scolding, there are no taints, vexation, and fever for one who refrains from spiteful scolding.’ ‘With the support of refraining from spiteful scolding, spiteful scolding is to be abandoned.’ So it was said with reference to this.

mula_pali: 39. ‘‘‘Akkodhūpāyāsaṃ nissāya kodhūpāyāso pahātabbo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu kodhūpāyāsī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana kodhūpāyāsī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya kodhūpāyāsapaccayā , anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ kodhūpāyāsapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā kodhūpāyāsapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ kodhūpāyāso. Ye ca kodhūpāyāsapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, akkodhūpāyāsissa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Akkodhūpāyāsaṃ nissāya kodhūpāyāso pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.
mula_english:
39. ‘“With the support of refraining from angry despair ( *akkodhūpāyāsaṃ*), angry despair ( *kodhūpāyāso*) is to be abandoned.” So it was said, but with reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: “Those fetters ( *saṃyojanānaṃ*) because of which I might be full of angry despair ( *kodhūpāyāsī*), I have undertaken the path for the abandoning and complete destruction ( *pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno*) of those fetters.”

If I were to be full of angry despair ( *kodhūpāyāsī assaṃ*), I would blame myself for this; the wise, having investigated, would censure me for this; and on the dissolution of the body ( *kāyassa bhedā*), after death ( *paraṃ maraṇā*), because of being full of angry despair ( *kodhūpāyāsapaccayā*), an unhappy destination ( *duggati pāṭikaṅkhā*) would be expected.

But this angry despair ( *kodhūpāyāso*) is itself a fetter ( *saṃyojanaṃ*) and a hindrance ( *nīvaraṇaṃ*).

And while taints ( *āsavā*), vexation ( *vighāta*), and fever ( *pariḷāhā*) might arise through angry despair, there are no taints, vexation, and fever for one who is not full of angry despair.’

‘“With the support of refraining from angry despair ( *akkodhūpāyāsaṃ nissāya*), angry despair ( *kodhūpāyāso*) is to be abandoned.”’ So it was said... with reference to this that it was said.

mula_pali: 40. ‘‘‘Anatimānaṃ nissāya atimāno pahātabbo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu atimānī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana atimānī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya atimānapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ atimānapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā atimānapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ atimāno. Ye ca atimānapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, anatimānissa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Anatimānaṃ nissāya atimāno pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.
mula_english:
40. “‘With the support of non-arrogance, arrogance is to be abandoned.’ So it was said. And with reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Those fetters for which I might be arrogant, I have undertaken the practice for the abandoning and complete destruction of those fetters.’

If I were to be arrogant, I would blame myself for this; the wise, having investigated, would censure me for this; and on the dissolution of the body, after death, because of being arrogant an unhappy destination would be expected.

But this arrogance is itself a fetter (saṃyojana) and a hindrance (nīvaraṇa).

And while taints (āsava), vexation, and fever might arise through arrogance, there are no taints, vexation, and fever for one who is not arrogant.’

‘With the support of non-arrogance, arrogance is to be abandoned.’ So it is with reference to this that it was said.

mula_pali:
41. ‘‘Ime kho, gahapati, aṭṭha dhammā saṃkhittena vuttā, vitthārena vibhattā avibhattā (syā. ka.), ye ariyassa vinaye vohārasamucchedāya saṃvattanti; na tveva tāva ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hotī’’ti.

‘‘Yathā kathaṃ pana, bhante, ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hoti? Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā tathā dhammaṃ desetu yathā ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hotī’’ti. ‘‘Tena hi, gahapati, suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī’’ti. ‘‘Evaṃ, bhante’’ti kho potaliyo gahapati bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

Kāmādīnavakathā
mula_english:
“These eight things, householder, that have been stated in brief and explained in detail, lead to the cutting off of affairs in the Noble One’s Discipline; but the cutting off of affairs in the Noble One’s Discipline has not yet been achieved entirely and in all ways.”

“But how, venerable sir, is the cutting off of affairs in the Noble One’s Discipline achieved entirely and in all ways? It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach the Dhamma in such a way that the cutting off of affairs in the Noble One’s Discipline would be achieved entirely and in all ways.”

“Then listen, householder, and attend closely to what I shall say.”

“Yes, venerable sir,” Potaliya the householder replied.

The Blessed One said this:

The Discourse on the Drawbacks of Sensual Pleasures

mula_pali:
42. ‘‘Seyyathāpi , gahapati, kukkuro jighacchādubbalyapareto goghātakasūnaṃ paccupaṭṭhito assa. Tamenaṃ dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ nimmaṃsaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ upasumbheyya upacchubheyya (sī. pī.), upacchūbheyya (syā. kaṃ.), upaccumbheyya (ka.). Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, api nu kho so kukkuro amuṃ aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ nimmaṃsaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ palehanto jighacchādubbalyaṃ paṭivineyyā’’ti?

‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’.

‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’?

‘‘Aduñhi, bhante, aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ nimmaṃsaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ. Yāvadeva pana so kukkuro kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assāti. Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā bahūpāyāsā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā taṃ abhinivajjetvā, yāyaṃ upekkhā ekattā ekattasitā yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhanti tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.

bahūpāyāsā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)
mula_english:
42. Just as, householder, a dog (kukkuro) overcome with hunger and weakness (jighacchādubbalyapareto) might approach a butcher's stall (goghātakasūnaṃ paccupaṭṭhito). Then a skilled butcher (dakkho goghātako) or his apprentice would toss him a skeleton of bones (aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ) stripped of flesh (nimmaṃsaṃ), well-cleaned (sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ), and smeared with blood (lohitamakkhitaṃ). What do you think, householder, would that dog, while licking that skeleton of bones stripped of flesh, well-cleaned and smeared with blood, get rid of his hunger and weakness?"

"No, venerable sir."

"What is the reason for that?"

"Because, venerable sir, it is a skeleton of bones, well-cleaned and stripped of flesh. The dog would only get a share of weariness and frustration (kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assāti)."

"In the same way (evameva kho), householder, a noble disciple (ariyasāvako) reflects thus: 'Sensual pleasures (kāmā) have been compared to a skeleton of bones (aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā) by the Blessed One (bhagavatā), [they are] full of much suffering (bahudukkhā) and much despair (bahupāyāsā), and the danger (ādīnava) in them is even greater (ettha bhiyyo).' Having seen this as it actually is (yathābhūtaṃ) with right wisdom (sammappaññāya), he avoids (abhinivajjetvā) the equanimity (upekkhā) that is diversified (nānattā), based on diversity (nānattasitā), and develops (bhāveti) the equanimity (upekkhā) that is unified (ekattā), based on unity (ekattasitā), where clinging to the material things of the world (lokāmisūpādānā) utterly ceases (aparisesā nirujjhanti) without remainder."

Notes: bahūpāyāsā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)
commentary_pali:
42. Vitthāradesanāyaṃ tamenaṃ dakkhoti padassa upasumbheyyāti iminā saddhiṃ sambandho veditabbo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, tamenaṃ kukkuraṃ upasumbheyya, tassa samīpe khipeyyāti attho. Aṭṭhikaṅkalanti uraṭṭhiṃ vā piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ vā sīsaṭṭhiṃ vā. Tañhi nimmaṃsattā kaṅkalanti vuccati. Sunikkantaṃnikkantanti yathā sunikkantaṃ hoti, evaṃ nikkantaṃ nillikhitaṃ, yadettha allīnamaṃsaṃ atthi, taṃ sabbaṃ nillikhitvā aṭṭhimattameva katanti attho. Tenevāha ‘‘nimmaṃsa’’nti. Lohitaṃ pana makkhitvā tiṭṭhati, tena vuttaṃ ‘‘lohitamakkhita’’nti.

Bahudukkhā bahupāyāsāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikehi dukkhehi bahudukkhā, upāyāsasaṃkilesehi bahupāyāsā. Yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitāti yā ayaṃ pañcakāmaguṇārammaṇavasena nānāsabhāvā, tāneva ca ārammaṇāni nissitattā ‘‘nānattasitā’’ti vuccati pañcakāmaguṇūpekkhā, taṃ abhinivajjetvā. Ekattā ekattasitāti catutthajjhānupekkhā, sā hi divasampi ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe uppajjanato ekasabhāvā, tadeva ekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ nissitattā ekattasitā nāma. Yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhantīti yattha catutthajjhānupekkhāyaṃ yaṃ upekkhaṃ āgamma yaṃ paṭicca sabbena sabbaṃ aparisesā lokāmisasaṅkhātā pañcakāmaguṇāmisā nirujjhanti. Pañcakāmaguṇāmisāti ca kāmaguṇārammaṇachandarāgā, gahaṇaṭṭhena teyeva ca upādānātipi vuttā. Tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāvetīti taṃ lokāmisūpādānānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ catutthajjhānupekkhameva vaḍḍheti.

Bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā Yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā Ekattā ekattasitā Yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhantī Pañcakāmaguṇāmisā Tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāvetī
commentary_english:
42. In the detailed explanation, the connection of the phrase "skilled in that" (*tamenaṃ dakkho*), with the word "should approach" (*upasumbheyyā*) should be understood in this way.

This means: one should approach that dog, one should throw [food] near it; this is the meaning.

"A skeleton" (*aṭṭhikaṅkala*) means a breast bone or a backbone or a head bone.

Because it is without flesh, it is called a skeleton.

"Well-scraped," "scraped" (*sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ*): Just as it is well-scraped, so it is scraped and made smooth, and whatever clinging flesh there is, all of that is scraped away, only the bones remain; this is the meaning.

Therefore, he said, "without flesh" (*nimmaṃsa*).

But blood having been smeared remains. Therefore, it is said, "smeared with blood" (*lohitamakkhita*).

"With much suffering, with much distress" (*bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā*) means with much suffering due to suffering in this very life and in the life to come, with much distress due to distress and defilements.

"Whatever equanimity is diverse, dependent on diversity" (*yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā*) means whatever equanimity is of diverse natures through the force of the five sense-qualities (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), and because those objects are dependent, it is called "dependent on diversity" (*nānattasitā*). Therefore, one should abandon equanimity with the five sense-qualities (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).

"Unified, dependent on unity" (*ekattā ekattasitā*) is the equanimity of the fourth *jhāna*; for that is of one nature, since it arises in a single object even for a day, and because it depends on that single object, it is called "dependent on unity" (*ekattasitā*).

"Where all grasping at worldly bait ceases without remainder" (*yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhantī*) means wherever, in the equanimity of the fourth *jhāna*, that equanimity is reached, and because of that, all the objects designated as worldly bait, the sense-qualities (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) as bait, cease without remainder.

"The sense-qualities as bait" (*pañcakāmaguṇāmisā*) are desire and passion for objects of the sense-qualities, and they themselves are also called grasping due to their characteristic of seizing.

"He cultivates that same equanimity" (*tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāvetī*) means he develops only the equanimity of the fourth *jhāna*, which is the opposite of the grasping at those worldly baits.

With much suffering, with much distress, whatever equanimity is diverse, dependent on diversity, unified, dependent on unity, where all grasping at worldly bait ceases without remainder, the sense-qualities as bait, he cultivates that same equanimity.

mula_pali:
43. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, gahapati, gijjho vā kaṅko vā kulalo vā maṃsapesiṃ ādāya uḍḍīyeyya uḍḍayeyya (syā. pī.). Tamenaṃ gijjhāpi kaṅkāpi kulalāpi anupatitvā anupatitvā vitaccheyyuṃ vissajjeyyuṃ virājeyyuṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, sace so gijjho vā kaṅko vā kulalo vā taṃ maṃsapesiṃ na khippameva paṭinissajjeyya, so tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha’’nti?

‘‘Evaṃ, bhante’’.

‘‘Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘maṃsapesūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā taṃ abhinivajjetvā yāyaṃ upekkhā ekattā ekattasitā yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhanti tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.
mula_english:
“Suppose, householder, a vulture (*gijjha*), a crow (*kaṅka*), or a hawk (*kulala*) seized a piece of meat (*maṃsapesiṃ*) and flew away. Then vultures, crows, and hawks flew up and pecked and clawed it.

What do you think, householder? If that vulture, crow, or hawk does not quickly let go of that piece of meat, wouldn’t it incur death or deadly suffering because of that?”

“Indeed, venerable sir.”

“So too, householder, a noble disciple (*ariyasāvako*) considers thus: ‘Sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) have been compared to a piece of meat (*maṃsapesūpamā*) by the Blessed One; they provide much suffering (*bahudukkhā*) and much despair (*bahupāyāsā*), while the danger (*ādīnava*) in them is great (*bhiyyo*) .’ Having seen this thus as it actually is (*yathābhūtaṃ*) with proper wisdom (*sammappaññāya*), he avoids the equanimity (*upekkhā*) that is diversified (*nānattā*), based on diversity (*nānattasitā*), and develops the equanimity (*upekkhā*) that is unified (*ekattā*), based on unity (*ekattasitā*), where clinging to the material things of the world (*lokāmisūpādānā*) utterly ceases without remainder (*aparisesā nirujjhanti*).
commentary_pali: 43.Uḍḍīyeyyāti uppatitvā gaccheyya. Anupatitvāti anubandhitvā. Vitaccheyyunti mukhatuṇḍakena ḍaṃsantā taccheyyuṃ. Vissajjeyyunti maṃsapesiṃ nakhehi kaḍḍhitvā pāteyyuṃ.
commentary_english:
43. *uḍḍīyeyyā* means "having flown up, one would go."
*anupatitvā* means "having followed".
*vitaccheyyu* means "biting with the beak, they would cut off."
*vissajjeyyu* means "having pulled off a lump of flesh with their nails, they would throw it down."

mula_pali:
44. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, gahapati, puriso ādittaṃ tiṇukkaṃ ādāya paṭivātaṃ gaccheyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, sace so puriso taṃ ādittaṃ tiṇukkaṃ na khippameva paṭinissajjeyya tassa sā ādittā tiṇukkā hatthaṃ vā daheyya bāhuṃ vā daheyya aññataraṃ vā aññataraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ daheyya. aññataraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅga (sī. pī.) daheyya, so tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha’’nti?

‘‘Evaṃ, bhante’’.

‘‘Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘tiṇukkūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.
mula_english:
“Householder, suppose a man took a blazing grass torch (ādittaṃ tiṇukkaṃ) and went against the wind.

What do you think, householder? If that man does not quickly let go of that blazing grass torch, wouldn’t that blazing grass torch burn his hand or his arm or some other part of his body, so that because of that he would come to death or deadly suffering (maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ)?”

“So it is, venerable sir.”

“So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus: ‘Sensual pleasures (kāmā) have been compared to a grass torch by the Blessed One; they provide much suffering (bahudukkhā) and much despair (bahupāyāsā), while the danger (ādīnava) in them is great.’ Having seen this thus as it actually is with proper wisdom… he develops equanimity (upekkhā).

mula_pali:
45. ‘‘Seyyathāpi , gahapati, aṅgārakāsu sādhikaporisā, pūrā aṅgārānaṃ vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya jīvitukāmo amaritukāmo sukhakāmo dukkhappaṭikkūlo. Tamenaṃ dve balavanto purisā nānābāhāsu gahetvā aṅgārakāsuṃ upakaḍḍheyyuṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, api nu so puriso iticiticeva kāyaṃ sannāmeyyā’’ti?

‘‘Evaṃ, bhante’’.

‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’?

‘‘Viditañhi , bhante, tassa purisassa imañcāhaṃ aṅgārakāsuṃ papatissāmi, tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigacchissāmi maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha’’nti. ‘‘Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.
mula_english:
45. "Householder, suppose there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height full of glowing coals without flame or smoke. Then a man came who wanted to live and not to die, who wanted pleasure and recoiled from pain, and two strong men seized him by both arms and dragged him towards that charcoal pit. What do you think, householder? Would that man twist his body this way and that?"

"Yes, venerable sir."

"Why is that?"

"Because that man knows that if he falls into that charcoal pit, he will incur death or deadly suffering because of that."

"So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus: 'Sensual pleasures are like a charcoal pit (aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā) by the Blessed One; they provide much suffering (bahu-dukhā) and much despair (bahu-upāyāsā), while the danger (ādīnava) in them is great.' Having seen this thus as it actually is (yathābhūtaṃ) with proper wisdom (sammappaññāya)…he develops equanimity (upekkhā).

mula_pali: 46. ‘‘Seyyathāpi , gahapati, puriso supinakaṃ passeyya ārāmarāmaṇeyyakaṃ vanarāmaṇeyyakaṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṃ pokkharaṇirāmaṇeyyakaṃ. So paṭibuddho na kiñci paṭipasseyya passeyya (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘supinakūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.
mula_english: “Householder, suppose a man might see in a dream lovely parks (*ārāma*), lovely groves (*vana*), lovely meadows (*bhūmi*), and lovely lakes (*pokkharaṇī*). But upon awakening, he would perceive nothing. So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures (*kāma*) have been compared to dreams; they are said by the Blessed One to be the source of much suffering (*dukkha*) and much despair (*upāyāsa*), while the danger (*ādīnava*) in them is great.’ …and so on… He cultivates equanimity (*upekkhā*) regarding them.

mula_pali:
47. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, gahapati, puriso yācitakaṃ bhogaṃ yācitvā yānaṃ vā yānaṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī.) poriseyyaṃ poroseyyaṃ (sī. pī. ka.), oropeyya (syā. kaṃ.) pavaramaṇikuṇḍalaṃ. So tehi yācitakehi bhogehi purakkhato parivuto antarāpaṇaṃ paṭipajjeyya. Tamenaṃ jano disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘bhogī vata, bho, puriso, evaṃ kira bhogino bhogāni bhuñjantī’ti. Tamenaṃ sāmikā yattha yattheva passeyyuṃ tattha tattheva sāni hareyyuṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, alaṃ nu kho tassa purisassa aññathattāyā’’ti?

‘‘Evaṃ, bhante’’.

‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’?

‘‘Sāmino hi, bhante, sāni harantī’’ti. ‘‘Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yācitakūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.
mula_english:
“Householder, suppose a man, having borrowed goods on loan, obtained a vehicle or excellent jeweled earrings. Preceded and surrounded by those borrowed goods, he would go to the marketplace. Seeing him, people would say, ‘Sirs, that is a rich man! That is how the rich enjoy their wealth!’ Then the owners, whenever and wherever they saw him, would take back their things. What do you think, householder? Would that be enough to make that man unhappy?”

“Yes, venerable sir.”

“Why is that?”

“Because, venerable sir, the owners would be taking back their things.”

“In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been described by the Blessed One as like borrowed goods, as bringing much suffering and much despair, and as having great danger in them.’ … He develops equanimity with regard to that.
commentary_pali: 47.Yānaṃ vā poriseyyanti purisānucchavikaṃ yānaṃ. Pavaramaṇikuṇḍalanti nānappakāraṃ uttamamaṇiñca kuṇḍalañca. Sāni harantīti attano bhaṇḍakāni gaṇhanti.
commentary_english: 47. yānaṃ vā poriseyyanti *purisānucchavikaṃ yānaṃ*. pavaramaṇikuṇḍalanti *nānappakāraṃ uttamamaṇiñca kuṇḍalañca*. sāni harantīti *attano bhaṇḍakāni gaṇhanti*.

mula_pali:
48. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, gahapati, gāmassa vā nigamassa vā avidūre tibbo vanasaṇḍo. Tatrassa rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo uppannaphalo (syā.) ca, na cassu kānici phalāni bhūmiyaṃ patitāni. Atha puriso āgaccheyya phalatthiko phalagavesī phalapariyesanaṃ caramāno. So taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā taṃ rukkhaṃ passeyya sampannaphalañca upapannaphalañca. Tassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo ca, natthi ca kānici phalāni bhūmiyaṃ patitāni. Jānāmi kho panāhaṃ rukkhaṃ ārohituṃ āruhituṃ (sī.). Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ rukkhaṃ ārohitvā yāvadatthañca khādeyyaṃ ucchaṅgañca pūreyya’nti. So taṃ rukkhaṃ ārohitvā yāvadatthañca khādeyya ucchaṅgañca pūreyya. Atha dutiyo puriso āgaccheyya phalatthiko phalagavesī phalapariyesanaṃ caramāno tiṇhaṃ kuṭhāriṃ kudhāriṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) ādāya. So taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā taṃ rukkhaṃ passeyya sampannaphalañca upapannaphalañca. Tassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo ca, natthi ca kānici phalāni bhūmiyaṃ patitāni. Na kho panāhaṃ jānāmi rukkhaṃ ārohituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ rukkhaṃ mūlato chetvā yāvadatthañca khādeyyaṃ ucchaṅgañca pūreyya’nti. So taṃ rukkhaṃ mūlatova chindeyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, amuko asu (sī. pī.) yo so puriso paṭhamaṃ rukkhaṃ ārūḷho sace so na khippameva oroheyya tassa so rukkho papatanto hatthaṃ vā bhañjeyya pādaṃ vā bhañjeyya aññataraṃ vā aññataraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ bhañjeyya, so tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha’’nti?

‘‘Evaṃ, bhante’’.

‘‘Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘rukkhaphalūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā taṃ abhinivajjetvā yāyaṃ upekkhā ekattā ekattasitā yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhanti tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.
mula_english:
48. “Householder, suppose there were a dense grove not far from some village or town.

Within it, there was a tree laden with fruit (**sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo**), and none of its fruits had fallen to the ground.

Then a man came, needing fruit (**phalatthiko**), seeking fruit (**phalagavesī**), wandering in search of fruit (**phalapariyesanaṃ caramāno**).

Having entered the grove, he saw the tree laden with fruit (**sampannaphalañca upapannaphalañca**).

He thought, ‘This tree is laden with fruit (**sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo**), and none of its fruits have fallen to the ground.

I know how to climb a tree.’

So, he climbed the tree, ate as much as he wanted, and filled his bag.

Then, a second man came, needing fruit (**phalatthiko**), seeking fruit (**phalagavesī**), wandering in search of fruit (**phalapariyesanaṃ caramāno**), and taking a sharp axe (**tiṇhaṃ kuṭhāriṃ**).

Having entered the grove, he saw the tree laden with fruit (**sampannaphalañca upapannaphalañca**).

He thought, ‘This tree is laden with fruit (**sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo**), and none of its fruits have fallen to the ground.

I do not know how to climb a tree.

So, let me cut this tree down at its root, eat as much fruit as I want, and fill my bag.’

And he cut that tree down at its root.

What do you think, householder? If that first man who had climbed the tree didn’t come down quickly, when the tree falls, wouldn’t he break his hand or his foot or some other part of his body, so that he might incur death or deadly suffering?”

“Yes, venerable sir.”

“So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared to a fruit tree (**rukkhaphalūpamā kāmā**) by the Blessed One; they provide much suffering (**bahudukkhā**) and much despair (**bahupāyāsā**), while the danger (**ādīnavo**) in them is great.’

Having seen this thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, he avoids the equanimity that is diversified, based on diversity (**yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā taṃ abhinivajjetvā**), and develops the equanimity that is unified, based on unity (**yāyaṃ upekkhā ekattā ekattasitā**), where clinging to the material things of the world utterly ceases without remainder (**yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhanti tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti**).
commentary_pali: 48.Sampannaphalanti madhuraphalaṃ. Upapannaphalanti phalūpapannaṃ bahuphalaṃ.
commentary_english: 48. sampannaphalanti: sweet fruit ( *madhuraphalaṃ*). upapannaphalanti: fruit endowed with qualities (*phalūpapannaṃ*), abundant fruit (*bahuphalaṃ*).

mula_pali:
49. ‘‘Sa kho so, gahapati, ariyasāvako imaṃyeva anuttaraṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ āgamma anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati.

‘‘Sa kho so, gahapati, ariyasāvako imaṃyeva anuttaraṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ āgamma dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānāti.

‘‘Sa kho so, gahapati, ariyasāvako imaṃyeva anuttaraṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ āgamma āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Ettāvatā kho, gahapati, ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hoti.
mula_english:
“And indeed, householder, when the noble disciple has arrived at that unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity, he recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births...and so on... Thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.

“And indeed, householder, when the noble disciple has arrived at that unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate…and so on… he understands how beings pass on according to their actions (yathākammūpage satte pajānāti).

“And indeed, householder, when the noble disciple has arrived at that unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity, by realizing for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints (āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati).

“At this point, householder, the cutting off of affairs in the Noble One’s Discipline has been achieved entirely and in all ways (ettāvatā kho, gahapati, ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hoti).”
commentary_pali: 49.Anuttaranti uttamaṃ pabhassaraṃ nirupakkilesaṃ.
commentary_english: 49. *anuttara* means: the highest, radiant, and free from defilements (*nirupakkilesaṃ*).

mula_pali:
50. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, yathā ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hoti, api nu tvaṃ evarūpaṃ vohārasamucchedaṃ attani samanupassasī’’ti? ‘‘Ko cāhaṃ, bhante, ko ca ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo! Ārakā ahaṃ, bhante, ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedā. Mayañhi, bhante, pubbe aññatitthiye paribbājake anājānīyeva samāne ājānīyāti amaññimha, anājānīyeva samāne ājānīyabhojanaṃ bhojimha, anājānīyeva samāne ājānīyaṭhāne ṭhapimha; bhikkhū pana mayaṃ, bhante, ājānīyeva samāne anājānīyāti amaññimha, ājānīyeva samāne anājānīyabhojanaṃ bhojimha, ājānīyeva samāne anājānīyaṭhāne ṭhapimha; idāni pana mayaṃ, bhante, aññatitthiye paribbājake anājānīyeva samāne anājānīyāti jānissāma, anājānīyeva samāne anājānīyabhojanaṃ bhojessāma, anājānīyeva samāne anājānīyaṭhāne ṭhapessāma. Bhikkhū pana mayaṃ, bhante, ājānīyeva samāne ājānīyāti jānissāma ājānīyeva samāne ājānīyabhojanaṃ bhojessāma, ājānīyeva samāne ājānīyaṭhāne ṭhapessāma. Ajanesi vata me, bhante, bhagavā samaṇesu samaṇappemaṃ, samaṇesu samaṇappasādaṃ, samaṇesu samaṇagāravaṃ. Abhikkantaṃ, bhante, abhikkantaṃ, bhante ! Seyyathāpi, bhante, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti; evamevaṃ kho, bhante, bhagavatā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata’’nti.

Potaliyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.
mula_english:
50. What do you think, householder? In the Noble One’s Discipline, is there a complete cutting off of all affairs, in every way? Do you see in yourself such a cutting off of affairs?” “Venerable sir, who am I, and what is the complete cutting off of all affairs in every way in the Noble One’s Discipline! Venerable sir, I am far removed from the complete cutting off of all affairs in every way in the Noble One’s Discipline.

For, venerable sir, though the wanderers of other sects are not thoroughbreds, we imagined that they are thoroughbreds; though they are not thoroughbreds, we fed them the food of thoroughbreds; though they are not thoroughbreds, we set them in the place of thoroughbreds. But though the *bhikkhus* are thoroughbreds, we imagined that they are not thoroughbreds; though they are thoroughbreds, we fed them the food of those who are not thoroughbreds; though they are thoroughbreds, we set them in the place of those who are not thoroughbreds. But now, venerable sir, though the wanderers of other sects are not thoroughbreds, we shall understand that they are not thoroughbreds; though they are not thoroughbreds, we shall feed them the food of those who are not thoroughbreds; though they are not thoroughbreds, we shall set them in the place of those who are not thoroughbreds.

But as the *bhikkhus* are thoroughbreds, we shall understand that they are thoroughbreds; as they are thoroughbreds, we shall feed them the food of thoroughbreds; as they are thoroughbreds, we shall set them in the place of those who are thoroughbreds.

Venerable sir, the Blessed One *Bhagavā* has inspired in me love for ascetics (*samaṇa*), confidence in ascetics, reverence for ascetics.

Excellent, venerable Sir! Excellent, venerable Sir! Just as, venerable Sir, one might set upright what has been overturned, or open up what has been closed, or show a path to one who is lost, or carry an oil lamp into the darkness, 'those with vision will see forms', just so has the *Dharma* been explained by the Blessed One *Bhagavata* in countless ways.

I go to the Blessed One (*bhagavantaṃ*) for refuge, and to the *Dharma* (*dhammañca*), and to the *Saṃgha* (*bhikkhusaṅghañca*), the community of monks.

May the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) accept me as a lay follower (*upāsakaṃ*) who has gone for refuge (*saraṇaṃ gataṃ*) from this day forward, for as long as life lasts."

The *Potaliyasutta* is finished, the fourth.
commentary_pali:
50.Ārakā ahaṃ, bhanteti pathavito nabhaṃ viya samuddassa orimatīrato paratīraṃ viya ca suvidūravidūre ahaṃ. Anājānīyeti gihivohārasamucchedanassa kāraṇaṃ ajānanake. Ājānīyabhojananti kāraṇaṃ jānantehi bhuñjitabbaṃ bhojanaṃ. Anājānīyabhojananti kāraṇaṃ ajānantehi bhuñjitabbaṃ bhojanaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Potaliyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
50. “I am far away, venerable sir,” [is] like the sky from the earth, like the far shore from the near shore of the ocean, I am very, very far.

“Not knowing,” [means] the cause of the destruction of the householder's affairs, to one who does not know.

“Knowing food” means food that should be eaten by those who know the cause.

“Not knowing food” means food that should be eaten by those who do not know the cause.

The rest is clear throughout.

The commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya* entitled *Papañcasūdanī*.

The commentary on the *Potaliyasutta* is finished.

mula_pali: 51. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavane. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi . Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho jīvako komārabhacco bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘sutaṃ metaṃ, bhante – ‘samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhanti ārambhanti (ka.), taṃ samaṇo gotamo jānaṃ uddissakataṃ uddissakaṭaṃ (sī. pī.) maṃsaṃ paribhuñjati paṭiccakamma’nti. Ye te, bhante, evamāhaṃsu – ‘samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhanti, taṃ samaṇo gotamo jānaṃ uddissakataṃ maṃsaṃ paribhuñjati paṭiccakamma’nti, kacci te, bhante, bhagavato vuttavādino, na ca bhagavantaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkhanti, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākaronti, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānuvādo gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgacchatī’’ti?
mula_english:
THUS HAVE I HEARD.

On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Mango Grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca.

Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side.

Seated to one side, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, I have heard this: 'They slaughter living beings for the *śramaṇa* Gotama; the *śramaṇa* Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared for him from animals killed for his sake.'"

"Venerable sir, do those who speak thus say what has been said by the Blessed One, and not misrepresent him with what is contrary to fact? Do they explain in accordance with the *dharma* in such a way that nothing which provides a ground for censure can be legitimately deduced from their assertions?"
commentary_pali:
51.Evaṃme sutanti jīvakasuttaṃ. Tattha jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavaneti ettha jīvatīti jīvako. Kumārena bhatoti komārabhacco. Yathāha ‘‘kiṃ etaṃ bhaṇe kākehi samparikiṇṇanti? Dārako devāti. Jīvati bhaṇeti? Jīvati devāti. Tena hi bhaṇe taṃ dārakaṃ amhākaṃ antepuraṃ netvā dhātīnaṃ detha posetunti. Tassa jīvatīti jīvakoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu, kumārena posāpitoti komārabhaccoti nāmaṃ akaṃsū’’ti (mahāva. 328). Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārena pana jīvakavatthu khandhake āgatameva. Vinicchayakathāpissa samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya vuttā.

Ayaṃ pana jīvako ekasmiṃ samaye bhagavato dosābhisannaṃ kāyaṃ virecetvā sīveyyakaṃ dussayugaṃ datvā vatthānumodanapariyosāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya cintesi – ‘‘mayā divasassa dvattikkhattuṃ buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ gantabbaṃ, idañca veḷuvanaṃ atidūre, mayhaṃ uyyānaṃ ambavanaṃ āsannataraṃ, yaṃnūnāhamettha bhagavato vihāraṃ kāreyya’’nti. So tasmiṃ ambavane rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaleṇakuṭimaṇḍapādīni sampādetvā bhagavato anucchavikaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ kāretvā ambavanaṃ aṭṭhārasahatthubbedhena tambapaṭṭavaṇṇena pākārena parikkhipāpetvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ cīvarabhattena santappetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ pātetvā vihāraṃ niyyātesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – ‘‘jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavane’’ti.

Ārabhantīti ghātenti. Uddissakatanti uddisitvā kataṃ. Paṭiccakammanti attānaṃ paṭicca kataṃ. Atha vā paṭiccakammanti nimittakammassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, taṃ paṭicca kammamettha atthīti maṃsaṃ ‘‘paṭiccakamma’’nti vuttaṃ hoti yo evarūpaṃ maṃsaṃ paribhuñjati, sopi tassa kammassa dāyādo hoti, vadhakassa viya tassāpi pāṇaghātakammaṃ hotīti tesaṃ laddhi. Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākarontīti bhagavatā vuttakāraṇassa anukāraṇaṃ kathenti. Ettha ca kāraṇaṃ nāma tikoṭiparisuddhamacchamaṃsaparibhogo, anukāraṇaṃ nāma mahājanassa tathā byākaraṇaṃ. Yasmā pana bhagavā uddissakataṃ na paribhuñjati, tasmā neva taṃ kāraṇaṃ hoti, na titthiyānaṃ tathā byākaraṇaṃ anukāraṇaṃ. Sahadhammiko vādānuvādoti parehi vuttakāraṇena sakāraṇo hutvā tumhākaṃ vādo vā anuvādo vā viññūhi garahitabbakāraṇaṃ koci appamattakopi kiṃ na āgacchati . Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ‘‘kiṃ sabbākārenapi tumhākaṃ vāde gārayhaṃ kāraṇaṃ natthī’’ti. Abbhācikkhantīti abhibhavitvā ācikkhanti.

Ārabhantī Uddissakata Paṭiccakamma paṭiccakamma Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākarontī Sahadhammiko vādānuvādo Abbhācikkhantī
commentary_english:
51. Thus have I heard: This is the Jīvaka Sūtra.

There, "at the Mango Grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca," the name Jīvaka means, “he lives.”

Komārabhacca means "reared by a prince."

As it was said: “What is this, sir, surrounded by crows?” “A boy, your highness.”

“Is he alive, I say?” “He is alive, your highness.”

“Well then, I say, take that boy into our palace and give him to the nurses to raise.”

Because it was said of him, “He is alive,” they gave him the name Jīvaka; and because he was raised by a prince, they gave him the name Komārabhacca” (Mahāvagga 328).

This is a brief account.

The story of Jīvaka is related at length in the Khandhakas.

The story of the judgment is also told in the *Samantapāsādikā Vinayaṭṭhakathā*.

Once, Jīvaka purged the body of the Blessed One when it was afflicted by a disorder of the humors, and having given a pair of Siveyyaka cloths, at the conclusion of the thanksgiving talk for the cloths, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry. He thought: “I should go to wait upon the Buddha two or three times a day, but the Bamboo Grove is too far away. My Mango Grove park is closer. Let me build a dwelling there for the Blessed One.”

He set up night-quarters, day-quarters, caves, huts, pavilions, etc, in that Mango Grove, built a Fragrant Cottage suitable for the Exalted One, and erected a copper-colored wall eighteen yards high surrounding the Mango Grove. He treated the Sangha of *bhikkhus* headed by the Buddha to an offering of a meal and robes, and after pouring the gift-water, presented the dwelling.

With reference to that, it was said: “at the Mango Grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca.”

*Ārabhantī* means they kill.

*Uddissakata* means done after having been intended.

*Paṭiccakamma* means done in relation to oneself.

Alternatively, *paṭiccakamma* is an appellation for an act based on a cause. Meat is called *paṭiccakamma* because an action is present in relation to it. Whoever consumes such meat is an heir to that action; like the butcher, that person also has an act of taking life, such is their view.

*Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākarontī* means they tell an imitation of the reason spoken by the Blessed One.

Here, *kāraṇaṃ* means the consumption of fish or meat that is pure in three respects, and *anukāraṇaṃ* means a similar explanation by the general populace.

Since the Blessed One does not consume what was done after having been intended, therefore that is not a reason, nor is that an imitation of the explanation of the Tīrthikas.

*Sahadhammiko vādānuvādo* means, having become causal by a reason spoken by others, does not even a small reason for which your speech or translation is to be censured by the wise come?

This is what was said: “Is there not in every way a reason in your speech that is censurable?”

*Abbhācikkhantī* means they speak after having overcome.

*Ārabhantī*, *uddissakata*, *paṭiccakamma*, *paṭiccakamma*, *dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākarontī*, *sahadhammiko vādānuvādo*, *abbhācikkhantī*

mula_pali: 52. ‘‘Ye te, jīvaka, evamāhaṃsu – ‘samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhanti, taṃ samaṇo gotamo jānaṃ uddissakataṃ maṃsaṃ paribhuñjati paṭiccakamma’nti na me te vuttavādino, abbhācikkhanti ca maṃ te asatā abhūtena. Tīhi kho ahaṃ, jīvaka, ṭhānehi maṃsaṃ aparibhoganti vadāmi. Diṭṭhaṃ, sutaṃ, parisaṅkitaṃ – imehi kho ahaṃ, jīvaka , tīhi ṭhānehi maṃsaṃ aparibhoganti vadāmi. Tīhi kho ahaṃ, jīvaka, ṭhānehi maṃsaṃ paribhoganti vadāmi. Adiṭṭhaṃ, asutaṃ, aparisaṅkitaṃ – imehi kho ahaṃ, jīvaka, tīhi ṭhānehi maṃsaṃ paribhoganti vadāmi.
mula_english:
“Jīvaka, those who speak thus, saying, ‘The *śramaṇa* Gotama slaughters living beings for the sake of (himself), the *śramaṇa* Gotama knowingly eats meat killed for his sake based on the causal principle’ do not speak according to what I have said; they misrepresent me with what is untrue and contrary to fact.

“Jīvaka, I say that there are three instances in which meat should not be eaten:

when it is seen (*dṛṣṭaṃ*), heard (*śrutaṃ*), or suspected (*parisaṅkitaṃ*) – Jīvaka, I say that meat should not be eaten in these three instances.

Jīvaka, I say that there are three instances in which meat may be eaten:

when it is not seen (*adṛṣṭaṃ*), not heard (*aśrutaṃ*), and not suspected (*aparisaṅkitaṃ*) – Jīvaka, I say that meat may be eaten in these three instances.
commentary_pali:
52.Ṭhānehīti kāraṇehi. Diṭṭhādīsu diṭṭhaṃ nāma bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya migamacche vadhitvā gayhamānaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. Sutaṃ nāma bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya migamacche vadhitvā gahitanti sutaṃ. Parisaṅkitaṃ nāma diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ sutaparisaṅkitaṃ tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitanti tividhaṃ hoti.

Tatrāyaṃ sabbasaṅgāhakavinicchayo – idha bhikkhū passanti manusse jālavāgurādihatthe gāmato vā nikkhamante araññe vā vicarante. Dutiyadivase ca nesaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhiharanti. Te tena diṭṭhena parisaṅkanti ‘‘bhikkhūnaṃ nu kho atthāya kata’’nti, idaṃ diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma, etaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana te manussā ‘‘kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā’’ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā ‘‘nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ atthāya vā kata’’nti vadanti, kappati.

diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ

Na heva kho bhikkhū passanti, apica suṇanti ‘‘manussā kira jālavāgurādihatthā gāmato vā nikkhamanti araññe vā vicarantī’’ti. Dutiyadivase ca nesaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhiharanti. Te tena sutena parisaṅkanti ‘‘bhikkhūnaṃ nu kho atthāya kata’’nti, idaṃ sutaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma, etaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana te manussā ‘‘kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā’’ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā ‘‘nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ atthāya vā kata’’nti vadanti, kappati.

sutaparisaṅkitaṃ

Na heva kho pana passanti na suṇanti, apica tesaṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ pattaṃ gahetvā samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā abhiharanti. Te parisaṅkanti ‘‘bhikkhūnaṃ nu kho atthāya kata’’nti, idaṃ tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma. Etampi gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati . Sace pana te manussā ‘‘kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā’’ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā ‘‘nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ atthāya vā kataṃ, pavattamaṃsaṃ vā kataṃ, kappiyameva labhitvā bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya sampādita’’nti vadanti, kappati.

tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitaṃ

Matānaṃ petakiccatthāya maṅgalādīnaṃ vā atthāya katepi eseva nayo. Yaṃ yañhi bhikkhūnaṃyeva atthāya akataṃ, yattha ca nibbematikā honti, taṃ sabbaṃ kappati. Sace pana ekasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhū uddissa kataṃ hoti, te ca attano atthāya katabhāvaṃ na jānanti, aññe jānanti. Ye jānanti, tesaṃ na vaṭṭati, itaresaṃ vaṭṭati. Aññe na jānanti, teyeva jānanti, tesaṃyeva na vaṭṭati, aññesaṃ vaṭṭati. Tepi ‘‘amhākaṃ atthāya kataṃ’’ti jānanti aññepi ‘‘etesaṃ atthāya kata’’nti jānanti, sabbesampi taṃ na vaṭṭati. Sabbe na jānanti, sabbesaṃ vaṭṭati. Pañcasu hi sahadhammikesu yassa kassaci vā atthāya uddissa kataṃ sabbesaṃ na kappati.

Sace pana koci ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ vadhitvā tassa pattaṃ pūretvā deti, so ce attano atthāya katabhāvaṃ jānaṃyeva gahetvā aññassa bhikkhuno deti, so tassa saddhāya paribhuñjati. Kassāpattīti? Dvinnampi anāpatti. Yañhi uddissa kataṃ, tassa abhuttatāya anāpatti, itarassa ajānanatāya. Kappiyamaṃsassa hi paṭiggahaṇe āpatti natthi. Uddissakatañca ajānitvā bhuttassa pacchā ñatvā āpattidesanākiccaṃ nāma natthi. Akappiyamaṃsaṃ pana ajānitvā bhuttena pacchā ñatvāpi āpatti desetabbā. Uddissakatañhi ñatvā bhuñjatova āpatti, akappiyamaṃsaṃ ajānitvā bhuttassāpi āpattiyeva. Tasmā āpattibhīrukena rūpaṃ sallakkhentenāpi pucchitvāva maṃsaṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ, paribhogakāle pucchitvā paribhuñjissāmīti vā gahetvā pucchitvāva paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Duviññeyyattā. Acchamaṃsañhi sūkaramaṃsasadisaṃ hoti, dīpimaṃsādīni ca migamaṃsasadisāni, tasmā pucchitvā gahaṇameva vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

Adiṭṭhanti bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya vadhitvā gayhamānaṃ adiṭṭhaṃ. Asutanti bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya vadhitvā gahitanti asutaṃ. Aparisaṅkitanti diṭṭhaparisaṅkitādivasena aparisaṅkitaṃ. Paribhoganti vadāmīti imehi tīhi kāraṇehi parisuddhaṃ tikoṭiparisuddhaṃ nāma hoti, tassa paribhogo araññe jātasūpeyyasākaparibhogasadiso hoti, tathārūpaṃ paribhuñjantassa mettāvihārissa bhikkhuno doso vā vajjaṃ vā natthi, tasmā taṃ paribhuñjitabbanti vadāmīti attho.

Adiṭṭha Asuta Aparisaṅkita Paribhoganti vadāmī tikoṭiparisuddhaṃ
commentary_english:
52. "For these reasons" means because of these causes. Among things seen, "seen" (*diṭṭhaṃ*) means that which is seen, that is, after hunting animals or fish for the sake of the *bhikkhus*. "Heard" (*sutaṃ*) means that which is heard, that is, after hunting animals or fish for the sake of the *bhikkhus*, it is taken. "Suspected" (*parisaṅkitaṃ*) means three kinds: suspected because of seeing (*diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ*), suspected because of hearing (*sutaparisaṅkitaṃ*), and suspected of being freed from both (*tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitanti*). There is this comprehensive judgment: Here, the *bhikkhus* see people going out from a village or wandering in a forest with nets, traps, etc., in their hands. On the second day, they bring alms-food mixed with meat to that village for the *bhikkhus* who have entered for alms. They suspect because of that seeing, "Was this done for the sake of the *bhikkhus*?" This is called "suspected because of seeing" (*diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ*), it is not proper to take this. Whatever is not suspected in this way, that is proper. If those people ask, "Venerable Sirs, why do you not accept?" and having heard the matter, say, "This was not done for the sake of the *bhikkhus*, but it was done by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials, etc.," it is allowable. Suspected because of seeing (*diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ*): The *bhikkhus* do not see, but they hear, "People are going out from a village or wandering in a forest with nets, traps, etc., in their hands." On the second day, they bring alms-food mixed with meat to that village for the *bhikkhus* who have entered for alms. They suspect because of that hearing, "Was this done for the sake of the *bhikkhus*?" This is called "suspected because of hearing" (*sutaparisaṅkitaṃ*), it is not proper to take this. Whatever is not suspected in this way, that is proper. If those people ask, "Venerable Sirs, why do you not accept?" and having heard the matter, say, "This was not done for the sake of the *bhikkhus*, but it was done by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials, etc.," it is allowable. Suspected because of hearing (*sutaparisaṅkitaṃ*): The *bhikkhus* neither see nor hear, but having entered that village for alms, they take the bowl, mix the alms-food with meat, and bring it. They suspect, "Was this done for the sake of the *bhikkhus*?" This is called "suspected of being freed from both" (*tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitaṃ*). It is not proper to take even this. Whatever is not suspected in this way, that is proper. If those people ask, "Venerable Sirs, why do you not accept?" and having heard the matter, say, "This was not done for the sake of the *bhikkhus*, but it was done by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials, etc., or it was made from meat already killed, having obtained what is allowable, it was prepared for the sake of the *bhikkhus*," it is allowable. Suspected of being freed from both (*tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitaṃ*): This same method applies even if it is done for the sake of deceased ancestors or for auspicious ceremonies, etc. Whatever is not done specifically for the sake of the *bhikkhus*, and in which there is no uncertainty, all of that is allowable. If, however, something is done in a certain monastery intending it for the *bhikkhus*, and they do not know that it was done for their own sake, but others know, those who know, it is not proper for them; for the others, it is proper. If others do not know, but they themselves know, it is not proper for them alone; for the others, it is proper. If they also know, "This was done for our sake," and others also know, "This was done for the sake of these ones," it is not proper for any of them. If all do not know, it is proper for all. Indeed, if something is done intending it for the sake of anyone among five fellow *dhamma*-practitioners, it is not allowable for all. If, however, someone kills a living being intending it for a certain *bhikkhu*, and having filled his bowl, gives it, and that *bhikkhu*, knowing that it was done for his own sake, takes it and gives it to another *bhikkhu*, that one enjoys it out of faith. To whom does the offense apply? There is no offense for either of the two. Indeed, because it was done intentionally, there is no offense for him because of not eating it; for the other, it is because of not knowing. Indeed, there is no offense in accepting allowable meat. And if, without knowing that it was done intentionally, it is eaten, afterwards, upon knowing, there is no matter of confession of the offense. However, if one unknowingly eats unsuitable meat (*akappiyamaṃsa*) and later realizes it, the offense (*āpatti*) should be confessed. Indeed, if one knows that [the meat] was specifically intended [for him] and then eats it, there is an offense (*āpatti*). Even if one unknowingly eats unsuitable meat (*akappiyamaṃsa*), there is still an offense (*āpattiyeva*). Therefore, one who is afraid of offenses (*āpattibhīrukena*) should carefully examine the appearance (*rūpaṃ sallakkhentenāpi*) and ask before accepting meat (*maṃsaṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ*), or, at the time of consumption (*paribhogakāle*) having taken it, should ask: "Will I consume it after asking?" (*pucchitvā paribhuñjissāmīti*) and then should consume it only after asking (*pucchitvāva paribhuñjitabbaṃ*). Why is that? Because it is difficult to discern (*duviññeyyattā*). For example, bear meat (*acchamaṃsaṃ*) is similar to pig meat (*sūkaramaṃsasadisaṃ hoti*), and leopard meat (*dīpimaṃsādīni*) etc., is similar to deer meat (*migamaṃsasadisāni*). Therefore, they say that it is only proper to take it after asking (*pucchitvā gahaṇameva vaṭṭatīti vadanti*).

Unseen (*adiṭṭha*) means that it was killed for the monks, but not received by them. Unheard (*asuta*) means that it was killed for the monks and received by them. Unsuspected (*aparisaṅkita*) means that it is free from suspicion due to having been seen, or other reasons. I declare it is proper to consume (*paribhoganti vadāmī*) - thus, because of these three reasons, it is called perfectly pure (*parisuddhaṃ*), "threefold-pure" (*tikoṭiparisuddhaṃ*). Its consumption (*paribhogo*) is like the consumption of soup and vegetables (*sūpeyyasākaparibhogasadiso*) that grow in the wilderness (*araññe*). For a monk who dwells in loving-kindness (*mettāvihārissa*), who consumes such [food], there is no fault (*doso*) or blame (*vajjaṃ*) (*bhikkhuno doso vā vajjaṃ vā natthi*). Therefore, the meaning (*attho*) is, "I declare that it is proper to consume it (*taṃ paribhuñjitabbanti vadāmīti*)."

Unseen Unheard Unsuspected I declare it is proper to consume Threefold-pure

mula_pali:
53. ‘‘Idha, jīvaka, bhikkhu aññataraṃ gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā upanissāya viharati. So mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharati. Tamenaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā upasaṅkamitvā svātanāya bhattena nimanteti. Ākaṅkhamānova ākaṅkhamāno (syā. kaṃ.), jīvaka, bhikkhu adhivāseti . So tassā rattiyā accayena pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena tassa gahapatissa vā gahapatiputtassa vā nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkamati; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdati. Tamenaṃ so gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā paṇītena piṇḍapātena parivisati. Tassa na evaṃ hoti – ‘sādhu vata māyaṃ maṃ + ayaṃ = māyaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā paṇītena piṇḍapātena pariviseyyāti! Aho vata māyaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā āyatimpi evarūpena paṇītena piṇḍapātena pariviseyyā’ti – evampissa na hoti. So taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ agathito agadhito (syā. kaṃ. ka.) amucchito anajjhopanno anajjhāpanno (syā. kaṃ. ka.) ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, jīvaka , api nu so bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye attabyābādhāya vā ceteti, parabyābādhāya vā ceteti, ubhayabyābādhāya vā cetetī’’ti?

‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’.

‘‘Nanu so, jīvaka, bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye anavajjaṃyeva āhāraṃ āhāretī’’ti?

‘‘Evaṃ, bhante. Sutaṃ metaṃ, bhante – ‘brahmā mettāvihārī’ti. Taṃ me idaṃ, bhante, bhagavā sakkhidiṭṭho; bhagavā hi, bhante, mettāvihārī’’ti. ‘‘Yena kho, jīvaka, rāgena yena dosena yena mohena byāpādavā assa so rāgo so doso so moho tathāgatassa pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato anabhāvakato (sī. pī.), anabhāvaṃgato (syā. kaṃ.) āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo. Sace kho te, jīvaka, idaṃ sandhāya bhāsitaṃ anujānāmi te eta’’nti. ‘‘Etadeva kho pana me, bhante, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ’’ bhāsitanti (syā.).

anabhāvakato (sī. pī.), anabhāvaṃgato (syā. kaṃ.) bhāsitanti (syā.)
mula_english:
Here, Jīvaka, a *bhikkhu* dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town.

He abides pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.

Thus above, below, around, everywhere, in its entirety, he dwells pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will.

Then a householder (*gṛhapati*) or a householder’s son approaches him and invites him for the next day’s meal.

If the *bhikkhu*, desiring, accepts,

when that night has passed, in the morning, having dressed, and taking his bowl (*pātra*) and robe (*cīvara*), he approaches the residence of that householder or householder’s son; having approached, he sits down on a seat made ready.

Then that householder or householder’s son serves him with choice almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*).

It does not occur to him: ‘How good that this householder or householder’s son serves me with choice almsfood!’ If only this householder or householder’s son might serve me with such choice almsfood in the future!’—it does not occur to him thus.

He partakes of that almsfood unattached, uninfatuated, not adhering to it, seeing the danger in it, understanding the escape from it.

What do you think, Jīvaka, would that *bhikkhu* on that occasion choose for his own affliction, or for another’s affliction, or for the affliction of both?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“Does not that *bhikkhu*, Jīvaka, on that occasion partake of food that is blameless?”

“Yes, venerable sir. I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘Brahmā abides in loving-kindness (*maitrī*)’”.

“Venerable sir, the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) is my visible witness to that; for the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) abides in loving-kindness (*maitrī*).”

“Jīvaka, any lust (*rāga*), any hate (*dveṣa*), any delusion (*moha*) whereby ill will (*vyāpāda*) might arise have been abandoned by the *Tathāgata*, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with so that they are no longer subject to future arising.

If what you said referred to that, then I allow it to you.”

“That is exactly what I meant, venerable sir.”
)
commentary_pali: 53. Idāni tādisassa paribhoge mettāvihārinopi anavajjataṃ dassetuṃ idha, jīvaka, bhikkhūtiādimāha. Tattha kiñcāpi aniyametvā bhikkhūti vuttaṃ, atha kho attānameva sandhāya etaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Bhagavatā hi mahāvacchagottasutte, caṅkīsutte, imasmiṃ sutteti tīsu ṭhānesu attānaṃyeva sandhāya desanā katā. Paṇītenapiṇḍapātenāti heṭṭhā anaṅgaṇasutte yo koci mahaggho piṇḍapāto paṇītapiṇḍapātoti adhippeto, idha pana maṃsūpasecanova adhippeto. Agathitoti taṇhāya agathito. Amucchitoti taṇhāmucchanāya amucchito. Anajjhopannoti na adhiopanno, sabbaṃ ālumpitvā ekappahāreneva gilitukāmo kāko viya na hotīti attho. Ādīnavadassāvīti ekarattivāsena udarapaṭalaṃ pavisitvā navahi vaṇamukhehi nikkhamissatītiādinā nayena ādīnavaṃ passanto. Nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjatīti idamatthamāhāraparibhogoti paññāya paricchinditvā paribhuñjati. Attabyābādhāya vā cetetīti attadukkhāya vā citeti. Sutametanti sutaṃ mayā etaṃ pubbe, etaṃ mayhaṃ savanamattamevāti dasseti. Sace kho te, jīvaka, idaṃ sandhāya bhāsitanti, jīvaka, mahābrahmunā vikkhambhanappahānena byāpādādayo pahīnā, tena so mettāvihārī mayhaṃ samucchedappahānena, sace te idaṃ sandhāya bhāsitaṃ, evaṃ sante tava idaṃ vacanaṃ anujānāmīti attho. So sampaṭicchi.
commentary_english:
53. Now, to show the faultlessness even in the use of such things by one abiding in loving-kindness, he said, "Here, Jīvaka, *bhikkhus*," and so forth.

There, although it is said vaguely, "*bhikkhus*," it should be understood that this was said referring to himself.

For the Blessed One, in the Mahāvacchagotta Sutta, the Caṅkī Sutta, and in this Sutta, in these three instances, the discourse was given referring to himself.

"*Paṇītena piṇḍapātena*": below, in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, any alms-food that is very valuable is intended as *paṇīta-piṇḍapāta*; here, however, only food with meat sauce is intended.

"*Agathito*": not attached to craving ( *taṇhā*).

"*Amucchito*": not infatuated with the infatuation of craving (*taṇhā*).

"*Anajjhopanno*": not adhering; not overcome, not desiring to swallow everything, having plundered it all, with a single strike, like a crow—this is the meaning.

"*Ādīnavadassāvī*": seeing the danger ( *ādīnava*) in the manner: "having entered the abdominal cavity in one night, it will exit through nine wound-openings," and so forth.

"*Nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjatī*": he consumes, having thoroughly analyzed with wisdom ( *paññā*) that this use of food is for this purpose.

"*Attabyābādhāya vā cetetī*": or he intends for his own suffering.

"*Sutameta*": "This was heard by me previously; this is merely my hearing," he shows.

"*Sace kho te, Jīvaka, idaṃ sandhāya bhāsita*": Jīvaka, the defilements, beginning with ill-will (*byāpāda*), are abandoned by Mahābrahmā by means of suppression ( *vikkhambhanappahāna*); therefore, that one abiding in loving-kindness [is faultless]. By my abandonment through eradication ( *samucchedappahāna*), if this was spoken by you intending this, in this case, I approve this statement of yours—this is the meaning.

He consented.

mula_pali:
54. ‘‘Idha, jīvaka, bhikkhu aññataraṃ gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā upanissāya viharati. So karuṇāsahagatena cetasā…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā…pe… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharati. Tamenaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā upasaṅkamitvā svātanāya bhattena nimanteti. Ākaṅkhamānova, jīvaka, bhikkhu adhivāseti. So tassā rattiyā accayena pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena gahapatissa vā gahapatiputtassa vā nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkamati; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdati. Tamenaṃ so gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā paṇītena piṇḍapātena parivisati. Tassa na evaṃ hoti – ‘sādhu vata māyaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā paṇītena piṇḍapātena pariviseyyāti! Aho vata māyaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā āyatimpi evarūpena paṇītena piṇḍapātena pariviseyyā’ti – evampissa na hoti. So taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ agathito amucchito anajjhopanno ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, jīvaka, api nu so bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye attabyābādhāya vā ceteti, parabyābādhāya vā ceteti, ubhayabyābādhāya vā cetetī’’ti?

‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’.

‘‘Nanu so, jīvaka, bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye anavajjaṃyeva āhāraṃ āhāretī’’ti?

‘‘Evaṃ, bhante. Sutaṃ metaṃ, bhante – ‘brahmā upekkhāvihārī’ti. Taṃ me idaṃ, bhante, bhagavā sakkhidiṭṭho; bhagavā hi, bhante, upekkhāvihārī’’ti. ‘‘Yena kho, jīvaka, rāgena yena dosena yena mohena vihesavā assa arativā assa paṭighavā assa so rāgo so doso so moho tathāgatassa pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo. Sace kho te, jīvaka, idaṃ sandhāya bhāsitaṃ, anujānāmi te eta’’nti. ‘‘Etadeva kho pana me, bhante, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ’’.
mula_english:
54. Here, Jivaka, a *bhikkhu* dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town.

He abides pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion…with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy…with a mind imbued with equanimity, likewise the second quarter, the third quarter, and the fourth quarter.

Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will.

Then a householder or a householder’s son comes to him and invites him for the next day’s meal.

The *bhikkhu* accepts, if he likes, Jivaka.

Then, when the night has ended, in the morning he dresses, and taking his bowl and outer robe, goes to the house of that householder or householder’s son and sits down on a seat made ready.

Then the householder or householder’s son serves him with good almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*).

He does not think: ‘How good that the householder or householder’s son serves me with good almsfood! If only a householder or householder’s son might serve me with such good almsfood in the future!’ He does not think thus.

He eats that almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*) without being tied to it, infatuated with it, and utterly committed to it, seeing the danger in it and understanding the escape from it.

What do you think, Jivaka? Would that *bhikkhu* on such an occasion choose for his own affliction, or for another’s affliction, or for the affliction of both?"

“No, venerable sir.”

“Does not that *bhikkhu* sustain himself with blameless food on that occasion?”

“Yes, venerable sir. I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘Brahmā abides in equanimity.’ Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my visible witness to that; for the Blessed One abides in equanimity.”

“Jivaka, any lust (*rāga*), any hate (*dosa*), any delusion (*moha*) whereby cruelty or discontent or aversion might arise have been abandoned by the *Tathāgata*, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with so that they are no longer subject to future arising.

If what you said, Jivaka, referred to this, I approve it.”

“Venerable sir, what I said referred to precisely that.”
commentary_pali: 54. Athassa bhagavā sesabrahmavihāravasenāpi uttari desanaṃ vaḍḍhento ‘‘idha, jīvaka, bhikkhū’’tiādimāha. Taṃ uttānatthameva.
commentary_english: 54. Then, the Blessed One (bhagavā), further increasing the teaching by means of the remaining abodes of Brahmā (brahmavihāra), said, "Here, Jīvaka, monks (bhikkhū)," and so on. The rest is clear (uttānatthameva).

mula_pali:
55. ‘‘Yo kho, jīvaka, tathāgataṃ vā tathāgatasāvakaṃ vā uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhati so pañcahi ṭhānehi bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yampi so, gahapati, evamāha – ‘gacchatha, amukaṃ nāma pāṇaṃ ānethā’ti, iminā paṭhamena ṭhānena bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yampi so pāṇo galappaveṭhakena galappavedhakena (bahūsu) ānīyamāno dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, iminā dutiyena ṭhānena bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yampi so evamāha – ‘gacchatha imaṃ pāṇaṃ ārabhathā’ti, iminā tatiyena ṭhānena bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yampi so pāṇo ārabhiyamāno dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti , iminā catutthena ṭhānena bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yampi so tathāgataṃ vā tathāgatasāvakaṃ vā akappiyena āsādeti, iminā pañcamena ṭhānena bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yo kho, jīvaka, tathāgataṃ vā tathāgatasāvakaṃ vā uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhati so imehi pañcahi ṭhānehi bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavatī’’ti.

Evaṃ vutte, jīvako komārabhacco bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Kappiyaṃ vata, bhante, bhikkhū āhāraṃ āhārenti ; anavajjaṃ vata, bhante, bhikkhū āhāraṃ āhārenti. Abhikkantaṃ, bhante, abhikkantaṃ, bhante…pe… upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata’’nti.

Jīvakasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.
mula_english:
55. “If anyone slaughters a living being for the *Tathāgata* or his disciple, he lays up much demerit in five instances.

When he says: ‘Go and fetch that living being,’ this is the first instance in which he lays up much demerit.

When that living being experiences pain and grief on being led along with a neck-halter, this is the second instance in which he lays up much demerit.

When he says: ‘Go and slaughter that living being,’ this is the third instance in which he lays up much demerit.

When that living being experiences pain and grief on being slaughtered, this is the fourth instance in which he lays up much demerit.

When he provides the *Tathāgata* or his disciple with food that is not permissible, this is the fifth instance in which he lays up much demerit.

Anyone who slaughters a living being for the *Tathāgata* or his disciple lays up much demerit in these five instances.”

When this was said, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said to the Blessed One: “Wonderful, O Lord, most excellent, O Lord! The *bhikkhus* sustain themselves with permissible food. The *bhikkhus* sustain themselves with blameless food.

Excellent, O Lord, most excellent, O Lord! May the Blessed Lord accept me from this day forth as a lay-follower as long as life shall last!”

The Jīvaka Sutta, the fifth, is ended.
commentary_pali:
55.Yokho jīvakāti ayaṃ pāṭiekko anusandhi. Imasmiñhi ṭhāne bhagavā dvāraṃ thaketi, sattānuddayaṃ dasseti. Sace hi kassaci evamassa ‘‘ekaṃ rasapiṇḍapātaṃ datvā kappasatasahassaṃ saggasampattiṃ paṭilabhanti, yaṃkiñci katvā paraṃ māretvāpi rasapiṇḍapātova dātabbo’’ti, taṃ paṭisedhento ‘‘yo kho, jīvaka, tathāgataṃ vā’’tiādimāha.

Tattha iminā paṭhamena ṭhānenāti iminā āṇattimatteneva tāva paṭhamena kāraṇena. Galappavedhakenāti yottena gale bandhitvā kaḍḍhito galena pavedhentena. Ārabhiyamānoti māriyamāno. Akappiyena āsādetīti acchamaṃsaṃ sūkaramaṃsanti, dīpimaṃsaṃ vā migamaṃsanti khādāpetvā – ‘‘tvaṃ kiṃ samaṇo nāma, akappiyamaṃsaṃ te khādita’’nti ghaṭṭeti. Ye pana dubbhikkhādīsu vā byādhiniggahaṇatthaṃ vā ‘‘acchamaṃsaṃ nāma sūkaramaṃsasadisaṃ, dīpimaṃsaṃ migamaṃsasadisa’’nti jānantā ‘‘sūkaramaṃsaṃ idaṃ, migamaṃsaṃ ida’’nti vatvā hitajjhāsayena khādāpenti, na te sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tesañhi bahupuññameva hoti. Esāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcāti ayaṃ āgataphalo viññātasāsano diṭṭhasacco ariyasāvako. Imaṃ pana dhammadesanaṃ ogāhanto pasādaṃ uppādetvā dhammakathāya thutiṃ karonto evamāha. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

iminā paṭhamena ṭhānenā Galappavedhakenā Ārabhiyamāno Akappiyena āsādetī Esāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcā

Jīvakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

mula_pali:
56. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā nāḷandāyaṃ viharati pāvārikambavane. Tena kho pana samayena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto nāthaputto (sī.), nātaputto (pī.) nāḷandāyaṃ paṭivasati mahatiyā nigaṇṭhaparisāya saddhiṃ. Atha kho dīghatapassī nigaṇṭho nāḷandāyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena pāvārikambavanaṃ yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho dīghatapassiṃ nigaṇṭhaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – ‘‘saṃvijjanti kho, tapassi dīghatapassi (syā. kaṃ. ka.), āsanāni; sace ākaṅkhasi nisīdā’’ti. Evaṃ vutte, dīghatapassī nigaṇṭho aññataraṃ nīcaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho dīghatapassiṃ nigaṇṭhaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – ‘‘kati pana, tapassi, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto kammāni paññapeti pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā’’ti?

‘‘Na kho, āvuso gotama, āciṇṇaṃ nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa ‘kammaṃ, kamma’nti paññapetuṃ; ‘daṇḍaṃ, daṇḍa’nti kho, āvuso gotama, āciṇṇaṃ nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa paññapetu’’nti.

‘‘Kati pana, tapassi, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto daṇḍāni paññapeti pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā’’ti?

‘‘Tīṇi kho, āvuso gotama, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto daṇḍāni paññapeti pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyāti, seyyathidaṃ – kāyadaṇḍaṃ, vacīdaṇḍaṃ, manodaṇḍa’’nti.

‘‘Kiṃ pana, tapassi, aññadeva kāyadaṇḍaṃ, aññaṃ vacīdaṇḍaṃ, aññaṃ manodaṇḍa’’nti?

‘‘Aññadeva , āvuso gotama, kāyadaṇḍaṃ, aññaṃ vacīdaṇḍaṃ, aññaṃ manodaṇḍa’’nti.

‘‘Imesaṃ pana, tapassi, tiṇṇaṃ daṇḍānaṃ evaṃ paṭivibhattānaṃ evaṃ paṭivisiṭṭhānaṃ katamaṃ daṇḍaṃ nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto mahāsāvajjataraṃ paññapeti pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā , yadi vā kāyadaṇḍaṃ, yadi vā vacīdaṇḍaṃ, yadi vā manodaṇḍa’’nti?

‘‘Imesaṃ kho, āvuso gotama, tiṇṇaṃ daṇḍānaṃ evaṃ paṭivibhattānaṃ evaṃ paṭivisiṭṭhānaṃ kāyadaṇḍaṃ nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto mahāsāvajjataraṃ paññapeti pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā, no tathā vacīdaṇḍaṃ, no tathā manodaṇḍa’’nti.

‘‘Kāyadaṇḍanti, tapassi, vadesi’’?

‘‘Kāyadaṇḍanti, āvuso gotama, vadāmi’’.

‘‘Kāyadaṇḍanti, tapassi, vadesi’’?

‘‘Kāyadaṇḍanti, āvuso gotama, vadāmi’’.

‘‘Kāyadaṇḍanti, tapassi, vadesi’’?

‘‘Kāyadaṇḍanti, āvuso gotama, vadāmī’’ti.

Itiha bhagavā dīghatapassiṃ nigaṇṭhaṃ imasmiṃ kathāvatthusmiṃ yāvatatiyakaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.
mula_english:
Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Nalanda in Pavarika’s mango-grove.

Now on that occasion the Nigantha Nataputta was staying at Nalanda with a large assembly of Niganthas.

Then, when the Nigantha named Digha Tapassi had wandered for alms in Nalanda and had returned from his almsround, after his meal he went to Pavarika’s Mango Grove to see the Blessed One; and after going, he exchanged greetings with the Fortunate One (bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi). After an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, he stood to one side. As he stood there, the Blessed One said to him: “There are seats, Tapassi, sit down if you like.”
