Ahaṃ kho pana, udāyi, appekadā iminā pattena samatittikampi bhuñjāmi bhiyyopi bhuñjāmi. ‘Appāhāro samaṇo gotamo, appāhāratāya ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā kosakāhārāpi aḍḍhakosakāhārāpi beluvāhārāpi aḍḍhabeluvāhārāpi na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ.

‘‘‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena cīvarena, itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, santi kho pana me, udāyi, sāvakā paṃsukūlikā lūkhacīvaradharā te susānā vā saṅkārakūṭā vā pāpaṇikā vā nantakāni pāpaṇikāni vā nantakāni vā (sī.) uccinitvā ucchinditvā (ka.) saṅghāṭiṃ karitvā dhārenti. Ahaṃ kho panudāyi, appekadā gahapaticīvarāni dhāremi daḷhāni satthalūkhāni alābulomasāni. ‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena cīvarena, itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā paṃsukūlikā lūkhacīvaradharā te susānā vā saṅkārakūṭā vā pāpaṇikā vā nantakāni uccinitvā saṅghāṭiṃ karitvā dhārenti, na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ.

pāpaṇikāni vā nantakāni vā (sī.) ucchinditvā (ka.)

‘‘‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena piṇḍapātena, itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, santi kho pana me, udāyi, sāvakā piṇḍapātikā sapadānacārino uñchāsake vate ratā, te antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhā samānā āsanenapi nimantiyamānā na sādiyanti. Ahaṃ kho panudāyi, appekadā nimantanepi nimantanassāpi (ka.) bhuñjāmi sālīnaṃ odanaṃ vicitakāḷakaṃ anekasūpaṃ anekabyañjanaṃ. ‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena piṇḍapātena, itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā piṇḍapātikā sapadānacārino uñchāsake vate ratā te antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhā samānā āsanenapi nimantiyamānā na sādiyanti, na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ.

nimantanassāpi (ka.)

‘‘‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena senāsanena, itarītarasenāsanasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, santi kho pana me, udāyi, sāvakā rukkhamūlikā abbhokāsikā, te aṭṭhamāse channaṃ na upenti. Ahaṃ kho panudāyi, appekadā kūṭāgāresupi viharāmi ullittāvalittesu nivātesu phusitaggaḷesu phussitaggaḷesu (sī. pī.) pihitavātapānesu. ‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena senāsanena, itarītarasenāsanasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā rukkhamūlikā abbhokāsikā te aṭṭhamāse channaṃ na upenti, na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ.

phussitaggaḷesu (sī. pī.)

‘‘‘Pavivitto samaṇo gotamo, pavivekassa ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, santi kho pana me, udāyi, sāvakā āraññikā pantasenāsanā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni ajjhogāhetvā viharanti, te anvaddhamāsaṃ saṅghamajjhe osaranti pātimokkhuddesāya. Ahaṃ kho panudāyi, appekadā ākiṇṇo viharāmi bhikkhūhi bhikkhunīhi upāsakehi upāsikāhi raññā rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi. ‘Pavivitto samaṇo gotamo, pavivekassa ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā āraññakā pantasenāsanā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni ajjhogāhetvā viharanti te anvaddhamāsaṃ saṅghamajjhe osaranti pātimokkhuddesāya, na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ.

‘‘Iti kho, udāyi, na mamaṃ sāvakā imehi pañcahi dhammehi sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.
mula_english:
242. “Suppose, Udayin, my disciples honored, respected, revered, and venerated me, and lived in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me, with the thought: ‘The recluse Gotama eats little and commends eating little.’ Now there are disciples of mine who live on a cupful or half a cupful of food, a *bilva* fruit’s or half a *bilva* fruit’s quantity of food.
I, Udayin, sometimes eat the full contents of my almsbowl or even more.
with the thought: ‘The recluse Gotama eats little and commends eating little,’ then those disciples of mine who live on a cupful of food…should not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this quality, nor should they live in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me.

“Suppose, Udayin, my disciples honored, respected, revered, and venerated me, and lived in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me, with the thought: ‘The recluse Gotama is content with any kind of robe and commends contentment with any kind of robe.’ Now there are disciples of mine who are refuse-rag wearers, wearers of coarse robes; they collect rags from the charnel ground, rubbish heaps, or shops, make them into patched robes (*saṃghāṭi*), and wear them.
I, Udayin, sometimes wear householder’s robes, strong, coarse, and made of bottle gourd fiber.
So if my disciples honored me…with the thought: ‘The recluse Gotama is content with any kind of robe and commends contentment with any kind of robe,’ then those disciples of mine who are refuse-rag wearers, wearers of coarse robes…should not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this quality, nor should they live in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me.

“Suppose, Udayin, my disciples honored, respected, revered, and venerated me, and lived in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me, with the thought: ‘The recluse Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood and commends contentment with any kind of almsfood.’ Now there are disciples of mine who are almsfood eaters, who go on unbroken almsround from house to house, who delight in gathering their food; when they have entered among the houses they will not consent even when invited to sit down.
I, Udayin, sometimes eat rice and curry with various sauces and relishes even when invited.
So if my disciples honored me… with the thought: ‘The recluse Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood and commends contentment with any kind of almsfood.’ then those disciples of mine who are almsfood eaters…should not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this quality, nor should they live in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me.

“Suppose, Udayin, my disciples honored, respected, revered, and venerated me, and lived in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me, with the thought: ‘The recluse Gotama is content with any kind of resting place and commends contentment with any kind of resting place.’ Now there are disciples of mine who are tree-root dwellers and open-air dwellers, who do not use a roof for eight months of the year.
I, Udayin, sometimes live in gabled mansions plastered within and without, protected against the wind, secured by door bolts, with shuttered windows.
So if my disciples honored me…with the thought: ‘The recluse Gotama is content with any kind of resting place and commends contentment with any kind of resting place.’ then those disciples of mine who are tree-root dwellers and open-air dwellers…should not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this quality, nor should they live in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me.

“Suppose, Udayin, my disciples honored, respected, revered, and venerated me, and lived in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me, with the thought: ‘The recluse Gotama is secluded and commends seclusion.’ Now there are disciples of mine who are forest dwellers, dwellers in remote resting places, who live withdrawn in remote jungle-thicket resting places and return to the midst of the *Saṅgha* once each half-month for the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*.
I, Udayin, sometimes live crowded with monks and nuns.
…by male lay followers (*upāsaka*) and female lay followers (*upāsikā*), by kings (*rājan*) and royal ministers (*rājamahāmatta*), by sectarians (*tīrthika*) and their disciples (*tīrthika-śrāvaka*).

So if my disciples honoured me…with the thought: ‘The ascetic Gotama is secluded (*pravivikta*) and commends seclusion (*praviveka*).’

…me, Udayin, my disciples should honor, respect, revere, and venerate, and live in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me, those disciples of mine who are forest dwellers (*āraññaka*), who frequent remote lodgings, who, resorting to remote forest thicket lodgings, live there; they return to the midst of the *saṃgha* once each half-month for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; they should not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this quality, nor should they live in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me.

Thus, Udayin, it is not because of these five qualities that my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me.
commentary_pali:
242.Kosakāhārāpīti dānapatīnaṃ ghare aggabhikkhāṭhapanatthaṃ khuddakasarāvā honti, dānapatino aggabhattaṃ vā tattha ṭhapetvā bhuñjanti, pabbajite sampatte taṃ bhattaṃ tassa denti. Taṃ sarāvakaṃ kosakoti vuccati. Tasmā ye ca ekeneva bhattakosakena yāpenti, te kosakāhārāti. Beluvāhārāti beluvamattabhattāhārā. Samatittikanti oṭṭhavaṭṭiyā heṭṭhimalekhāsamaṃ . Iminā dhammenāti iminā appāhāratādhammena. Ettha pana sabbākāreneva bhagavā anappāhāroti na vattabbo. Padhānabhūmiyaṃ chabbassāni appāhārova ahosi, verañjāyaṃ tayo māse patthodaneneva yāpesi pālileyyakavanasaṇḍe tayo māse bhisamuḷāleheva yāpesi. Idha pana etamatthaṃ dasseti – ‘‘ahaṃ ekasmiṃ kāle appāhāro ahosiṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāvakā dhutaṅgasamādānato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na bhindantī’’ti. Tasmā yadi te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ, mayā hi te visesatarā. Añño ceva pana dhammo atthi, yena maṃ te sakkarontīti dasseti. Iminā nayena sabbavāresu yojanā veditabbā.

Paṃsukūlikāti samādinnapaṃsukūlikaṅgā. Lūkhacīvaradharāti satthasuttalūkhāni cīvarāni dhārayamānā. Nantakānīti antavirahitāni vatthakhaṇḍāni, yadi hi nesaṃ anto bhaveyya, pilotikāti saṅkhaṃ gaccheyyuṃ. Uccinitvāti phāletvā dubbalaṭṭhānaṃ pahāya thiraṭṭhānameva gahetvā. Alābulomasānīti alābulomasadisasuttāni sukhumānīti dīpeti. Ettāvatā ca satthā cīvarasantosena asantuṭṭhoti na vattabbo. Atimuttakasusānato hissa puṇṇadāsiyā pārupitvā pātitasāṇapaṃsukūlaṃ gahaṇadivase udakapariyantaṃ katvā mahāpathavī akampi. Idha pana etamatthaṃ dasseti – ‘‘ahaṃ ekasmiṃyeva kāle paṃsukūlaṃ gaṇhiṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāvakā dhutaṅgasamādānato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na bhindantī’’ti.

Paṃsukūlikā Lūkhacīvaradharā Nantakānī Uccinitvā Alābulomasānī

Piṇḍapātikāti atirekalābhaṃ paṭikkhipitvā samādinnapiṇḍapātikaṅgā. Sapadānacārinoti loluppacāraṃ paṭikkhipitvā samādinnasapadānacārā. Uñchāsake vate ratāti uñchācariyasaṅkhāte bhikkhūnaṃ pakativate ratā, uccanīcagharadvāraṭṭhāyino hutvā kabaramissakaṃ bhattaṃ saṃharitvā paribhuñjantīti attho. Antaragharanti brahmāyusutte ummārato paṭṭhāya antaragharaṃ, idha indakhīlato paṭṭhāya adhippetaṃ. Ettāvatā ca satthā piṇḍapātasantosena asantuṭṭhoti na vattabbo, appāhāratāya vuttaniyāmeneva pana sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Idha pana etamatthaṃ dasseti – ‘‘ahaṃ ekasmiṃyeva kāle nimantanaṃ na sādayiṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāvakā dhutaṅgasamādānato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na bhindantī’’ti.

Piṇḍapātikā Sapadānacārino Uñchāsake vate ratā Antaraghara

Rukkhamūlikāti channaṃ paṭikkhipitvā samādinnarukkhamūlikaṅgā. Abbhokāsikāti channañca rukkhamūlañca paṭikkhipitvā samādinnaabbhokāsikaṅgā. Aṭṭhamāseti hemantagimhike māse. Antovasse pana cīvarānuggahatthaṃ channaṃ pavisanti. Ettāvatā ca satthā senāsanasantosena asantuṭṭhoti na vattabbo, senāsanasantoso panassa chabbassikamahāpadhānena ca pālileyyakavanasaṇḍena ca dīpetabbo. Idha pana etamatthaṃ dasseti – ‘‘ahaṃ ekasmiṃyeva kāle channaṃ na pāvisiṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāvakā dhutaṅgasamādānato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na bhindantī’’ti.

Rukkhamūlikā Abbhokāsikā Aṭṭhamāse

Āraññikāti gāmantasenāsanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā samādinnaāraññikaṅgā. Saṅghamajjhe osarantīti abaddhasīmāya kathitaṃ, baddhasīmāyaṃ pana vasantā attano vasanaṭṭhāneyeva uposathaṃ karonti. Ettāvatā ca satthā no pavivittoti na vattabbo, ‘‘icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhave, aḍḍhamāsaṃ paṭisalliyitu’’nti (pārā. 162; 565) evañhissa paviveko paññāyati. Idha pana etamatthaṃ dasseti ‘‘ahaṃ ekasmiṃyeva tathārūpe kāle paṭisalliyiṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāvakā dhutaṅgasamādānato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na bhindantī’’ti. Mamaṃ sāvakāti maṃ sāvakā.

Āraññikā Saṅghamajjhe osarantī Mamaṃ sāvakā
commentary_english:
242. *Kosakāhārāpī* means small bowls are kept in the houses of donors for the purpose of placing the first portion of alms-food. The donors, having placed the first portion of food there, eat, and when an ascetic arrives, they give that food to him.

That bowl is called *kosaka*.

Therefore, those who live on only one food-bowl are called *kosakāhāra*.

*Beluvāhārā* means those who eat food the size of a *beluva* fruit.

*Samatittika* means even with the lower line of the lip.

*Iminā dhammenā* means by this practice of eating little food.

Here, however, the Blessed One is not to be described as one who eats little food in every way.

For six years at the base of the tree he was one who ate very little. In Verañjā he spent three months with only coarse barley-meal, and in the Pāḷileyyaka forest grove, he spent three months with only lotus roots and stalks.

Here it shows this meaning: “At one time, I was one who ate little food, but my disciples, from the undertaking of the dhutaṅga, do not break the dhutaṅga as long as they live.”

Therefore, if they were to honor you by this practice, they would be more distinguished than me.

Moreover, there is another teaching, by which they honor me, it shows.

In this way, the connection should be understood in all instances.

*Paṃsukūlikā* means those who have undertaken the *paṃsukūlika* practice.

*Lūkhacīvaradharā* means those who wear rough robes made of rags picked from dust heaps.

*Nantakānī* means cloths that are without ends. For if they had ends, they would go to the count of rags (*pilotikā*).

*Uccinitvā* means having discarded weak places by splitting [the cloth], having taken only the strong places.

*Alābulomasānī* means it indicates threads as fine as the fibers of a gourd.

To this extent, the Teacher is not to be described as dissatisfied with robes.

From the *atimuttaka* cemetery, after Puṇṇadāsī had draped [the robe] and offered the cast-off hempen rag-robe, the great earth trembled, after making the limit of water on the day of acceptance.

Here, however, it shows this meaning: “At one time, I accepted a rag-robe, but my disciples, from the undertaking of the *dhutaṅga*, do not break the *dhutaṅga* as long as they live.”

*Paṃsukūlikā*. *Lūkhacīvaradharā*. *Nantakānī*. *Uccinitvā*. *Alābulomasānī*. *Piṇḍapātikā* means having refused extra gain, those who have undertaken the alms-food eating practice.

*Sapadānacārino* means having refused greedy conduct, those who have undertaken the practice of walking for alms from house to house.

*Uñchāsake vate ratā* means those who delight in the habitual practice of monks, known as gleaning, after becoming those who stand at the doors of high and low houses, and having gathered mixed-up food, they eat it, is the meaning.

*Antaraghara* means in the Brahmāyu Sutta, *antaragharaṃ* [means] from the threshold onward; here it is intended from the *indakhīla* pillar onward.

To this extent, the Teacher is not to be described as dissatisfied with alms-food, but everything should be explained only by the rule that has been stated regarding eating little food.

Here, however, it shows this meaning: “At one time, I did not accept an invitation, but my disciples, from the undertaking of the *dhutaṅga*, do not break the *dhutaṅga* as long as they live.”

*Piṇḍapātikā*. *Sapadānacārino*. *Uñchāsake vate ratā*. *Antaraghara*. *Rukkhamūlikā* means having refused shelter, those who have undertaken the practice of dwelling at the foot of a tree.

*Abbhokāsikā* means having refused both shelter and the foot of a tree, those who have undertaken the practice of dwelling in the open air.

*Aṭṭhamāse* means in the winter and hot months.

During the rains, however, they enter shelter for the sake of protecting robes.

To this extent, the Teacher is not to be described as dissatisfied with dwellings, but satisfaction with dwellings is to be explained by his six-year great exertion, and by the Pāḷileyyaka forest grove.
Here, however, he shows this meaning: "I did not enter a covered place at any time; but my disciples, from the undertaking of the ascetic practices onward, do not violate the ascetic practices as long as they live."

Root-dweller, open-air dweller…

In the eighth month…

"Dweller in the woods"… having rejected a village dwelling, he undertook the practice of dwelling in the woods.

"Descending into the midst of the *saṃgha*," it is said of one who has no defined boundary; but those who dwell within a defined boundary perform the *uposatha* right in their own dwelling place.

Thus, the Teacher should not be called not secluded; "I desire, monks, to retire for half a month" (Parā.

162; 565) in this way, seclusion is known to him.

Here, however, he shows this meaning: "I retired at one time in such a place; but my disciples, from the undertaking of the ascetic practices onward, do not violate the ascetic practices as long as they live."

"My disciples" means my disciples.

Dweller in the woods…

Descending into the midst of the *saṃgha*, my disciples…

mula_pali: 243. ‘‘Atthi kho, udāyi, aññe ca pañca dhammā yehi pañcahi dhammehi mamaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti , sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti. Katame pañca? Idhudāyi, mamaṃ sāvakā adhisīle sambhāventi – ‘sīlavā samaṇo gotamo paramena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato’ti. Yampudāyi yamudāyi (syā. ka.), mamaṃ sāvakā adhisīle sambhāventi – ‘sīlavā samaṇo gotamo paramena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato’ti, ayaṃ kho, udāyi , paṭhamo dhammo yena mamaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.
mula_english:
“However, Udayin, there are other five qualities because of which my disciples honour, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me, honouring and respecting me.

“Which five? Here, Udayin, my disciples esteem me for the higher virtue thus: ‘The recluse Gotama is virtuous, he possesses the supreme aggregate of virtue ( *paramena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato* ).’

Udayin, my disciples esteem me for the higher virtue thus: ‘The recluse Gotama is virtuous, he possesses the supreme aggregate of virtue.’ This is the first quality because of which my disciples honour, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me, honouring and respecting me.

mula_pali: 244. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, mamaṃ sāvakā abhikkante ñāṇadassane sambhāventi – ‘jānaṃyevāha samaṇo gotamo – jānāmīti, passaṃyevāha samaṇo gotamo – passāmīti; abhiññāya samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no anabhiññāya; sanidānaṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no anidānaṃ; sappāṭihāriyaṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no appāṭihāriya’nti. Yampudāyi, mamaṃ sāvakā abhikkante ñāṇadassane sambhāventi – ‘jānaṃyevāha samaṇo gotamo – jānāmīti, passaṃyevāha samaṇo gotamo – passāmīti; abhiññāya samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no anabhiññāya; sanidānaṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no anidānaṃ; sappāṭihāriyaṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no appāṭihāriya’nti, ayaṃ kho, udāyi, dutiyo dhammo yena mamaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.
mula_english:
244. Again, Udayin, my disciples esteem me for my excellent knowledge and vision thus: ‘When the *śramaṇa* (ascetic) Gotama says “I know (*jānāmi*)”, he truly knows; when he says “I see (*passāmi*)”, he truly sees. The *śramaṇa* Gotama teaches the *dharma* (law, teaching) through direct knowledge (*abhijñāya*), not without direct knowledge; he teaches the *dharma* (law, teaching) with a sound basis (*sanidānaṃ*), not without a sound basis; he teaches the *dharma* (law, teaching) in a convincing manner (*sappāṭihāriyaṃ*), not in an unconvincing manner.’

O Udayin, the reason why my disciples esteem me for my excellent knowledge and vision, thinking "When the *śramaṇa* (ascetic) Gotama says, 'I know (*jānāmīti*)', he knows. When he says, 'I see (*passāmīti*)', he sees," and the reason why they esteem me because the *śramaṇa* Gotama teaches the *dharma* (law, teaching) with direct knowledge (*abhijñāya*), and not without direct knowledge, with a basis (*sanidānaṃ*), and not without a basis, with convincing miracles (*sappāṭihāriyaṃ*), and not without miracles, is the following. This, Udayin, is the second quality by which my disciples, honoring, respecting, esteeming and venerating me, and having honored and respected me, live in dependence.
commentary_pali: 244.Sanidānanti sappaccayaṃ. Kiṃ pana appaccayaṃ nibbānaṃ na desetīti. No na deseti, sahetukaṃ pana taṃ desanaṃ katvā deseti, no ahetukanti. Sappāṭihāriyanti purimassevetaṃ vevacanaṃ, sakāraṇanti attho. Taṃ vatāti ettha vatāti nipātamattaṃ.
commentary_english:
244. *Sanidāna* means with conditions (*sa-pratyaya*).

Why then does he not teach unconditioned (*a-pratyaya*) *nirvāṇa*?

No, he does teach it, but he teaches it having made that teaching with a cause (*sahetuka*), not without a cause (*ahetuka*).

*Sappāṭihāriya* is a synonym of the former, meaning with a reason (*sa-kāraṇa*).

*Taṃ vatā*—here, *vatā* is merely a particle (*nipāta-mātra*).

mula_pali:
245. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, mamaṃ sāvakā adhipaññāya sambhāventi – ‘paññavā samaṇo gotamo paramena paññākkhandhena samannāgato; taṃ vata anāgataṃ vādapathaṃ na dakkhati, uppannaṃ vā parappavādaṃ na sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggaṇhissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati’. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, api nu me sāvakā evaṃ jānantā evaṃ passantā antarantarā kathaṃ opāteyyu’’nti?

‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’.

‘‘Na kho panāhaṃ, udāyi, sāvakesu anusāsaniṃ paccāsīsāmi paccāsiṃsāmi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.); aññadatthu mamayeva sāvakā anusāsaniṃ paccāsīsanti.

paccāsiṃsāmi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)

‘‘Yampudāyi, mamaṃ sāvakā adhipaññāya sambhāventi – ‘paññavā samaṇo gotamo paramena paññākkhandhena samannāgato; taṃ vata anāgataṃ vādapathaṃ na dakkhati, uppannaṃ vā parappavādaṃ na sahadhammena niggahitaṃ niggaṇhissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati’. Ayaṃ kho, udāyi, tatiyo dhammo yena mamaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.
mula_english:
245. “Again, Udayin, my disciples esteem me for the higher wisdom thus: ‘The recluse Gotama is wise; he possesses the supreme aggregate of wisdom. It is impossible that he should not foresee the future courses of doctrine or that he should not be able to confute with reasons the current doctrines of others.’

What do you think, Udayin? Would my disciples, knowing and seeing thus, break in and interrupt me?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“I do not expect instruction from my disciples; invariably, it is my disciples who expect instruction from me.

“Again, Udayin, my disciples esteem me for the higher wisdom thus: ‘The recluse Gotama is wise; he possesses the supreme aggregate of wisdom. It is impossible that he should not foresee the future courses of doctrine or that he should not be able to confute with reasons the current doctrines of others.’

This, Udayin, is the third quality because of which my disciples honour, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me, honouring and respecting me.
commentary_pali: 245.Anāgataṃ vādapathanti ajja ṭhapetvā sve vā punadivase vā aḍḍhamāse vā māse vā saṃvacchare vā tassa tassa pañhassa upari āgamanavādapathaṃ. Nadakkhatīti yathā saccako nigaṇṭho attano niggahaṇatthaṃ āgatakāraṇaṃ visesetvā vadanto na addasa, evaṃ na dakkhatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Sahadhammenāti sakāraṇena. Antarantarā kathaṃ opāteyyunti mama kathāvāraṃ pacchinditvā antarantare attano kathaṃ paveseyyunti attho. Na kho panāhaṃ, udāyīti, udāyi, ahaṃ ambaṭṭhasoṇadaṇḍakūṭadantasaccakanigaṇṭhādīhi saddhiṃ mahāvāde vattamānepi – ‘‘aho vata me ekasāvakopi upamaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ vā āharitvā dadeyyā’’ti evaṃ sāvakesu anusāsaniṃ na paccāsīsāmi. Mamayevāti evarūpesu ṭhānesu sāvakā mamayeva anusāsaniṃ ovādaṃ paccāsīsanti.
commentary_english:
245. “The path of future debate” means establishing today, or tomorrow, or the next day, or in a half-month, or in a month, or in a year, the path of future debate regarding that particular question.

“He does not see” means just as Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha, while speaking in detail about the reason for his arrival for the purpose of refuting [others], did not see [his own faults], so too, he will not see. This situation exists.

“With a justified teaching” means with a reason.

“How should they interrupt repeatedly?” means cutting off my turn to speak, how should they insert their own speech in the middle? This is the meaning.

“I, Udayi, do not” means, Udayi, even while I am engaged in a great debate with Ambaṭṭha, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha, and others, I do not expect from my disciples an instruction such as, “Oh, may even one of my disciples bring forth a comparison or a reason.”

“Mine alone” means in such situations, the disciples expect an instruction or advice from me alone.

mula_pali: 246. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, mama sāvakā yena dukkhena dukkhotiṇṇā dukkhaparetā te maṃ upasaṅkamitvā dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pucchanti, tesāhaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ puṭṭho byākaromi, tesāhaṃ cittaṃ ārādhemi pañhassa veyyākaraṇena; te maṃ dukkhasamudayaṃ… dukkhanirodhaṃ… dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pucchanti, tesāhaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ puṭṭho byākaromi , tesāhaṃ cittaṃ ārādhemi pañhassa veyyākaraṇena. Yampudāyi, mama sāvakā yena dukkhena dukkhotiṇṇā dukkhaparetā te maṃ upasaṅkamitvā dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pucchanti, tesāhaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ puṭṭho byākaromi, tesāhaṃ cittaṃ ārādhemi pañhassa veyyākaraṇena. Te maṃ dukkhasamudayaṃ … dukkhanirodhaṃ… dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pucchanti. Tesāhaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ puṭṭho byākaromi. Tesāhaṃ cittaṃ ārādhemi pañhassa veyyākaraṇena. Ayaṃ kho, udāyi, catuttho dhammo yena mamaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.
mula_english:
“Furthermore, Udayin, my disciples, afflicted and overwhelmed by suffering, approach me and ask about the noble truth of suffering (*duḥkhaṃ āryasatyaṃ*). When asked about the noble truth of suffering, I explain it to them, and I satisfy their minds with my explanation. They ask me about the noble truth of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudayaṃ*), the noble truth of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodhaṃ*), and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodhagāminiṃ pratipadāṃ āryasatyaṃ*). When asked about the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, I explain it to them, and I satisfy their minds with my explanation.

Again, Udayin, my disciples, afflicted and overwhelmed by suffering, approach me and ask about the noble truth of suffering. When asked about the noble truth of suffering, I explain it to them, and I satisfy their minds with my explanation. They ask me about the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. When asked about the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, I explain it to them, and I satisfy their minds with my explanation.

This, Udayin, is the fourth quality because of which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me.
commentary_pali: 246.Tesāhaṃcittaṃ ārādhemīti tesaṃ ahaṃ tassa pañhassa veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ gaṇhāmi sampādemi paripūremi, aññaṃ puṭṭho aññaṃ na byākaromi, ambaṃ puṭṭho labujaṃ viya labujaṃ vā puṭṭho ambaṃ viya. Ettha ca ‘‘adhisīle sambhāventī’’ti vuttaṭṭhāne buddhasīlaṃ nāma kathitaṃ, ‘‘abhikkante ñāṇadassane sambhāventī’’ti vuttaṭṭhāne sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, ‘‘adhipaññāya sambhāventī’’ti vuttaṭṭhāne ṭhānuppattikapaññā, ‘‘yena dukkhenā’’ti vuttaṭṭhāne saccabyākaraṇapaññā. Tattha sabbaññutaññāṇañca saccabyākaraṇapaññañca ṭhapetvā avasesā paññā adhipaññaṃ bhajati.
commentary_english:
246. “I would appease their minds”: I take, produce, and fulfill their minds with the explanation of that question. When asked one thing, I do not explain another, like being asked about a mango and [answering about] a breadfruit, or being asked about a breadfruit and [answering about] a mango.

And here, in the place where it is said, "cultivating in higher morality (adhisīle)," what is stated is the Buddha's morality (Buddhasīla); in the place where it is said, "cultivating in superior knowledge and vision (abhikkante ñāṇadassane)," it is the knowledge of omniscience (sarvajñutaññāṇaṃ); in the place where it is said, "cultivating in higher wisdom (adhipaññāya)," it is the wisdom of arising in the proper place (ṭhānuppattikapaññā); in the place where it is said, "by which suffering (dukkhenā)," it is the wisdom of explaining the truth (saccabyākaraṇapaññā).

There, having set aside the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ) and the wisdom of explaining the truth (saccabyākaraṇapaññañca), the remaining wisdoms partake of higher wisdom (adhipaññaṃ).

mula_pali:
247. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati… citte cittānupassī viharati… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā cattāro sammappadhāne bhāventi. Idhudāyi , bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, vīriyaṃ ārabhati, cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, padahati; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, vīriyaṃ ārabhati, cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, padahati; anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, vīriyaṃ ārabhati, cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, padahati; uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, vīriyaṃ ārabhati, cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, padahati. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā cattāro iddhipāde bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, cittasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīmaṃsāsamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā pañcindriyāni bhāventi. Idhudāyi , bhikkhu saddhindriyaṃ bhāveti upasamagāmiṃ sambodhagāmiṃ; vīriyindriyaṃ bhāveti…pe… satindriyaṃ bhāveti… samādhindriyaṃ bhāveti… paññindriyaṃ bhāveti upasamagāmiṃ sambodhagāmiṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā pañca balāni bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu saddhābalaṃ bhāveti upasamagāmiṃ sambodhagāmiṃ; vīriyabalaṃ bhāveti…pe… satibalaṃ bhāveti… samādhibalaṃ bhāveti… paññābalaṃ bhāveti upasamagāmiṃ sambodhagāmiṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā sattabojjhaṅge bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ; dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… pītisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti, sammāsaṅkappaṃ bhāveti, sammāvācaṃ bhāveti , sammākammantaṃ bhāveti, sammāājīvaṃ bhāveti, sammāvāyāmaṃ bhāveti, sammāsatiṃ bhāveti, sammāsamādhiṃ bhāveti. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.
mula_english:
247. Again, Udayin, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way to develop the four foundations of mindfulness ( *cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāventi*).

Here, Udayin, a *bhikkhu* abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly aware and mindful, having put aside hankering and fretting for the world; he abides contemplating feelings as feelings…he abides contemplating mind as mind…he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects, ardent, clearly aware and mindful, having put aside hankering and fretting for the world.

And thereby many disciples of mine abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.

Again, Udayin, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way to develop the four right kinds of striving ( *cattāro sammappadhāne bhāventi*).

Here, Udayin, a *bhikkhu* awakens zeal for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states, and he makes effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He awakens zeal for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states, and he makes effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He awakens zeal for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and he makes effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He awakens zeal for the continuance, non-disappearance, strengthening, increase, and fulfilment by development of arisen wholesome states, and he makes effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives.

And thereby many disciples of mine abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.

Again, Udayin, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way to develop the four bases for spiritual power ( *cattāro iddhipāde bhāventi*).

Here, Udayin, a *bhikkhu* develops the basis for spiritual power consisting in concentration due to zeal (*chanda*) and determined striving. He develops the basis for spiritual power consisting in concentration due to energy (*vīriya*) and determined striving. He develops the basis for spiritual power consisting in concentration due to purity of mind (*citta*) and determined striving. He develops the basis for spiritual power consisting in concentration due to investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) and determined striving.

And thereby many disciples of mine abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.

Again, Udayin, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way to develop the five spiritual faculties ( *pañcindriyāni bhāventi*).

Here, Udayin, a *bhikkhu* develops the faculty of faith ( *saddhindriya*), which leads to peace, leads to enlightenment. He develops the faculty of energy ( *vīriyindriya*)…He develops the faculty of mindfulness ( *satindriya*)…He develops the faculty of concentration ( *samādhindriya*)…He develops the faculty of wisdom ( *paññindriya*), which leads to peace, leads to enlightenment.

And thereby many disciples of mine abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.

Again, Udayin, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way to develop the five powers ( *pañca balāni bhāventi*).

Here, Udayin, a *bhikkhu* develops the power of faith ( *saddhābala*), which leads to peace, leads to enlightenment. He develops the power of energy ( *vīriyabala*)…He develops the power of mindfulness ( *satibala*)…He develops the power of concentration ( *samādhibala*)…He develops the power of wisdom ( *paññābala*), which leads to peace, leads to enlightenment.

And thereby many disciples of mine abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.

Again, Udayin, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way to develop the seven enlightenment factors ( *sattabojjhaṅge bhāventi*).

Here, Udayin, a *bhikkhu* develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor ( *satisambojjhaṅga*), which is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and results in relinquishment. He develops the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor ( *dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*)…He develops the energy enlightenment factor ( *vīriyasambojjhaṅga*)…He develops the rapture enlightenment factor ( *pītisambojjhaṅga*)…He develops the tranquility enlightenment factor ( *passaddhisambojjhaṅga*)…He develops the concentration enlightenment factor ( *samādhisambojjhaṅga*)…He develops the equanimity enlightenment factor ( *upekkhāsambojjhaṅga*), which is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and results in relinquishment.

And thereby many disciples of mine abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.

Again, Udayin, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way to develop the Noble Eightfold Path ( *ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāventi*).

Here, Udayin, a *bhikkhu* develops right view (*sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti*), right intention (*sammāsaṅkappaṃ bhāveti*), right speech (*sammāvācaṃ bhāveti*), right action (*sammākammantaṃ bhāveti*), right livelihood (*sammāājīvaṃ bhāveti*), right effort (*sammāvāyāmaṃ bhāveti*), right mindfulness (*sammāsatiṃ bhāveti*), and right concentration ( *sammāsamādhiṃ bhāveti*).

And thereby many disciples of mine abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
commentary_pali:
247. Idāni tesaṃ tesaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ paṭipadaṃ ācikkhanto puna caparaṃ udāyītiādimāha. Tattha abhiññāvosānapāramippattāti abhiññāvosānasaṅkhātañceva abhiññāpāramīsaṅkhātañca arahattaṃ pattā.

Sammappadhāneti upāyapadhāne. Chandaṃ janetīti kattukamyatākusalacchandaṃ janeti. Vāyamatīti vāyāmaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti vīriyaṃ pavatteti. Cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti cittaṃ ukkhipati. Padahatīti upāyapadhānaṃ karoti. Bhāvanāya pāripūriyāti vaḍḍhiyā paripūraṇatthaṃ. Apicettha – ‘‘yā ṭhiti, so asammoso…pe… yaṃ vepullaṃ, sā bhāvanāpāripūrī’’ti (vibha. 406) evaṃ purimaṃ purimassa pacchimaṃ pacchimassa atthotipi veditabbaṃ.

Sammappadhāne Chandaṃ janetī Vāyamatī Vīriyaṃ ārabhatī Cittaṃ paggaṇhātī Padahatī Bhāvanāya pāripūriyā

Imehi pana sammappadhānehi kiṃ kathitaṃ? Kassapasaṃyuttapariyāyena sāvakassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadā kathitā. Vuttañhetaṃ tattha –

‘‘Cattārome , āvuso, sammappadhānā. Katame cattāro? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu, anuppannā me pāpakā akusalā dhammā uppajjamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyunti ātappaṃ karoti. Uppannā me pāpakā akusalā dhammā appahīyamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyunti ātappaṃ karoti. Anuppannā me kusalā dhammā anuppajjamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyunti ātappaṃ karoti. Uppannā me kusalā dhammā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyunti ātappaṃ karotī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 2.145).

Ettha ca pāpakā akusalāti lobhādayo veditabbā. Anuppannā kusalā dhammāti samathavipassanā ceva maggo ca, uppannā kusalā nāma samathavipassanāva. Maggo pana sakiṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhamāno anatthāya saṃvattanako nāma natthi. So hi phalassa paccayaṃ datvāva nirujjhati. Purimasmimpi vā samathavipassanāva gahetabbāti vuttaṃ, taṃ pana na yuttaṃ.

Tattha ‘‘uppannā samathavipassanā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvattantī’’ti atthassa āvibhāvatthamidaṃ vatthu – eko kira khīṇāsavatthero ‘‘mahācetiyañca mahābodhiñca vandissāmī’’ti samāpattilābhinā bhaṇḍagāhakasāmaṇerena saddhiṃ janapadato mahāvihāraṃ āgantvā vihārapariveṇaṃ pāvisi. Sāyanhasamaye mahābhikkhusaṅghe cetiyaṃ vandamāne cetiyaṃ vandanatthāya na nikkhami. Kasmā? Khīṇāsavānañhi tīsu ratanesu mahantaṃ gāravaṃ hoti. Tasmā bhikkhusaṅghe vanditvā paṭikkamante manussānaṃ sāyamāsabhuttavelāyaṃ sāmaṇerampi ajānāpetvā ‘‘cetiyaṃ vandissāmī’’ti ekakova nikkhami. Sāmaṇero – ‘‘kiṃ nu kho thero avelāya ekakova gacchati, jānissāmī’’ti upajjhāyassa padānupadiko nikkhami. Thero anāvajjanena tassa āgamanaṃ ajānanto dakkhiṇadvārena cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ āruhi. Sāmaṇeropi anupadaṃyeva āruḷho.

Mahāthero mahācetiyaṃ ulloketvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā haṭṭhapahaṭṭho cetiyaṃ vandati. Sāmaṇero therassa vandanākāraṃ disvā ‘‘upajjhāyo me ativiya pasannacitto vandati, kiṃ nu kho pupphāni labhitvā pūjaṃ kareyyā’’ti cintesi. Thero vanditvā uṭṭhāya sirasi añjaliṃ ṭhapetvā mahācetiyaṃ ulloketvā ṭhito. Sāmaṇero ukkāsitvā attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpesi. Thero parivattetvā olokento ‘‘kadā āgatosī’’ti pucchi. Tumhākaṃ cetiyaṃ vandanakāle, bhante. Ativiya pasannā cetiyaṃ vandittha kiṃ nu kho pupphāni labhitvā pūjeyyāthāti? Āma sāmaṇera imasmiṃ cetiye viya aññatra ettakaṃ dhātūnaṃ nidhānaṃ nāma natthi, evarūpaṃ asadisaṃ mahāthūpaṃ pupphāni labhitvā ko na pūjeyyāti. Tena hi, bhante, adhivāsetha, āharissāmīti tāvadeva jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā iddhiyā himavantaṃ gantvā vaṇṇagandhasampannapupphāni parissāvanaṃ pūretvā mahāthere dakkhiṇamukhato pacchimaṃ mukhaṃ asampatteyeva āgantvā pupphaparissāvanaṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā ‘‘pūjetha, bhante,’’ti āha . Thero ‘‘atimandāni no sāmaṇera pupphānī’’ti āha. Gacchatha, bhante, bhagavato guṇe āvajjitvā pūjethāti.

Thero pacchimamukhanissitena sopāṇena āruyha kucchivedikābhūmiyaṃ pupphapūjaṃ kātuṃ āraddho. Vedikābhūmiyaṃ paripuṇṇāni pupphāni patitvā dutiyabhūmiyaṃ jaṇṇupamāṇena odhinā pūrayiṃsu. Tato otaritvā pādapiṭṭhikapantiṃ pūjesi. Sāpi paripūri. Paripuṇṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā heṭṭhimatale vikiranto agamāsi. Sabbaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ paripūri. Tasmiṃ paripuṇṇe ‘‘sāmaṇera pupphāni na khīyantī’’ti āha. Parissāvanaṃ, bhante, adhomukhaṃ karothāti. Adhomukhaṃ katvā cālesi, tadā pupphāni khīṇāni. Parissāvanaṃ sāmaṇerassa datvā saddhiṃ hatthipākārena cetiyaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā pariveṇaṃ gacchanto cintesi – ‘‘yāva mahiddhiko vatāyaṃ sāmaṇero, sakkhissati nu kho imaṃ iddhānubhāvaṃ rakkhitu’’nti. Tato ‘‘na sakkhissatī’’ti disvā sāmaṇeramāha – ‘‘sāmaṇera tvaṃ idāni mahiddhiko, evarūpaṃ pana iddhiṃ nāsetvā pacchimakāle kāṇapesakāriyā hatthena madditakañjiyaṃ pivissasī’’ti. Daharakabhāvassa nāmesa dosoyaṃ, so upajjhāyassa kathāyaṃ saṃvijjitvā – ‘‘kammaṭṭhānaṃ me, bhante, ācikkhathā’’ti na yāci, amhākaṃ upajjhāyo kiṃ vadatīti taṃ pana asuṇanto viya agamāsi.

Thero mahācetiyañca mahābodhiñca vanditvā sāmaṇeraṃ pattacīvaraṃ gāhāpetvā anupubbena kuṭeḷitissamahāvihāraṃ agamāsi. Sāmaṇero upajjhāyassa padānupadiko hutvā bhikkhācāraṃ na gacchati, ‘‘kataraṃ gāmaṃ pavisatha, bhante,’’ti pucchitvā pana ‘‘idāni me upajjhāyo gāmadvāraṃ patto bhavissatī’’ti ñatvā attano ca upajjhāyassa ca pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā ākāsena gantvā therassa pattacīvaraṃ datvā piṇḍāya pavisati. Thero sabbakālaṃ ovadati – ‘‘sāmaṇera mā evamakāsi, puthujjaniddhi nāma calā anibaddhā, asappāyaṃ rūpādiārammaṇaṃ labhitvā appamattakeneva bhijjati, santāya samāpattiyā parihīnāya brahmacariyavāso santhambhituṃ na sakkotī’’ti. Sāmaṇero ‘‘kiṃ katheti mayhaṃ upajjhāyo’’ti sotuṃ na icchati, tatheva karoti. Thero anupubbena cetiyavandanaṃ karonto kammubinduvihāraṃ nāma gato. Tattha vasantepi there sāmaṇero tatheva karoti.

Athekadivasaṃ ekā pesakāradhītā abhirūpā paṭhamavaye ṭhitā kammabindugāmato nikkhamitvā padumassaraṃ oruyha gāyamānā pupphāni bhañjati. Tasmiṃ samaye sāmaṇero padumassaramatthakena gacchati, gacchanto pana silesikāya kāṇamacchikā viya tassā gītasadde bajjhi. Tāvadevassa iddhi antarahitā, chinnapakkhakāko viya ahosi. Santasamāpattibalena pana tattheva udakapiṭṭhe apatitvā simbalitūlaṃ viya patamānaṃ anupubbena padumasaratīre aṭṭhāsi. So vegena gantvā upajjhāyassa pattacīvaraṃ datvā nivatti. Mahāthero ‘‘pagevetaṃ mayā diṭṭhaṃ, nivāriyamānopi na nivattissatī’’ti kiñci avatvā piṇḍāya pāvisi.

Sāmaṇero gantvā padumasaratīre aṭṭhāsi tassā paccuttaraṇaṃ āgamayamāno. Sāpi sāmaṇeraṃ ākāsena gacchantañca puna āgantvā ṭhitañca disvā ‘‘addhā esa maṃ nissāya ukkaṇṭhito’’ti ñatvā ‘‘paṭikkama sāmaṇerā’’ti āha. So paṭikkami. Itarā paccuttaritvā sāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘‘kiṃ, bhante,’’ti pucchi. So tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Sā bahūhi kāraṇehi gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ brahmacariyavāse ānisaṃsañca dassetvā ovadamānāpi tassa ukkaṇṭhaṃ vinodetuṃ asakkontī – ‘‘ayaṃ mama kāraṇā evarūpāya iddhiyā parihīno, na dāni yuttaṃ pariccajitu’’nti idheva tiṭṭhāti vatvā gharaṃ gantvā mātāpitūnaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Tepi āgantvā nānappakāraṃ ovadamānā vacanaṃ aggaṇhantaṃ āhaṃsu – ‘‘tvaṃ amhe uccakulāti sallakkhesi, mayaṃ pesakārā. Sakkhissasi pesakārakammaṃ kātu’’nti sāmaṇero āha – ‘‘upāsaka gihibhūto nāma pesakārakammaṃ vā kareyya naḷakārakammaṃ vā, kiṃ iminā sāṭakamattena lobhaṃ karothā’’ti. Pesakāro udare baddhasāṭakaṃ datvā gharaṃ netvā dhītaraṃ adāsi.

So pesakārakammaṃ uggaṇhitvā pesakārehi saddhiṃ sālāya kammaṃ karoti. Aññesaṃ itthiyo pātova bhattaṃ sampādetvā āhariṃsu, tassa bhariyā na tāva āgacchati. So itaresu kammaṃ vissajjetvā bhuñjamānesu tasaraṃ vaṭṭento nisīdi. Sā pacchā agamāsi. Atha naṃ so ‘‘aticirena āgatāsī’’ti tajjesi. Mātugāmo ca nāma api cakkavattirājānaṃ attani paṭibaddhacittaṃ ñatvā dāsaṃ viya sallakkheti. Tasmā sā evamāha – ‘‘aññesaṃ ghare dārupaṇṇaloṇādīni sannihitāni, bāhirato āharitvā dāyakā pesanatakārakāpi atthi, ahaṃ pana ekikāva, tvampi mayhaṃ ghare idaṃ atthi idaṃ natthīti na jānāsi. Sace icchasi, bhuñja, no ce icchasi, mā bhuñjā’’ti. So ‘‘na kevalañca ussūre bhattaṃ āharasi, vācāyapi maṃ ghaṭṭesī’’ti kujjhitvā aññaṃ paharaṇaṃ apassanto tameva tasaradaṇḍakaṃ tasarato luñcitvā khipi. Sā taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā īsakaṃ parivatti. Tasaradaṇḍakassa ca koṭi nāma tikhiṇā hoti, sā tassā parivattamānāya akkhikoṭiyaṃ pavisitvā aṭṭhāsi. Sā ubhohi hatthehi vegena akkhiṃ aggahesi, bhinnaṭṭhānato lohitaṃ paggharati. So tasmiṃ kāle upajjhāyassa vacanaṃ anussari – ‘‘idaṃ sandhāya maṃ upajjhāyo ‘anāgate kāle kāṇapesakāriyā hatthehi madditakañjiyaṃ pivissasī’ti āha, idaṃ therena diṭṭhaṃ bhavissati, aho dīghadassī ayyo’’ti mahāsaddena rodituṃ ārabhi. Tamenaṃ aññe – ‘‘alaṃ, āvuso, mā rodi, akkhi nāma bhinnaṃ na sakkā rodanena paṭipākatikaṃ kātu’’nti āhaṃsu. So ‘‘nāhametamatthaṃ rodāmi, apica kho imaṃ sandhāya rodāmī’’ti sabbaṃ paṭipāṭiyā kathesi. Evaṃ uppannā samathavipassanā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvattanti.

Aparampi vatthu – tiṃsamattā bhikkhū kalyāṇimahācetiyaṃ vanditvā aṭavimaggena mahāmaggaṃ otaramānā antarāmagge jhāmakhette kammaṃ katvā āgacchantaṃ ekaṃ manussaṃ addasaṃsu. Tassa sarīraṃ masimakkhitaṃ viya ahosi. Masimakkhitaṃyeva ekaṃ kāsāvaṃ kacchaṃ pīḷetvā nivatthaṃ, olokiyamāno jhāmakhāṇuko viya khāyati. So divasabhāge kammaṃ katvā upaḍḍhajjhāyamānānaṃ dārūnaṃ kalāpaṃ ukkhipitvā piṭṭhiyaṃ vippakiṇṇehi kesehi kummaggena āgantvā bhikkhūnaṃ sammukhe aṭṭhāsi. Sāmaṇerā disvā aññamaññaṃ olokayamānā, – ‘‘āvuso, tuyhaṃ pitā tuyhaṃ mahāpitā tuyhaṃ mātulo’’ti hasamānā gantvā ‘‘konāmo tvaṃ upāsakā’’ti nāmaṃ pucchiṃsu. So nāmaṃ pucchito vippaṭisārī hutvā dārukalāpaṃ chaḍḍetvā vatthaṃ saṃvidhāya nivāsetvā mahāthere vanditvā ‘‘tiṭṭhatha tāva, bhante,’’ti āha. Mahātherā aṭṭhaṃsu.

Daharasāmaṇerā āgantvā mahātherānaṃ sammukhāpi parihāsaṃ karonti. Upāsako āha – ‘‘bhante, tumhe maṃ passitvā parihasatha, ettakeneva matthakaṃ pattamhāti mā sallakkhetha. Ahampi pubbe tumhādisova samaṇo ahosiṃ. Tumhākaṃ pana cittekaggatāmattakampi natthi, ahaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo ahosiṃ, ākāsaṃ gahetvā pathaviṃ karomi, pathaviṃ ākāsaṃ. Dūraṃ gaṇhitvā santikaṃ karomi, santikaṃ dūraṃ. Cakkavāḷasatasahassaṃ khaṇena vinivijjhāmi. Hatthe me passatha, idāni makkaṭahatthasadisā, ahaṃ imeheva hatthehi idha nisinnova candimasūriye parāmasiṃ. Imesaṃyeva pādānaṃ candimasūriye pādakathalikaṃ katvā nisīdiṃ. Evarūpā me iddhi pamādena antarahitā, tumhe mā pamajjittha. Pamādena hi evarūpaṃ byasanaṃ pāpuṇanti. Appamattā viharantā jātijarāmaraṇassa antaṃ karonti. Tasmā tumhe maññeva ārammaṇaṃ karitvā appamattā hotha, bhante,’’ti tajjetvā ovādamadāsi. Te tassa kathentasseva saṃvegaṃ āpajjitvā vipassamānā tiṃsajanā tattheva arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti. Evampi uppannā samathavipassanā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvattantīti veditabbā.

Anuppannānaṃ pāpakānanti cettha ‘‘anuppanno vā kāmāsavo na uppajjatī’’tiādīsu vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Uppannānaṃ pāpakānanti ettha pana catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ vattamānuppannaṃ bhutvāvigatuppannaṃ, okāsakatuppannaṃ, bhūmiladdhuppannanti. Tattha ye kilesā vijjamānā uppādādisamaṅgino, idaṃ vattamānuppannaṃ nāma. Kamme pana javite ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavitvā niruddhavipāko bhutvā vigataṃ nāma. Kammaṃ uppajjitvā niruddhaṃ bhavitvā vigataṃ nāma. Tadubhayampi bhutvāvigatuppannanti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ aññassa kammassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karoti, evaṃ kate okāse vipāko uppajjamāno okāsakaraṇato paṭṭhāya uppannoti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Idaṃ okāsakatuppannaṃ nāma. Pañcakkhandhā pana vipassanāya bhūmi nāma. Te atītādibhedā honti. Tesu anusayitakilesā pana atītā vā anāgatā vā paccuppannā vāti na vattabbā. Atītakhandhesu anusayitāpi hi appahīnāva honti, anāgatakhandhesu, paccuppannakhandhesu anusayitāpi appahīnāva honti. Idaṃ bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāma. Tenāhu porāṇā – ‘‘tāsu tāsu bhūmīsu asamugghātitakilesā bhūmiladdhuppannāti saṅkhaṃ gacchantī’’ti.

Anuppannānaṃ pāpakāna Uppannānaṃ pāpakāna vattamānuppannaṃ bhutvāvigatuppanna okāsakatuppannaṃ bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ

Aparampi catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ samudācāruppannaṃ, ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ, avikkhambhituppannaṃ asamugghātituppannanti. Tattha sampati vattamānaṃyeva samudācāruppannaṃ nāma. Sakiṃ cakkhūni ummīletvā ārammaṇe nimitte gahite anussaritānussaritakkhaṇe kilesā nuppajjissantīti na vattabbā. Kasmā? Ārammaṇassa adhigahitattā. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā khīrarukkhassa kuṭhāriyā āhatāhataṭṭhāne khīraṃ na nikkhamissatīti na vattabbaṃ, evaṃ. Idaṃ ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ nāma. Samāpattiyā avikkhambhitā kilesā pana imasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne nuppajjissantīti na vattabbā. Kasmā? Avikkhambhitattā. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā sace khīrarukkhe kuṭhāriyā āhaneyyuṃ, imasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne khīraṃ na nikkhameyyāti na vattabbaṃ, evaṃ. Idaṃ avikkhambhituppannaṃ nāma. Maggena asamugghātitakilesā pana bhavagge nibbattassāpi uppajjantīti purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Idaṃ asamugghātituppannaṃ nāma.

samudācāruppannaṃ ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ avikkhambhituppannaṃ asamugghātituppannaṃ

Imesu uppannesu vattamānuppannaṃ bhutvāvigatuppannaṃ okāsakatuppannaṃ samudācāruppannanti catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ na maggavajjhaṃ, bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ avikkhambhituppannaṃ asamugghātituppannanti catubbidhaṃ maggavajjhaṃ. Maggo hi uppajjamāno ete kilese pajahati. So ye kilese pajahati, te atītā vā anāgatā vā paccuppannā vāti na vattabbā. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

‘‘Hañci atīte kilese pajahati, tena hi khīṇaṃ khepeti, niruddhaṃ nirodheti, vigataṃ vigameti atthaṅgataṃ atthaṅgameti. Atītaṃ yaṃ natthi, taṃ pajahati. Hañci anāgate kilese pajahati, tena hi ajātaṃ pajahati, anibbattaṃ, anuppannaṃ, apātubhūtaṃ pajahati. Anāgataṃ yaṃ natthi, taṃ pajahati, hañci paccuppanne kilese pajahati, tena hi ratto rāgaṃ pajahati , duṭṭho dosaṃ, mūḷho mohaṃ, vinibaddho mānaṃ, parāmaṭṭho diṭṭhiṃ, vikkhepagato uddhaccaṃ, aniṭṭhaṅgato vicikicchaṃ, thāmagato anusayaṃ pajahati. Kaṇhasukkadhammā yuganaddhā samameva vattanti. Saṃkilesikā maggabhāvanā hoti…pe… tena hi natthi maggabhāvanā, natthi phalasacchikiriyā, natthi kilesappahānaṃ, natthi dhammābhisamayoti. Atthi maggabhāvanā…pe… atthi dhammābhisamayoti. Yathā kathaṃ viya, seyyathāpi taruṇo rukkho ajātaphalo…pe… apātubhūtāyeva na pātubhavantī’’ti.

Iti pāḷiyaṃ ajātaphalarukkho āgato, jātaphalarukkhena pana dīpetabbaṃ. Yathā hi saphalo taruṇambarukkho, tassa phalāni manussā paribhuñjeyyuṃ, sesāni pātetvā pacchiyo pūreyyuṃ . Athañño puriso taṃ pharasunā chindeyya, tenassa neva atītāni phalāni nāsitāni honti, na anāgatapaccuppannāni nāsitāni. Atītāni hi manussehi paribhuttāni, anāgatāni anibbattāni, na sakkā nāsetuṃ. Yasmiṃ pana samaye so chinno, tadā phalāniyeva natthīti paccuppannānipi anāsitāni. Sace pana rukkho acchinno, athassa pathavīrasañca āporasañca āgamma yāni phalāni nibbatteyyuṃ, tāni nāsitāni honti. Tāni hi ajātāneva na jāyanti, anibbattāneva na nibbattanti, apātubhūtāneva na pātubhavanti, evameva maggo nāpi atītādibhede kilese pajahati, nāpi na pajahati. Yesañhi kilesānaṃ maggena khandhesu apariññātesu uppatti siyā, maggena uppajjitvā khandhānaṃ pariññātattā te kilesā ajātāva na jāyanti, anibbattāva na nibbattanti, apātubhūtāva na pātubhavanti, taruṇaputtāya itthiyā puna avijāyanatthaṃ, byādhitānaṃ rogavūpasamanatthaṃ pītabhesajjehi cāpi ayamattho vibhāvetabbo. Evaṃ maggo ye kilese pajahati, te atītā vā anāgatā vā paccuppannā vāti na vattabbā, na ca maggo kilese na pajahati. Ye pana maggo kilese pajahati, te sandhāya ‘‘uppannānaṃ pāpakāna’’ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Na kevalañca maggo kileseyeva pajahati, kilesānaṃ pana appahīnattā ye ca uppajjeyyuṃ upādinnakakkhandhā, tepi pajahatiyeva. Vuttampi cetaṃ – ‘‘sotāpattimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena satta bhave ṭhapetvā anamatagge saṃsāre ye uppajjeyyuṃ nāmañca rūpañca, etthete nirujjhantī’’ti (cūḷani. 6) vitthāro. Iti maggo upādinnaanupādinnato vuṭṭhāti. Bhavavasena pana sotāpattimaggo apāyabhavato vuṭṭhāti, sakadāgāmimaggo sugatibhavekadesato, anāgāmimaggo sugatikāmabhavato, arahattamaggo rūpārūpabhavato vuṭṭhāti. Sabbabhavehi vuṭṭhātiyevātipi vadanti.

Atha maggakkhaṇe kathaṃ anuppannānaṃ uppādāya bhāvanā hoti, kathaṃ vā uppannānaṃ ṭhitiyāti. Maggappavattiyāyeva. Maggo hi pavattamāno pubbe anuppannapubbattā anuppanno nāma vuccati. Anāgatapubbañhi ṭhānaṃ āgantvā ananubhūtapubbaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ anubhavitvā vattāro bhavanti ‘‘anāgataṭṭhānaṃ āgatamhā, ananubhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ anubhavāmā’’ti. Yā cassa pavatti, ayameva ṭhiti nāmāti ṭhitiyā bhāvetītipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Iddhipādesu saṅkhepakathā cetokhilasutte (ma. ni. 1.185 ādayo) vuttā. Upasamamānaṃ gacchati, kilesūpasamatthaṃ vā gacchatīti upasamagāmī. Sambujjhamānā gacchati, maggasambodhatthāya vā gacchatīti sambodhagāmī.

Iddhipādesu upasamagāmī sambodhagāmī

Vivekanissitādīni sabbāsavasaṃvare vuttāni. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panāyaṃ bodhipakkhiyakathā visuddhimagge vuttā.

Vivekanissitā visuddhimagge

247. Now, while indicating the practice for the attainment of those various distinctions, he said, beginning with "Furthermore, Udāyī." There, *abhiññāvosānapāramippattā* means having attained arahantship, which is reckoned as the culmination of direct knowledge (*abhiññāvosāna*) and reckoned as the perfection of direct knowledge (*abhiññāpāramī*). *Sammappadhāne* means in the exertion of skillful means (*upāyapadhāne*). *Chandaṃ janeti* means he generates the desire-to-do (*kattukamyatā*) which is a wholesome desire (*kusalacchandaṃ*). *Vāyamati* means he makes an effort (*vāyāmaṃ karoti*). *Vīriyaṃ ārabhati* means he rouses energy (*vīriyaṃ pavatteti*). *Cittaṃ paggaṇhāti* means he uplifts his mind (*cittaṃ ukkhipati*). *Padahati* means he makes the exertion of skillful means (*upāyapadhānaṃ karoti*). *Bhāvanāya pāripūriyā* means for the sake of the fullness of growth (*vaḍḍhiyā paripūraṇatthaṃ*). Moreover, in this regard, it should be understood that the meaning of each later [factor] is [connected to] each earlier one, as it is said, "That which is stability is non-confusion…pe…that which is abundance is the fullness of cultivation (*bhāvanāpāripūrī*)" (Vibha. 406). *Sammappadhāne chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati bhāvanāya pāripūriyā* Now, what is described by these right exertions (*sammappadhānehi*)? The preliminary practice (*pubbabhāgapaṭipadā*) of a disciple is described in the section connected with Kassapa (*kassapasaṃyuttapariyāyena*). For it was said there: "There are these four right exertions, friend. What four? Here, friend, a bhikkhu generates enthusiasm (*ātappaṃ karoti*) thinking, 'May evil, unwholesome states not arise that, arising, would lead to harm.' He generates enthusiasm thinking, 'May evil, unwholesome states that have arisen not be abandoned and lead to harm.' He generates enthusiasm thinking, 'May wholesome states that have not arisen not arise and lead to harm.' He generates enthusiasm thinking, 'May wholesome states that have arisen not cease and lead to harm'" (Saṃ. Ni. 2. 145). Here, evil, unwholesome states (*pāpakā akusalā*) should be understood as greed and so forth. Wholesome states that have not arisen (*anuppannā kusalā dhammā*) are tranquility (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) as well as the path (*maggo*), and wholesome states that have arisen (*uppannā kusalā*) are tranquility and insight. But there is no path (*maggo*) that, arising once and ceasing, would lead to harm. For it ceases only after giving the condition for the fruit. Or it has been said that tranquility and insight should be taken even in the former [case], but that is not fitting. There, this story [is told] for the sake of revealing the meaning of "tranquility and insight that have arisen cease and lead to harm": It seems that a certain elder, one whose outflows were exhausted (*khīṇāsavatthero*), went from the countryside to the Great Monastery (*mahāvihāraṃ*) with a novice attendant, one who had gained attainments (*samāpattilābhinā bhaṇḍagāhakasāmaṇerena saddhiṃ*), thinking, "I will venerate the Great Shrine (*mahācetiyañca*) and the Great Bodhi Tree (*mahābodhiñca*)," and entered the monastery precinct (*vihārapariveṇaṃ pāvisi*). In the evening, when the great community of monks was venerating the shrine, he did not go out to venerate the shrine. Why? For those whose outflows are exhausted have great respect for the three jewels. Therefore, after the community of monks had venerated and were returning at the time of the evening meal for the people, without informing even the novice, he went out alone thinking, "I will venerate the shrine." The novice: "Why is the elder going alone at an unseemly time? I will find out," and he followed closely behind his preceptor (*upajjhāyassa padānupadiko nikkhami*). The elder, not knowing of his arrival due to non-attention, ascended to the shrine courtyard (*cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ āruhi*) by the southern gate (*dakkhiṇadvārena*). The novice also ascended immediately afterwards. The great elder, having looked up at the great *cetiya* (shrine), taking joy in focusing on the Buddha, gathering all of his mind, being delighted and elated, reverently worships the *cetiya*. The novice, having seen the elder's manner of worship, thought, "My preceptor is reverently worshipping with a very clear mind. What if I were to obtain flowers and perform a *pūjā* (offering)?" The elder, having worshipped, rose, placed his hands together in reverence on his head, and stood gazing at the great *cetiya*. The novice, having cleared his throat, made known his arrival. The elder, having turned around and looking, asked, "When did you arrive?" "During the time of your *cetiya* worship, venerable sir." "You are very clear-minded, you reverently worshipped the *cetiya*. What if you were to obtain flowers and perform a *pūjā*?" "Yes, novice. In this *cetiya*, as in no other place, there is such a collection of relics. Who would not perform a *pūjā* with flowers, having obtained such an incomparable great *stūpa*?" "Then, venerable sir, please consent. I will bring [flowers]," and just then, having attained *jhāna* (meditative absorption), by means of his power, having gone to the Himavant (Himalayas), having filled a *parissāvana* (water-strainer) with flowers endowed with color and fragrance, having returned before the great elder had reached the western side from the southern side, having placed the flower-strainer in his hand, he said, "Worship, venerable sir." The elder said, "The flowers are not very fresh, novice." "Go, venerable sir, reflect on the qualities of the Blessed One and perform a *pūjā*." Having ascended by the stairs situated on the western side, on the *kucchivedikābhūmi* (terrace), he began to perform a flower *pūjā*. The perfectly full flowers, having fallen on the *vedikābhūmi* (altar terrace), filled the second level with a layer as high as the knees. Then, having descended, he worshipped the row of foot-rests. That too became completely full. Having known the state of being completely full, scattering [flowers] on the lower level, he went away. The entire *cetiyaṅgaṇa* (shrine courtyard) became completely full. When that was completely full, he said, "Novice, the flowers are not exhausted." "Venerable sir, turn the *parissāvana* (water strainer) upside down." Having turned [it] upside down, he shook [it], then the flowers were exhausted. Having given the *parissāvana* (water strainer) to the novice, together with the elephant fence, having circumambulated the *cetiya* three times, having worshipped in the four places, while going to the enclosure, he thought, "This novice is very powerful. Will he be able to protect this power?" Then, having seen that "He will not be able," he said to the novice, "Novice, you are now very powerful, but without developing this power, in the future, you will be drinking *madditakañjiyaṃ* (fermented rice water) crushed by the hand of a one-eyed female weaver." This is a fault of youth. He, having been alarmed by the words of his preceptor, did not ask, "Venerable sir, tell me [about a subject] for meditation." He went away as if not hearing what our preceptor was saying. The elder, having worshipped the great *cetiya* and the great *bodhi* (enlightenment tree), having had the novice take the bowl and robes, gradually went to the Kuṭeḷitissa Great Monastery. The novice, being obedient to the elder, does not go for alms. "Which village are you entering, venerable sir?" Having asked, then knowing that "Now my preceptor will have arrived at the village gate," having taken his own bowl and robes and those of his preceptor, having gone through the sky, having given the bowl and robes to the elder, he enters for alms. The elder always advises, "Novice, do not do thus. The power of an ordinary person is unsteady and unbound. Having obtained an unsuitable object such as forms etc., it is destroyed by a small matter. With tranquility and attainment diminished, dwelling in the holy life is not able to be supported." The novice does not want to hear, "What is my preceptor saying?" He does just that. The elder, gradually performing *cetiyavandanaṃ* (shrine worship), went to a place called the Kammubindu Monastery. Even while the elder was dwelling there, the novice did just that. Then, one day, a beautiful weaver's daughter, standing at a young age, having gone out from Kammubindu village, having descended to the Paduma pond, singing, was breaking flowers. At that time, the novice was going along the top of the lotus pond, and as he was going, he was caught by her singing voice like a blind fly in the *silesikā*. Immediately, his psychic power disappeared, and he became like a crow with clipped wings. However, by the power of serenity and *samāpatti*, without falling on the surface of the water right there, he hovered like cotton from a silk-cotton tree, and gradually stood on the shore of the lotus pond. He quickly went, gave the bowl and robe to his preceptor, and returned. The elder said, "This was seen by me beforehand; even when being restrained, he will not turn back," and without saying anything, he entered for alms. The novice, having gone, stood on the shore of the lotus pond, awaiting her return. She also, having seen the novice going in the sky, and again having come and stood, knowing, "Indeed, this one is longing for me, relying on me," said, "Go back, novice!" He went back. The other, having returned, put on her garment, approached him, and asked, "What is it, *bhante*?" He told her that matter. She, having shown the misery of household life and the benefit of living a celibate life with many reasons, even though advising him, was unable to dispel his longing. Saying, "This one has declined from psychic power because of me; now it is not proper to abandon him," and having said that she would stay right there, she went to the house and told her parents that event. They also, having come, advising in various ways, said to him who did not accept their word, "You regarded us as being from a high family; we are weavers. You will be able to do weaving work?" The novice said, "Is it that a lay follower, having become a householder, would do weaving work or reed-mat making work? Why are you making a desire for gain with just this one garment?" The weaver, having given a garment tied to his belly, took him to the house and gave him his daughter. He, having learned weaving work, does work in the workshop together with the weavers. Other women brought food early in the morning, having prepared it, but his wife did not come yet. He, having dismissed the work among the others, while they were eating, sat turning the shuttle. She came later. Then he scolded her, "You have come too late!" A woman, knowing that even a *cakravartin* king has his mind bound to herself, regards him like a slave. Therefore, she said thus: "In the house of other people, firewood, leaves, salt, and so on are prepared, and there are also donors and message-delivering servants, but I am all alone, and you also do not know what is in my house and what is not. If you want, eat; if you don't want, don't eat!" He, angered, "Not only do you bring food late, but you also strike me with your words!" not seeing another weapon, having plucked that very shuttle rod from the shuttle, threw it. She, having seen him coming, turned aside slightly. And indeed, the tip of the shuttle rod was sharp, and it, entering the corner of her eye as she was turning, remained stuck there. She grabbed her eye forcefully with both hands, and blood flowed from the broken place. At that time, he remembered the word of his preceptor: "With reference to this, my preceptor said, 'In the future, you will drink pounded gruel with the hands of a blind weaver woman.' This will have been seen by the elder; oh, the venerable one is far-seeing!" and he began to cry with a loud voice. Then others said to him, "Enough, friend! Do not cry! It is not possible to make an eye that is broken become as it was originally through crying." He said, "I am not crying for this matter, but rather I am crying with reference to this!" and he told everything in order. Thus, *samatha* and *vipassanā* that have arisen, being obstructed, conduce to disadvantage. Here is another account: Approximately thirty monks, after venerating the auspicious, great *cetiya*, were descending the great road via the forest path. On the road in between, they saw a man coming who had been working in a burnt field. His body was as if smeared with soot. He wore a single soot-smeared ochre robe, tucking up the end, and looked like a burnt stump. Having worked during the day, he had lifted up a bundle of partially burnt timber and, with his hair scattered across his back, came by a bad road and stood before the monks. The novices, seeing [him], looked at each other and said, “Friend, [is he] your father? Your grandfather? Your uncle?” Laughing, they went and asked, “What is your name, lay follower?” Being asked his name, he became remorseful and, throwing away the bundle of wood, arranged his robe, and, having robed himself, venerated the elder monks and said, “Wait a moment, venerable sirs.” The elder monks waited. The young novices came and even ridiculed the elder monks. The lay follower said, “Venerable sirs, do not assume that you have reached the summit just because you see me laughing at you. I, too, was formerly a *śramaṇa* like you. But you do not even have a modicum of one-pointedness of mind. In this Dispensation, I was powerful and of great influence. I could take the sky and make it earth, or [take] the earth [and make it] sky. Having taken what is far, I can make it near; [and take] what is near [and make it] far. I can pierce a hundred thousand world-systems in an instant. Look at my hands; now they are like monkey’s paws, but, sitting here, I can touch the moon and sun with these very hands. Making the moon and sun footstools for these very feet, I have sat. My psychic power is such that it is unimpeded by negligence; do not be negligent! For it is through negligence that such misfortune is reached. Those who abide diligently make an end to birth, aging, and death. Therefore, making me your object [of meditation], be diligent, venerable sirs!” Thus, having threatened them, he gave [them] counsel. They, having experienced agitation just from his speaking and contemplating, thirty people then and there attained *arhatship*. Even so, it should be understood that concentration and insight that have arisen in this way, when ceasing, lead to harm. In "[preventing] unarisen evil," here, the meaning should be understood in the manner stated in the [passages beginning] “‘Or, unarisen is the outflow of sensual desire, it does not arise,’ etc.” However, in "[abandoning] arisen evil," there are four kinds of arising: arising in the present, arising after having been, arising from opportunity, and arising having gained a basis. There, those defilements that are present and furnished with arising, etc., this is called “arising in the present.” However, in the case of action, when speeded up, after experiencing the taste of the object, what is past having been stopped is called “having been and ceased.” Action, having arisen, stopped, and become past, is called “having been and ceased.” Both of these go by the designation “arising after having been and ceased.” A wholesome or unwholesome action, having resisted the result of another action, makes an opportunity for its own result. When a result is produced on that opportunity having been made, it goes by the designation “arisen,” starting from the making of the opportunity. This is called “arising from opportunity.” The five aggregates, however, are called the basis for insight. They have the distinctions of past, etc. Among them, the defilements lying dormant cannot be called past, future, or present. For even in the past aggregates the dormant [defilements] are unabandoned; [so it is] in the future aggregates, [and] in the present aggregates. 0174"/> But the latent tendencies are not yet abandoned. This is called "produced by attainment of the ground" (*bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ*). Therefore, the ancients said: "On those grounds, the defilements that have not been eradicated are called "produced by attainment of the ground" (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*)."

Of unarisen evil things. 0251"/> Of arisen evil things, of things arisen in the present, of things arisen having ceased, of things arisen from opportunity. 0174"/> "Produced by attainment of the ground" (*bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ*). Moreover, there are four kinds of arising: arising from behavior (*samudācāruppannaṃ*), arising from the appropriation of an object (*ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ*), arising from non-obstruction (*avikkhambhituppannaṃ*), and arising from non-eradication (*asamugghātituppannaṃ*). Therein, what is presently happening is called "arising from behavior" (*samudācāruppannaṃ*). Having once opened the eyes and seized upon an object as a sign, in the moment of recollecting and re-recollecting, defilements. 0252"/> will not arise, it should not be said. 0178"/> should not be said. Why? Because of the appropriation of the object (*ārammaṇassa adhigahitattā*). What is the example? Just as it should not be said that milk will not come out at a place struck and struck by an axe on a milk-tree, even so. This is called "arising from the appropriation of an object" (*ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ*). Because of concentration, defilements that are unobstructable will not arise in this place, it should not be said. Why? Because of non-obstruction (*avikkhambhitattā*). What is the example? Just as, if they were to strike a milk-tree with an axe, it should not be said that milk will not come out in this place, even so. This is called "arising from non-obstruction" (*avikkhambhituppannaṃ*). Defilements that have not been eradicated by the path, even for one born in the highest existence, will arise, thus it should be expanded in the same way as before. This is called "arising from non-eradication" (*asamugghātituppannaṃ*).

Arising from behavior (*samudācāruppannaṃ*). 0252"/> 0178"/> Arising from the appropriation of an object (*ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ*), arising from non-obstruction (*avikkhambhituppannaṃ*), and arising from non-eradication (*asamugghātituppannaṃ*). Of these arisings, arising in the present, arising having ceased, arising from opportunity, and arising from behavior (*samudācāruppannaṃ*) are four kinds of arising that are not liable to the path (*maggavajjhaṃ*). Produced by attainment of the ground (*bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ*), arising from the appropriation of an object (*ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ*), arising from non-obstruction (*avikkhambhituppannaṃ*), and arising from non-eradication (*asamugghātituppannaṃ*) are four kinds of what is liable to the path (*maggavajjhaṃ*). For the path, arising, abandons these defilements. So, those defilements that he abandons, whether they are past, future, or present, it should not be said. This was also said: "If he abandons past defilements, then he causes what is exhausted to be exhausted, he causes what is stopped to be stopped, he causes what is gone to be gone, he causes what has set to set. He abandons the past, which does not exist. If he abandons future defilements, then he abandons what is unborn, he abandons what has not occurred, he abandons what has not arisen, he abandons what has not become manifest. He abandons the future, which does not exist. If he abandons present defilements, then the passionate one abandons passion. 0253"/>, the corrupt one abandons corruption, the deluded one abandons delusion, the bound one abandons conceit, the attached one abandons wrong views, the agitated one abandons excitement, the one gone to what is undesirable abandons doubt, the one gone to fortitude abandons latent tendency. Dark and bright states occur coupled together (*yuganaddhā samameva vattanti*). A path-development that has defilement …pe… therefore, there is no path-development, there is no realization of fruition, there is no abandoning of defilements, there is no penetration to the Dhamma. There is 0175"/> path-development…pe… there is penetration to the Dhamma. Just how is it like, as, for example, a young tree that is without fruit…pe… they do not appear even though they have not appeared."

0253"/> 0175"/> Iti, in the Pāḷi, a tree without fruit has come, but it should be explained with a tree that has fruit. Just as, indeed, a young mango tree is fruitful, people would enjoy its fruits, and having felled the remaining ones, they would fill their baskets. 0179"/>. Then another person would cut it down with an axe, but by that, neither would its past fruits be destroyed, nor would its future and present fruits be destroyed. Indeed, past things have been used by people, future things have not arisen, it is not possible to destroy them. However, at whatever time that [tree] is cut, then, since the fruits themselves do not exist, even the present ones are not consumed. If, however, the tree is not cut, then, when it obtains the flavor of earth and the flavor of water, the fruits that would arise from it, those would be destroyed. Indeed, those do not arise even without being born, they do not come into being even without being brought forth, they do not appear even without appearing; just so, the path also does not abandon the defilements in the divisions beginning with the past, nor does it not abandon them. Indeed, if there would be arising through the path in the aggregates when the defilements have not been fully understood, those defilements, having arisen through the path, because of the aggregates having been fully understood, do not arise even without being born, they do not come into being even without being brought forth, they do not appear even without appearing, for a young woman for the sake of not conceiving again, for the sick for the purpose of calming the disease, this meaning should also be illustrated with drunk medicines. Thus, the path abandons whatever defilements, those should not be said to be past or future or present, and the path does not not abandon the defilements. But those defilements which the path abandons, referring to those it is said, "arisen evil ones," and so on. The abbreviated talk in the Ceto-khila Sutta (M. N. 1. 185 and so on) has been spoken. Going to appeasement, or because it goes for the sake of the appeasement of the defilements, [it is called] *upasamagāmī* (leading to appeasement). Going to perfect enlightenment, or because it goes for the sake of the perfect enlightenment of the path, [it is called] *sambodhagāmī* (leading to perfect enlightenment). The concise story is told in the Ceto-khila Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya, 1. 185, et cetera). Approaching tranquility or going to the purpose of the tranquility of the defilements is called *upasamagāmī* (leading to tranquility). Proceeding to perfect awakening, or going for the purpose of the perfect awakening of the path, is called *sambodhagāmī* (leading to perfect awakening). That path rises up from the grasped and the ungrasped. However, by the force of existence, the stream-enterer's path rises up from the plane of misery, the once-returner's path [rises up] from a part of the plane of the good destiny, the non-returner's path [rises up] from the plane of the good destiny of desire, the *arhat*'s path rises up from the plane of form and formlessness. Some say that it rises up from all existences. Now, at the moment of the path, how is there cultivation for the arising of the unarisen, or how is there stability for the arisen? Just by the proceeding of the path. Indeed, the path, while proceeding, because of the previous state of not having arisen, is called unarisen. Indeed, having come to a place that was not previously come to, or having experienced an object that was not previously experienced, speakers become saying, "We have come to a place that was not come to, we experience an object that was not experienced." And whatever its proceeding, this itself is called stability, so it is fitting to say that one cultivates by stability. That which is based on seclusion, and other [qualities], are stated in the restraint of all the āsravas. This is the summary here; however, this talk of the qualities pertaining to enlightenment is stated in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. Based on discernment, in the *Visuddhimagga*.

mula_pali: 248. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā aṭṭha vimokkhe bhāventi.
