Then Pañcakaṅga the carpenter thought: “It is not the right time to see the Blessed One; he is still in retreat. And it is not the right time to see bhikkhus worthy of esteem; they are still in retreat. Suppose I went to Mallikā’s Park, to the debating hall near the Tinduka tree to see the wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamuṇḍikaputta?” And he went to Mallikā’s Park.

Now on that occasion the wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamuṇḍikaputta was sitting together with a large following of wanderers, making a great noise and uproar, engaged in manifold frivolous talk, such as: talk about kings, robbers, and ministers of state; talk about armies, dangers, and wars; talk about food, drink, garments, and lodgings; talk about garlands and scents; talk about relations, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; talk about women and talk about heroes; street talk and talk by the well; talk about those departed in days gone by; rambling chit-chat; speculations about the world and about the sea; talk about gain and loss.

The wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamuṇḍikaputta saw the carpenter Pañcakaṅga coming in the distance. Seeing him, he quieted his own assembly thus: “Sirs, be quiet; sirs make no noise. Here comes the carpenter Pañcakaṅga, a disciple of the recluse Gotama. As many as there are lay disciples of the recluse Gotama, dressed in white, staying at Sāvatthī, this carpenter Pañcakaṅga is one of them. These venerable ones like quiet; they are disciplined in quiet; they commend quiet. Perhaps if he finds our assembly a quiet one, he will think to join us.” Then the wanderers became silent.
commentary_pali: 260.Evaṃme sutanti samaṇamuṇḍikasuttaṃ. Tattha uggāhamānoti tassa paribbājakassa nāmaṃ. Sumanoti pakatināmaṃ. Kiñci kiñci pana uggahituṃ uggāhetuṃ samatthatāya uggāhamānoti naṃ sañjānanti. Samayaṃ pavadanti etthāti samayappavādakaṃ. Tasmiṃ kira ṭhāne caṅkītārukkhapokkharasātippabhutayo brāhmaṇā nigaṇṭhācelakaparibbājakādayo ca pabbajitā sannipatitvā attano attano samayaṃ pavadanti kathenti dīpenti, tasmā so ārāmo samayappavādakoti vuccati. Sveva tindukācīrasaṅkhātāya timbarūsakarukkhapantiyā parikkhittattā tindukācīraṃ. Yasmā panettha paṭhamaṃ ekā sālā ahosi, pacchā mahāpuññaṃ poṭṭhapādaparibbājakaṃ nissāya bahū sālā katā, tasmā tameva ekaṃ sālaṃ upādāya laddhanāmavasena ekasālakoti vuccati. Mallikāya pana pasenadirañño deviyā uyyānabhūto so pupphaphalasañchanno ārāmoti katvā mallikāya ārāmoti saṅkhaṃ gato. Tasmiṃ samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme. Paṭivasatīti vāsaphāsutāya vasati. Divā divassāti divasassa divā nāma majjhanhātikkamo, tasmiṃ divasassapi divābhūte atikkantamatte majjhanhike nikkhamīti attho. Paṭisallīnoti tato tato rūpādigocarato cittaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā līno, jhānaratisevanavasena ekībhāvaṃ gato. Manobhāvanīyānanti manavaḍḍhanakānaṃ, ye āvajjato manasikaroto cittaṃ vinīvaraṇaṃ hoti unnamati vaḍḍhati. Yāvatāti yattakā. Ayaṃ tesaṃ aññataroti ayaṃ tesaṃ abbhantaro eko sāvako. Appeva nāmāti tassa upasaṅkamanaṃ patthayamāno āha. Patthanākāraṇaṃ pana sandakasutte vuttameva.
commentary_english:
260. Thus I have heard, the *samaṇamuṇḍika* discourse.

There, *uggāhamāno* means the name of that wanderer (*parivrājaka*).

*sumano* means the natural name.

Because of the ability to grasp and cause to grasp a little, they recognize him as *uggāhamāno*.

They declare the *samayaṃ* there, therefore *samayappavādakaṃ*.

In that place, brāhmaṇas, *nigaṇṭhācelaka parivrājakas*, and other renunciates, such as *caṅkītārukkhapokkharasātippabhuta*, having gathered, declare, speak, and illuminate their own doctrines (*samaya*). Therefore, that *ārāma* is called *samayappavādako*.

Because it is surrounded by a row of *timbarūsakarukkhapanti*, known as *tindukācīra*, it is called *tindukācīraṃ*.

Because here previously there was one hall (*sālā*), later many halls were made relying on the greatly meritorious *poṭṭhapāda parivrājaka*, therefore, taking up that same one hall, according to the name received, it is called *ekasālako*.

Mallikā's, the *pasenadirañño devī*'s, garden-like, that flower and fruit covered park, having made it an *ārāma*, it went to the designation *mallikāya ārāmo*.

In that *samayappavādaka tindukācīra ekasālaka mallikāya ārāme*.

*paṭivasatī* means dwells in comfort.

*divā divassā* means by day of the day, namely after midday, at that time when the day has become day, when the midday has passed, he goes out, is the meaning.

*paṭisallīno* means having withdrawn and secluded the mind (*citta*) from this and that object of sense, such as form (*rūpa*), having gone to oneness through cultivating delight in meditation (*jhāna*).

*manobhāvanīyāna* means of those that increase the mind, which, when reflecting and attending, the mind becomes without hindrances, rises up, grows.

*yāvatā* means as much as.

*ayaṃ tesaṃ aññataro* means this one is another, an inner disciple of those.

*appeva nāmā* means wishing to approach him, he says.

But the cause of wishing has already been spoken in the *sandakasutta*.

mula_pali:
261. Atha kho pañcakaṅgo thapati yena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā uggāhamānena paribbājakena samaṇamuṇḍikāputtena saddhiṃ sammodi . Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto etadavoca – ‘‘catūhi kho ahaṃ, gahapati, dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi sampannakusalaṃ paramakusalaṃ uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjhaṃ. Katamehi catūhi? Idha, gahapati, na kāyena pāpakammaṃ karoti, na pāpakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, na pāpakaṃ saṅkappaṃ saṅkappeti, na pāpakaṃ ājīvaṃ ājīvati – imehi kho ahaṃ, gahapati, catūhi dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi sampannakusalaṃ paramakusalaṃ uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjha’’nti.

Atha kho pañcakaṅgo thapati uggāhamānassa paribbājakassa samaṇamuṇḍikāputtassa bhāsitaṃ neva abhinandi nappaṭikkosi. Anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi – ‘‘bhagavato santike etassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānissāmī’’ti. Atha kho pañcakaṅgo thapati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho pañcakaṅgo thapati yāvatako ahosi uggāhamānena paribbājakena samaṇamuṇḍikāputtena saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato ārocesi.
mula_english:
Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga went to the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta, and exchanged greetings with Uggāhamāna, the wanderer, the Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta. When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side.

The wanderer Uggāhamāna, the Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta, then said to the carpenter Pañcakaṅga who was sitting to one side: "Householder, when a man possesses four qualities, I describe him as accomplished in what is wholesome (**sampannakusalaṃ**), perfected in what is wholesome (**paramakusalaṃ**), attained to the supreme attainment (**uttamapattipattaṃ**), an invincible ascetic (**samaṇaṃ ayojjhaṃ**). Which four? Here, householder, he does no evil bodily actions, he utters no evil speech, he has no evil intentions, and he does not make his living by any evil livelihood. When a man possesses these four qualities, I describe him as accomplished in what is wholesome, perfected in what is wholesome, attained to the supreme attainment, an invincible ascetic."

Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga neither approved nor disapproved of the words of the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta. Without approving or disapproving, he rose from his seat and went away, thinking: “I shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One (**bhagavato**)."

Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga went to the Blessed One; and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side. As he sat there, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga reported to the Blessed One his entire conversation with the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta.
commentary_pali:
261.Etadavocāti dandapañño ayaṃ gahapati, dhammakathāya naṃ saṅgaṇhitvā attano sāvakaṃ karissāmīti maññamāno etaṃ ‘‘catūhi kho’’tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha paññapemīti dassemi ṭhapemi. Sampannakusalanti paripuṇṇakusalaṃ. Paramakusalanti uttamakusalaṃ. Ayojjhanti vādayuddhena yujjhitvā cāletuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ acalaṃ nikkampaṃ thiraṃ. Na karotīti akaraṇamattameva vadati, ettha pana saṃvarappahānaṃ vā paṭisevanappahānaṃ vā na vadati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

Neva abhinandīti titthiyā nāma jānitvāpi ajānitvāpi yaṃ vā taṃ vā vadantīti maññamāno nābhinandi. Na paṭikkosīti sāsanassa anulomaṃ viya pasannākāraṃ viya vadatīti maññamāno na paṭisedheti.

Neva abhinandī Na paṭikkosī
commentary_english:
261. *etadavocā* means: "the wise householder, thinking, 'having gathered him with a *dharma*-talk, I will make him my disciple,' spoke this saying beginning with, 'by means of these four.'"
*paññapemī* means: "I will show," "I will establish."
*sampannakusala* means: complete merit.
*paramakusala* means: supreme merit, or *uttamakusala*.
*ayojjha* means: "having striven in verbal battle, [it is] impossible to move, unshakeable, unmoving, firm."
*na karotī* means: "he does not do" merely abstaining from action; here he does not speak of restraint-abandoning or recourse-abandoning.
The same method [applies] in the remaining phrases.

*neva abhinandī* means: thinking, "the *tīrthikas* speak thus, whether knowing or not knowing," he did not rejoice.
*na paṭikkosī* means: thinking, "he speaks as if in accordance with the teaching, as if with a pleased manner," he does not reject.

*neva abhinandī na paṭikkosī*

mula_pali: 262. Evaṃ vutte, bhagavā pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ etadavoca – ‘‘evaṃ sante kho, thapati, daharo kumāro mando uttānaseyyako sampannakusalo bhavissati paramakusalo uttamapattipatto samaṇo ayojjho, yathā uggāhamānassa paribbājakassa samaṇamuṇḍikāputtassa vacanaṃ. Daharassa hi, thapati, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa kāyotipi na hoti, kuto pana kāyena pāpakammaṃ karissati, aññatra phanditamattā! Daharassa hi, thapati, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa vācātipi na hoti, kuto pana pāpakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsissati, aññatra roditamattā ! Daharassa hi, thapati, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa saṅkappotipi na hoti, kuto pana pāpakaṃ saṅkappaṃ saṅkappissati, aññatra vikūjitamattā vikujjitamattā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)! Daharassa hi, thapati, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa ājīvotipi na hoti, kuto pana pāpakaṃ ājīvaṃ ājīvissati, aññatra mātuthaññā! Evaṃ sante kho, thapati, daharo kumāro mando uttānaseyyako sampannakusalo bhavissati paramakusalo uttamapattipatto samaṇo ayojjho, yathā uggāhamānassa paribbājakassa samaṇamuṇḍikāputtassa vacanaṃ.
mula_english:
262. Thus spoken, the Blessed One said the following to the carpenter Pañcakaṅga: "If that were so, carpenter, then a young, tender infant lying prone would be accomplished in what is wholesome, perfected in what is wholesome, attained to the supreme attainment, an invincible *śramaṇa* (ascetic), according to the statement of the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the son of a *śramaṇa* (ascetic) Muṇḍikā.

For a young, tender infant lying prone does not even have the notion 'body' (*kāya*), so how should he do an evil action (*pāpakarma*) with the body (*kāya*) beyond mere wriggling? For a young, tender infant lying prone does not even have speech, so how should he utter evil speech (*pāpakaṃ vācaṃ*) beyond mere crying? For a young, tender infant lying prone does not even have intention (*saṅkappa*), so how should he have an evil intention (*pāpakaṃ saṅkappaṃ*) beyond mere cooing? For a young, tender infant lying prone does not even have a livelihood (*ājīva*), so how should he make a living with an evil livelihood (*pāpakaṃ ājīvaṃ*) beyond his mother's milk? If that were so, carpenter, then a young, tender infant lying prone would be accomplished in what is wholesome, perfected in what is wholesome, attained to the supreme attainment, an invincible *śramaṇa* (ascetic), according to the statement of the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the son of a *śramaṇa* (ascetic) Muṇḍikā."
commentary_pali: 262.Yathā uggāhamānassāti yathā tassa vacanaṃ, evaṃ sante uttānaseyyako kumāro ayojjhasamaṇo thirasamaṇo bhavissati, mayaṃ pana evaṃ na vadāmāti dīpeti. Kāyotipi na hotīti sakakāyo parakāyotipi visesañāṇaṃ na hoti. Aññatraphanditamattāti paccattharaṇe valisamphassena vā maṅguladaṭṭhena vā kāyaphandanamattaṃ nāma hoti. Taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ kāyena karaṇakammaṃ nāma natthi. Tampi ca kilesasahagatacitteneva hoti. Vācātipi na hotīti micchāvācā sammāvācātipi nānattaṃ na hoti. Roditamattāti jighacchāpipāsāparetassa pana roditamattaṃ hoti. Tampi kilesasahagatacitteneva. Saṅkappoti micchāsaṅkappo sammāsaṅkappotipi nānattaṃ na hoti. Vikūjitamattāti vikūjitamattaṃ rodanahasitamattaṃ hoti. Daharakumārakānañhi cittaṃ atītārammaṇaṃ pavattati, nirayato āgatā nirayadukkhaṃ saritvā rodanti, devalokato āgatā hasanti, tampi kilesasahagatacitteneva hoti. Ājīvoti micchājīvo sammājīvotipi nānattaṃ na hoti. Aññatra mātuthaññāti thaññacoradārakā nāma honti, mātari khīraṃ pāyantiyā apivitvā aññavihitakāle piṭṭhipassena āgantvā thaññaṃ pivanti. Ettakaṃ muñcitvā añño micchājīvo natthi. Ayampi kilesasahagatacitteneva hotīti dasseti.
commentary_english:
262. "Just as [it is] for one who is learning," that is, just as his word [is]; thus, while he exists, the infant lying on his back will become non-contentious and stable; this is what he is explaining when he says, "But we do not speak thus."
"There is no body either," that is, there is no specific knowledge of one's own body or another's body.
"Except for a trembling," that is, at the time of spreading out a covering, either by the touch of a wrinkle or by the bite of a *maṅgula*, there is merely a bodily trembling.
Having set that aside, there is no other act of doing with the body.
Moreover, that too occurs only with a mind accompanied by defilements (kleśa).
"There is no speech either," that is, there is no difference between false speech and true speech.
"There is only crying," that is, for one overcome by hunger and thirst, there is only crying.
Moreover, that too [occurs] only with a mind accompanied by defilements.
"*Saṅkappa*," that is, there is no difference between wrong intention (*micchāsaṅkappa*) and right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*).
"There is only humming," that is, there is only humming, only crying and laughing.
For the mind of young children tends towards past objects; those coming from hell cry, remembering the suffering of hell; those coming from the world of the gods laugh; moreover, that too occurs only with a mind accompanied by defilements.
"*Ājīva*," that is, there is no difference between wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*) and right livelihood (*sammājīva*).
"Except for the mother's breast," that is, they are called breast-thieving children; while the mother is giving milk, without drinking, they come to the side of her back at another prescribed time and drink milk.
Having abandoned so much, there is no other wrong livelihood.
He shows that even this occurs only with a mind accompanied by defilements.

mula_pali:
263. ‘‘Catūhi kho ahaṃ, thapati, dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi na ceva sampannakusalaṃ na paramakusalaṃ na uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjhaṃ, api cimaṃ daharaṃ kumāraṃ mandaṃ uttānaseyyakaṃ samadhigayha tiṭṭhati. Katamehi catūhi? Idha, thapati, na kāyena pāpakammaṃ karoti, na pāpakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, na pāpakaṃ saṅkappaṃ saṅkappeti, na pāpakaṃ ājīvaṃ ājīvati – imehi kho ahaṃ, thapati, catūhi dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi na ceva sampannakusalaṃ na paramakusalaṃ na uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjhaṃ, api cimaṃ daharaṃ kumāraṃ mandaṃ uttānaseyyakaṃ samadhigayha tiṭṭhati.

‘‘Dasahi kho ahaṃ, thapati, dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi sampannakusalaṃ paramakusalaṃ uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjhaṃ. Ime akusalā sīlā; tamahaṃ kahaṃ (sī.), tahaṃ (pī.), thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Itosamuṭṭhānā akusalā sīlā; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Idha akusalā sīlā aparisesā nirujjhanti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Evaṃ paṭipanno akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi.

kahaṃ (sī.), tahaṃ (pī.)

‘‘Ime kusalā sīlā; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Itosamuṭṭhānā kusalā sīlā; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Idha kusalā sīlā aparisesā nirujjhanti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Evaṃ paṭipanno kusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi.

‘‘Ime akusalā saṅkappā; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Itosamuṭṭhānā akusalā saṅkappā ; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Idha akusalā saṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Evaṃ paṭipanno akusalānaṃ saṅkappānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi.

‘‘Ime kusalā saṅkappā; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Itosamuṭṭhānā kusalā saṅkappā ; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Idha kusalā saṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Evaṃ paṭipanno kusalānaṃ saṅkappānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi.
mula_english:
263. “When a man possesses four qualities, carpenter, I describe him, not as accomplished in what is wholesome or perfected in what is wholesome or attained to the supreme attainment or an ascetic invincible, but as one who stands in the same category as the young tender infant lying prone.

Which four? Here he does no evil bodily actions, he utters no evil speech, he has no evil intentions, and he does not make his living by any evil livelihood. When a man possesses these four qualities, I describe him, not as accomplished…but as one who stands in the same category as the young tender infant lying prone.

“When a man possesses ten qualities, carpenter, I describe him as accomplished in what is wholesome, perfected in what is wholesome, attained to the supreme attainment, an ascetic invincible.

These are unwholesome habits; but first of all I say, it must be understood thus: ‘These are unwholesome habits,’ and thus: ‘Unwholesome habits originate from this’, and thus: ‘Unwholesome habits cease without remainder here’, and thus: ‘One practising in this way is practising the way to the cessation of unwholesome habits.’

“And I say, it must be understood thus: “These are wholesome habits’, and thus: ‘Wholesome habits originate from this,’ and thus: ‘Wholesome habits cease without remainder here’, and thus: ‘One practising in this way is practising the way to the cessation of wholesome habits.’

“And I say, it must be understood thus: ‘These are unwholesome intentions’, and thus: ‘Unwholesome intentions originate from this’, and thus: ‘Unwholesome intentions cease without remainder here’, and thus ‘One practising in this way is practising the way to the cessation of unwholesome intentions.’

“And l say, it must be understood thus: ‘These are wholesome intentions’, and thus: ‘Wholesome intentions originate from this’, and thus: ‘Wholesome intentions cease without remainder here’, and thus: ‘One practising in this way is practising the way to the cessation of wholesome intentions.’
commentary_pali:
263. Evaṃ paribbājakavādaṃ paṭikkhipitvā idāni sayaṃ sekkhabhūmiyaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapento catūhi kho ahantiādimāha. Tattha samadhigayha tiṭṭhatīti visesetvā tiṭṭhati. Nakāyena pāpa kammantiādīsu na kevalaṃ akaraṇamattameva, bhagavā pana ettha saṃvarappahānapaṭisaṅkhā paññapeti. Taṃ sandhāyevamāha. Na ceva sampannakusalantiādi pana khīṇāsavaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Idāni asekkhabhūmiyaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapento dasahi kho ahantiādimāha. Tattha tīṇi padāni nissāya dve paṭhamacatukkā ṭhapitā, ekaṃ padaṃ nissāya dve pacchimacatukkā. Ayaṃ sekkhabhūmiyaṃ mātikā.

dasahi kho aha
commentary_english:
263. Having thus refuted the doctrine of the wandering ascetics, now, establishing the matrix in the ground of the learner, he says, "By four, indeed, I..." etc.

There, "Having fully attained, he stands," thus, distinguishing, he stands.

Not.
Abstaining from evil deeds by body, etc., it is not merely non-doing alone; the Blessed One, however, here enjoins restraint, abandonment, and reflection.

Having considered that, he spoke thus.

Not even possessing wholesome qualities, etc., but this was said referring to one whose outflows are destroyed ( *khīṇāsava*).

Now, establishing the matrix in the ground of the non-learner, he says, "By ten, indeed, I..." etc.

There, relying on three words, two first tetrads are established; relying on one word, two last tetrads.

This is the matrix in the ground of the learner.

By ten, indeed, I...

mula_pali:
264. ‘‘Katame ca, thapati, akusalā sīlā? Akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ, akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ, pāpako ājīvo – ime vuccanti, thapati, akusalā sīlā.

‘‘Ime ca, thapati, akusalā sīlā kiṃsamuṭṭhānā? Samuṭṭhānampi nesaṃ vuttaṃ. ‘Cittasamuṭṭhānā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Katamaṃ cittaṃ? Cittampi hi bahuṃ anekavidhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ. Yaṃ cittaṃ sarāgaṃ sadosaṃ samohaṃ, itosamuṭṭhānā akusalā sīlā.

‘‘Ime ca, thapati, akusalā sīlā kuhiṃ aparisesā nirujjhanti? Nirodhopi nesaṃ vutto. Idha, thapati, bhikkhu kāyaduccaritaṃ pahāya kāyasucaritaṃ bhāveti, vacīduccaritaṃ pahāya vacīsucaritaṃ bhāveti, manoduccaritaṃ pahāya manosucaritaṃ bhāveti, micchājīvaṃ pahāya sammājīvena jīvitaṃ kappeti – etthete akusalā sīlā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

‘‘Kathaṃ paṭipanno, thapati, akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti? Idha, thapati, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Evaṃ paṭipanno kho, thapati, akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.
mula_english:
264. "What, O householder (thapati), are unwholesome habits (*akusalā sīlā*)? Unwholesome bodily action (*akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ*), unwholesome verbal action (*akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ*), and evil livelihood (*pāpako ājīvo*) - these are called unwholesome habits, O householder.

"And these unwholesome habits, O householder, from what do they originate? Their origin, too, has been stated.
'They should be said to originate from mind (cittasamuṭṭhānā'tissa vacanīyaṃ).'
What is that mind (*cittaṃ*)? Though mind (*cittampi*) is multiple, varied (*anekavidhaṃ*), and of different aspects (*nānappakārakaṃ*), the mind (*cittaṃ*) affected by lust (*sarāgaṃ*), by hate (*sadosaṃ*), or by delusion (*samohaṃ*), unwholesome habits (*akusalā sīlā*) originate from this.

"And where do these unwholesome habits (*akusalā sīlā*), O householder, cease without remainder (*aparisesā nirujjhanti*)? Their cessation (*nirodho*), too, has been stated.
Here, O householder, a *bhikkhu* abandons bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccaritaṃ pahāya*) and develops good bodily conduct (*kāyasucaritaṃ bhāveti*); he abandons verbal misconduct (*vacīduccaritaṃ pahāya*) and develops good verbal conduct (*vacīsucaritaṃ bhāveti*); he abandons mental misconduct (*manoduccaritaṃ pahāya*) and develops good mental conduct (*manosucaritaṃ bhāveti*); he abandons wrong livelihood (*micchājīvaṃ pahāya*) and gains a living by right livelihood (*sammājīvena jīvitaṃ kappeti*)—it is here that these unwholesome habits (*akusalā sīlā*) cease without remainder (*aparisesā nirujjhanti*).

"How, O householder, does one practicing, practice the way to the cessation (*nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti*) of unwholesome habits (*akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ*)? Here, O householder, a *bhikkhu* awakens zeal (*chandaṃ janeti*) for the non-arising (*anuppādāya*) of unarisen evil unwholesome states (*anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ*), and he makes effort (*vāyamati*), arouses energy (*vīriyaṃ ārabhati*), exerts his mind (*cittaṃ paggaṇhāti*), and strives (*padahati*). He awakens zeal (*chandaṃ janeti*) for the abandoning (*pahānāya*) of arisen evil unwholesome states (*uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ*)...He awakens zeal (*chandaṃ janeti*) for the arising (*uppādāya*) of unarisen wholesome states (*anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ*)...He awakens zeal (*chandaṃ janeti*) for the continuance (*ṭhitiyā*), non-disappearance (*asammosāya*), strengthening (*bhiyyobhāvāya*), increase (*vepullāya*), and fulfilment by development (*bhāvanāya pāripūriyā*) of arisen wholesome states (*uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ*), and he makes effort (*vāyamati*), arouses energy (*vīriyaṃ ārabhati*), exerts his mind (*cittaṃ paggaṇhāti*), and strives (*padahati*).
One so practicing (*evaṃ paṭipanno*) practices the way to the cessation (*nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti*) of unwholesome habits (*akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ*), O householder.
commentary_pali:
264. Idāni taṃ vibhajanto katame ca thapati akusalasīlātiādimāha. Tattha sarāganti aṭṭhavidhaṃ lobhasahagatacittaṃ. Sadosanti paṭighasampayuttacittadvayaṃ. Samohanti vicikicchuddhaccasahagatacittadvayampi vaṭṭati, sabbākusalacittānipi. Moho sabbākusale uppajjatīti hi vuttaṃ. Itosamuṭṭhānāti ito sarāgādicittato samuṭṭhānaṃ uppatti etesanti itosamuṭṭhānā.

Kuhinti kataraṃ ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇitvā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Ettheteti sotāpattiphale bhummaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlañhi sotāpattiphale paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā akusalasīlaṃ asesaṃ nirujjhati. Akusalasīlanti ca dussīlassetaṃ adhivacananti veditabbaṃ.

Kuhi Etthete

Akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipannoti ettha yāva sotāpattimaggā nirodhāya paṭipanno nāma hoti, phalapatte pana te nirodhitā nāma honti.

Akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno
commentary_english:
264. Now, dividing that, he says beginning with, "Which, Thapati, are unwholesome moralities ( *akusalasīlā*)?"

There, *sarāga* means the eight types of mind accompanied by greed ( *lobha*).

*Sadosa* means the two types of mind associated with aversion (*paṭigha*).

*Samoha* means the two types of mind accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā*) and excitement (*uddhacca*), and also all unwholesome minds.

For it was said that delusion (*moha*) arises in all unwholesome [states].

*Itosamuṭṭhānā* means their arising (*samuṭṭhānaṃ*) and origination (*uppatti*) is from this, from minds such as greed (*sarāga*) etc.; therefore, it is *itosamuṭṭhānā*.

What place (*ṭhānaṃ*) having reached, do they cease (*nirujjhanti*) without remainder (*aparisesā*)?

*Etthete* means the earth (*bhummaṃ*) at the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphale*).

For morality (*sīla*) consisting of the *pātimokkha-saṃvara* is fully complete (*paripuṇṇaṃ*) at the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphale*); having attained that place (*ṭhānaṃ*), unwholesome morality (*akusalasīlaṃ*) ceases (*nirujjhhati*) entirely (*asesaṃ*).

And *akusalasīla* should be understood as an appellation (*adhivacanaṃ*) for bad morality (*dussīlassa*).

Where? In this?

"*Akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno* (one who has undertaken to cease unwholesome moralities)" means here, up to the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimaggā*), he is said to be "*nirodhāya paṭipanno* (one who has undertaken to cease)," but when the fruit (*phalapatte*) is attained, they are said to be "*nirodhitā* (ceased)."

*Akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno* (one who has undertaken to cease unwholesome moralities)

mula_pali:
265. ‘‘Katame ca, thapati, kusalā sīlā? Kusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ, kusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ, ājīvaparisuddhampi kho ahaṃ, thapati, sīlasmiṃ vadāmi. Ime vuccanti, thapati, kusalā sīlā.

‘‘Ime ca, thapati, kusalā sīlā kiṃsamuṭṭhānā? Samuṭṭhānampi nesaṃ vuttaṃ. ‘Cittasamuṭṭhānā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Katamaṃ cittaṃ? Cittampi hi bahuṃ anekavidhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ. Yaṃ cittaṃ vītarāgaṃ vītadosaṃ vītamohaṃ, itosamuṭṭhānā kusalā sīlā.

‘‘Ime ca, thapati, kusalā sīlā kuhiṃ aparisesā nirujjhanti? Nirodhopi nesaṃ vutto. Idha, thapati, bhikkhu sīlavā hoti no ca sīlamayo, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; yatthassa te kusalā sīlā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

‘‘Kathaṃ paṭipanno ca, thapati, kusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti? Idha, thapati, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati ; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya…pe… anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya…pe… uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Evaṃ paṭipanno kho, thapati, kusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.
mula_english:
265. "And what, householder, are wholesome habits? Wholesome bodily action (kuśalaṃ kāyakammaṃ), wholesome verbal action (kuśalaṃ vacīkammaṃ), and I say, householder, purity of livelihood is also included in habits. These are called wholesome habits.

"And what do these wholesome habits originate from? Their origin has been stated: ‘They should be said to originate from mind (cittasamuṭṭhānā’tissa vacanīyaṃ).' What is that mind? Though mind is multiple, varied, and of different aspects, there is mind unaffected by lust, by hate, or by delusion. Wholesome habits originate from this.

"And where do these wholesome habits cease without remainder? Their cessation has been stated: Here a bhikkhu is virtuous, but he does not identify with his virtue, and he understands as it actually is that deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom where these wholesome habits cease without remainder.

"And how practising does he practise the way to the cessation of wholesome habits? Here, householder, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, stirs up energy, exerts his mind and strives to prevent the arising of unarisen evil unwholesome mental states; he generates desire... for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome mental states... he generates desire... for the production of unarisen wholesome mental states... he generates desire, makes an effort, stirs up energy, exerts his mind and strives to maintain wholesome mental states that have arisen, not to let them fade, to increase them, to expand them, and to bring them to fulfilment by development. One so practising, householder, practises the way to the cessation of wholesome habits.
commentary_pali:
265.Vītarāgantiādīhi aṭṭhavidhaṃ kāmāvacarakusalacittameva vuttaṃ. Etena hi kusalasīlaṃ samuṭṭhāti.

Sīlavā hotīti sīlasampanno hoti guṇasampanno ca. No ca sīlamayoti alamettāvatā, natthi ito kiñci uttari karaṇīyanti evaṃ sīlamayo na hoti. Yatthassa teti arahattaphale bhummaṃ. Arahattaphalañhi patvā akusalasīlaṃ asesaṃ nirujjhati.

Sīlavā hotī No ca sīlamayo Yatthassa te

Nirodhāya paṭipannoti ettha yāva arahattamaggā nirodhāya paṭipanno nāma hoti, phalapatte pana te nirodhitā nāma honti.

Nirodhāya paṭipanno
commentary_english:
265. *Vītarāga*- and so forth, aṭṭhavidhaṃ, is said to be only wholesome mind pertaining to the desire realm (kāmāvacara-kusala-citta).
Through this, wholesome conduct (kusala-śīla) arises.

*Sīlavā hotī* means he is accomplished in morality (śīla-sampanna) and accomplished in qualities (guṇa-sampanna).
*No ca sīlamayo* means enough with just that much; there is nothing further to do; thus, he is not merely composed of morality (śīlamayo na hoti).
*Yatthassa te* means the state resting on the fruit of Arhatship (arahattaphale bhummaṃ).
Having attained the fruit of Arhatship (arahattaphalañhi patvā), unwholesome conduct (akusala-śīla) ceases entirely (asesaṃ nirujjhati).

*Sīlavā hotī*, *no ca sīlamayo*, *yatthassa te*
*Nirodhāya paṭipanno* means here, up to the path of Arhatship, he is called one who has entered upon cessation (nirodhāya paṭipanno nāma hoti), but upon attaining the fruit (phalapatte pana te), they are called those who have brought about cessation (nirodhitā nāma honti).

*Nirodhāya paṭipanno*

mula_pali:
266. ‘‘Katame ca, thapati, akusalā saṅkappā? Kāmasaṅkappo, byāpādasaṅkappo, vihiṃsāsaṅkappo – ime vuccanti, thapati, akusalā saṅkappā.

‘‘Ime ca, thapati, akusalā saṅkappā kiṃsamuṭṭhānā? Samuṭṭhānampi nesaṃ vuttaṃ. ‘Saññāsamuṭṭhānā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Katamā saññā? Saññāpi hi bahū anekavidhā nānappakārakā. Kāmasaññā, byāpādasaññā, vihiṃsāsaññā – itosamuṭṭhānā akusalā saṅkappā.

‘‘Ime ca, thapati, akusalā saṅkappā kuhiṃ aparisesā nirujjhanti? Nirodhopi nesaṃ vutto. Idha, thapati, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati; etthete akusalā saṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

‘‘Kathaṃ paṭipanno ca, thapati, akusalānaṃ saṅkappānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti? Idha, thapati, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya…pe… anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya…pe… uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Evaṃ paṭipanno kho, thapati, akusalānaṃ saṅkappānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.
mula_english:
266. “And what, householder, are unwholesome intentions ( *akusalā saṅkappā* )? The intention of sensual desire ( *kāmasaṅkappo* ), the intention of ill will ( *byāpādasaṅkappo* ), and the intention of cruelty ( *vihiṃsāsaṅkappo* ) - these are called, householder, unwholesome intentions.

“And from what do these unwholesome intentions originate? Their origin has also been stated. ‘They originate from perception ( *saññāsamuṭṭhānā* ),’ should be the reply. What perception? Though perception (*saññā*) is multiple, varied, and of different aspects, there is perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*), perception of ill will (*byāpādasaññā*), and perception of cruelty (*vihiṃsāsaññā*) - unwholesome intentions originate from this.

“And where do these unwholesome intentions cease without remainder? Their cessation has also been stated. Here, householder, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first *jhāna* (meditative absorption); it is here that these unwholesome intentions cease without remainder.

“And how, householder, does one practicing practise the way to the cessation of unwholesome intentions? Here, householder, a *bhikkhu* (monk) generates desire ( *chandaṃ janeti* ), endeavors ( *vāyamati* ), activates persistence ( *vīriyaṃ ārabhati* ), upholds & exerts his intent (*cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati*) for the sake of the non-arising of evil, unskillful qualities ( *pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ* ) that have not yet arisen... for the sake of the abandoning of evil, unskillful qualities that have arisen... for the sake of the arising of skillful qualities ( *kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ* ) that have not yet arisen... for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, plenitude, development, & culmination of skillful qualities that have arisen. One so practising, householder, practises the way to the cessation of unwholesome intentions.
commentary_pali:
266.Kāmasaññādīsu kāmasaññā aṭṭhalobhasahagatacittasahajātā, itarā dve domanassasahagatacittadvayena sahajātā.

Paṭhamaṃjhānanti anāgāmiphalapaṭhamajjhānaṃ. Ettheteti anāgāmiphale bhummaṃ. Anāgāmiphalañhi patvā akusalasaṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

Paṭhamaṃ jhāna Etthete

Nirodhāya paṭipannoti ettha yāva anāgāmimaggā nirodhāya paṭipanno nāma hoti, phalapatte pana te nirodhitā nāma honti. Nekkhammasaññādayo hi tissopi aṭṭhakāmāvacarakusalasahajātasaññāva.

Nirodhāya paṭipanno
commentary_english:
266. Among the *kāmasaññā*s (perceptions of sense-desires), the *kāmasaññā* arises together with eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed ( *aṭṭhalobhasahagatacitta*), while the other two arise together with two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure (*domanassasahagatacitta*).

*paṭhamaṃ jhāna* means the first *jhāna* (meditative absorption) associated with the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).

*etthete* means in the state of the fruit of non-returning. For, having attained the fruit of non-returning, unwholesome thoughts are completely stopped without remainder.

*nirodhāya paṭipanno*: Here, "one who has entered upon the way to cessation" (*nirodhāya paṭipanno*) is so called until the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*); however, upon attaining the fruit, they are called "those who have ceased" (*nirodhitā*).

Indeed, the three perceptions beginning with the perception of renunciation (*nekkhammasaññā*) are also perceptions that arise together with eight wholesome consciousnesses pertaining to the sense-sphere (*aṭṭhakāmāvacarakusalasahajātasaññā*).

mula_pali:
267. ‘‘Katame ca, thapati, kusalā saṅkappā? Nekkhammasaṅkappo, abyāpādasaṅkappo, avihiṃsāsaṅkappo – ime vuccanti, thapati, kusalā saṅkappā.

‘‘Ime ca, thapati, kusalā saṅkappā kiṃsamuṭṭhānā? Samuṭṭhānampi nesaṃ vuttaṃ. ‘Saññāsamuṭṭhānā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Katamā saññā? Saññāpi hi bahū anekavidhā nānappakārakā. Nekkhammasaññā, abyāpādasaññā, avihiṃsāsaññā – itosamuṭṭhānā kusalā saṅkappā.

‘‘Ime ca, thapati, kusalā saṅkappā kuhiṃ aparisesā nirujjhanti? Nirodhopi nesaṃ vutto. Idha, thapati, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati; etthete kusalā saṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

‘‘Kathaṃ paṭipanno ca, thapati, kusalānaṃ saṅkappānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti? Idha, thapati, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya…pe… anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya…pe… uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Evaṃ paṭipanno kho, thapati, kusalānaṃ saṅkappānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.
mula_english:
267. “And what, householder, are wholesome intentions ( *kusalā saṅkappā* )? They are the intention of renunciation ( *nekkhammasaṅkappo* ), the intention of non-ill will ( *abyāpādasaṅkappo* ), and the intention of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsāsaṅkappo*) . These, householder, are called wholesome intentions.

“And what is the origin of these wholesome intentions, householder? Their origin, too, has been stated.
‘They should be said to originate from perception ( *saññāsamuṭṭhānā’tissa vacanīyaṃ* ).’
What is perception ( *saññā* )? Perception is varied, of many kinds, and diverse.
There is perception of renunciation ( *nekkhammasaññā* ), perception of non-ill will ( *abyāpādasaññā* ), and perception of non-cruelty ( *avihiṃsāsaññā* ). Wholesome intentions originate from this.

“And where do these wholesome intentions cease without remainder, householder? Their cessation, too, has been stated.
Here, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought ( *vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā* )…a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second *jhāna* ( *dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati* ); it is here that these wholesome intentions cease without remainder.

“And how, householder, does one practice the way to the cessation of wholesome intentions? Here, a bhikkhu awakens zeal (*chandaṃ janeti*) for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states (*anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya*), and he makes effort ( *vāyamati* ), arouses energy ( *vīriyaṃ ārabhati* ), exerts his mind ( *cittaṃ paggaṇhāti* ), and strives ( *padahati* ); for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states (*uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya*)…for the arising of unarisen wholesome states (*anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya*)…for the continuance, non-disappearance, strengthening, increase, and fulfilment by development of arisen wholesome states (*uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā*), he awakens zeal, makes effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives.
One so practising, householder, practises the way to the cessation of wholesome intentions.
commentary_pali:
267.Ettheteti arahattaphale bhummaṃ. Dutiyajjhānikaṃ arahattaphalañhi pāpuṇitvā kusalasaṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Nirodhāya paṭipannoti ettha yāva arahattamaggā nirodhāya paṭipanno nāma hoti, phalapatte pana te nirodhitā nāma honti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Samaṇamuṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
"Here, there," means grounded in the fruit of Arahatship (arhattaphala).
Indeed, having attained the fruit of Arahatship in the second jhana, wholesome thoughts are completely stopped without remainder.
"Entered upon cessation" means here, up to the path of Arahatship, he is called "entered upon cessation"; but when the fruit is attained, they are called "those who have caused cessation."
All the rest is clear.

The Samaṇamuṇḍikasutta Commentary in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary to the Middle Length Discourses, is finished.

mula_pali:
268. ‘‘Katamehi cāhaṃ, thapati, dasahi dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi sampannakusalaṃ paramakusalaṃ uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjhaṃ? Idha, thapati, bhikkhu asekhāya sammādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāsaṅkappena samannāgato hoti, asekhāya sammāvācāya samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammākammantena samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāājīvena samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāvāyāmena samannāgato hoti, asekhāya sammāsatiyā samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāsamādhinā samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāñāṇena samannāgato hoti, asekhāya sammāvimuttiyā samannāgato hoti – imehi kho ahaṃ, thapati, dasahi dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi sampannakusalaṃ paramakusalaṃ uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjha’’nti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano pañcakaṅgo thapati bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

Samaṇamuṇḍikasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.
mula_english:
268. “And furthermore, carpenter, by possessing which ten qualities do I describe an individual as accomplished in the good, supremely good, as having attained the highest attainment, an invincible *samaṇa*? Here, carpenter, a *bhikkhu* possesses the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*), the right intention of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyaksaṃkalpa*), the right speech of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagvāc*), the right action of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyakkarmānta*), the right livelihood of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagājīva*), the right effort of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagvyāyāma*), the right mindfulness of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyaksmṛti*), the right concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyaksamādhi*), the right knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagjñāna*), and the right deliverance of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagvimukti*). It is by possessing these ten qualities that I describe an individual as accomplished in the good, supremely good, as having attained the highest attainment, an invincible *samaṇa*.”

Thus spoke the Blessed One. The carpenter Pañcakaṅga was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

The Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta, the eighth, is finished.

mula_pali:
269. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Tena kho pana samayena sakuludāyī paribbājako moranivāpe paribbājakārāme paṭivasati mahatiyā paribbājakaparisāya saddhiṃ. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Atha kho bhagavato etadahosi – ‘‘atippago kho tāva rājagahe piṇḍāya carituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yena moranivāpo paribbājakārāmo yena sakuludāyī paribbājako tenupasaṅkameyya’’nti. Atha kho bhagavā yena moranivāpo paribbājakārāmo tenupasaṅkami.

Tena kho pana samayena sakuludāyī paribbājako mahatiyā paribbājakaparisāya saddhiṃ nisinno hoti unnādiniyā uccāsaddamahāsaddāya anekavihitaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathentiyā, seyyathidaṃ – rājakathaṃ corakathaṃ mahāmattakathaṃ senākathaṃ bhayakathaṃ yuddhakathaṃ annakathaṃ pānakathaṃ vatthakathaṃ sayanakathaṃ mālākathaṃ gandhakathaṃ ñātikathaṃ yānakathaṃ gāmakathaṃ nigamakathaṃ nagarakathaṃ janapadakathaṃ itthikathaṃ sūrakathaṃ visikhākathaṃ kumbhaṭṭhānakathaṃ pubbapetakathaṃ nānattakathaṃ lokakkhāyikaṃ samuddakkhāyikaṃ itibhavābhavakathaṃ iti vā. Addasā kho sakuludāyī paribbājako bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna sakaṃ parisaṃ saṇṭhāpesi – ‘‘appasaddā bhonto hontu, mā bhonto saddamakattha. Ayaṃ samaṇo gotamo āgacchati; appasaddakāmo kho pana so āyasmā appasaddassa vaṇṇavādī. Appeva nāma appasaddaṃ parisaṃ viditvā upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññeyyā’’ti. Atha kho te paribbājakā tuṇhī ahesuṃ .
mula_english:
269. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary ( *kalandakanivāpe*).

Now on that occasion the wanderer Sakuludāyin was staying in the Peacocks’ Sanctuary, the wanderers’ park (*moranivāpe paribbājakārāme*), with a large assembly of wanderers.

Then, when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe (*pattacīvaramādāya*), went into Rajagaha for alms.

Then the thought occurred to the Blessed One: “It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha. Suppose I went to the wanderer Sakuludāyin in the Peacocks’ Sanctuary, the wanderers’ park (*moranivāpo paribbājakārāmo*).”

Then the Blessed One went to the Peacocks’ Sanctuary, the wanderers’ park (*moranivāpo paribbājakārāmo*).

At that time, the wanderer Sakuludāyin was sitting with a large company of wanderers, making a great noise and commotion, engaged in various kinds of irrelevant talk, such as talk about kings, robbers, and ministers of state; armies, dangers, and wars; food, drink, garments, and lodgings; garlands and scents; relatives, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; women and heroes; street talk; talk about those who have passed away; miscellaneous talk; stories about the world and the sea; and talk about existence and non-existence.

Then the wanderer Sakuludāyin saw the Blessed One coming in the distance. Seeing him, he quieted his own assembly thus: “Sirs, be quiet; sirs, make no noise. Here comes the *śramaṇa* Gotama; that venerable one likes quiet and praises quiet. Maybe, if he perceives our group as quiet, he will consider it worth his while to come our way.”

Then those wanderers were silent.

mula_pali: 270. Atha kho bhagavā yena sakuludāyī paribbājako tenupasaṅkami. Atha kho sakuludāyī paribbājako bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘etu kho, bhante, bhagavā. Svāgataṃ, bhante, bhagavato. Cirassaṃ kho, bhante, bhagavā imaṃ pariyāyamakāsi yadidaṃ idhāgamanāya. Nisīdatu, bhante, bhagavā; idamāsanaṃ paññatta’’nti. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Sakuludāyīpi kho paribbājako aññataraṃ nīcaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho sakuludāyiṃ paribbājakaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – ‘‘kāya nuttha, udāyi, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā, kā ca pana vo antarākathā vippakatā’’ti? ‘‘Tiṭṭhatesā, bhante, kathā yāya mayaṃ etarahi kathāya sannisinnā. Nesā, bhante, kathā bhagavato dullabhā bhavissati pacchāpi savanāya. Yadāhaṃ, bhante, imaṃ parisaṃ anupasaṅkanto homi athāyaṃ parisā anekavihitaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathentī nisinnā hoti; yadā ca kho ahaṃ, bhante, imaṃ parisaṃ upasaṅkanto homi athāyaṃ parisā mamaññeva mukhaṃ ullokentī nisinnā hoti – ‘yaṃ no samaṇo udāyī dhammaṃ bhāsissati taṃ taṃ no (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) sossāmā’ti; yadā pana , bhante, bhagavā imaṃ parisaṃ upasaṅkanto hoti athāhañceva ayañca parisā bhagavato mukhaṃ ullokentā olokentī (syā. kaṃ. ka.) nisinnā homa – ‘yaṃ no bhagavā dhammaṃ bhāsissati taṃ sossāmā’’’ti.
mula_english:
Then the Blessed One went to the wanderer Sakuludayin.

Then the wanderer Sakuludayin said this to the Blessed One: “Come, Blessed One, venerable sir!

Welcome, venerable sir, to the Blessed One!

It’s been a long time since the Blessed One has gone out of his way to come here.

Be seated, Lord; this seat is ready.”

The Blessed One sat down on the seat made ready.

The wanderer Sakuludayin took a low seat and sat down at one side.

As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the wanderer Sakuludayin: “Udayin, what were you gathered here talking about, and what discussion was interrupted?” “Let that matter rest, venerable sir, that we were gathered here talking about.

It won’t be difficult for the Blessed One to hear about that later.

Venerable sir, when I do not come to this assembly, then it sits talking many kinds of pointless talk. But when I have come to this assembly, then it sits looking up to me, thinking: ‘Let us hear the *dharma* that the recluse Udayin expounds.’ However, when the Blessed One comes, then both I and this assembly sit looking up to the Blessed One, thinking: ‘Let us hear the *dharma* that the Blessed One expounds.’”
commentary_pali: 270.Evaṃme sutanti cūḷasakuludāyisuttaṃ. Tattha yadā pana, bhante, bhagavāti idaṃ paribbājako dhammakathaṃ sotukāmo bhagavato dhammadesanāya sālayabhāvaṃ dassento āha.
commentary_english:
270.
Thus, the *Cūḷasakuludāyisutta*, "[This] I have heard."
There, the wanderer, wishing to hear a talk on the *dharma*, showing reverence for the *Bhagavat's* teaching of the *dharma*, said, "When, venerable sir, the *Bhagavat*..."

mula_pali:
271. ‘‘Tenahudāyi, taṃyevettha paṭibhātu yathā maṃ paṭibhāseyyā’’si. ‘‘Purimāni , bhante, divasāni purimatarāni sabbaññū sabbadassāvī aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānamāno ‘carato ca me tiṭṭhato ca suttassa ca jāgarassa ca satataṃ samitaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhita’nti. So mayā paccupaṭṭhita’’nti mayā (?) pubbantaṃ ārabbha pañhaṃ puṭṭho samāno aññenaññaṃ paṭicari, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmesi, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātvākāsi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃyeva ārabbha sati udapādi – ‘aho nūna bhagavā, aho nūna sugato! Yo imesaṃ dhammānaṃ sukusalo’’’ti. ‘‘Ko pana so, udāyi, sabbaññū sabbadassāvī aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānamāno ‘carato ca me tiṭṭhato ca suttassa ca jāgarassa ca satataṃ samitaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhita’nti, yo tayā pubbantaṃ ārabbha pañhaṃ puṭṭho samāno aññenaññaṃ paṭicari, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmesi kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātvākāsī’’ti? ‘Nigaṇṭho, bhante, nāṭaputto’ti.

‘‘Yo kho, udāyi, anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussareyya, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussareyya, so vā maṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbha pañhaṃ puccheyya, taṃ vāhaṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbha pañhaṃ puccheyyaṃ; so vā me pubbantaṃ ārabbha pañhassa veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ ārādheyya, tassa vāhaṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbha pañhassa veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ ārādheyyaṃ.

‘‘Yo so (sī. pī.) kho, udāyi, dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passeyya cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajāneyya, so vā maṃ aparantaṃ ārabbha pañhaṃ puccheyya, taṃ vāhaṃ aparantaṃ ārabbha pañhaṃ puccheyyaṃ; so vā me aparantaṃ ārabbha pañhassa veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ ārādheyya, tassa vāhaṃ aparantaṃ ārabbha pañhassa veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ ārādheyyaṃ.

so (sī. pī.)

‘‘Api ca, udāyi, tiṭṭhatu pubbanto, tiṭṭhatu aparanto. Dhammaṃ te desessāmi – imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati; imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī’’ti.

‘‘Ahañhi, bhante, yāvatakampi me iminā attabhāvena paccanubhūtaṃ tampi nappahomi sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anussarituṃ, kuto panāhaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarissāmi, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarissāmi, seyyathāpi bhagavā? Ahañhi, bhante, etarahi paṃsupisācakampi na passāmi, kuto panāhaṃ dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passissāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānissāmi, seyyathāpi bhagavā? Yaṃ pana maṃ, bhante, bhagavā evamāha – ‘api ca, udāyi, tiṭṭhatu pubbanto, tiṭṭhatu aparanto; dhammaṃ te desessāmi – imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati; imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī’ti tañca pana me bhiyyosomattāya na pakkhāyati. Appeva nāmāhaṃ, bhante, sake ācariyake bhagavato cittaṃ ārādheyyaṃ pañhassa veyyākaraṇenā’’ti.
mula_english:
271. “Then, Udayin, suggest something that I should speak about.”

“Venerable sir, in recent days there was one claiming to be omniscient and all-seeing, to have complete knowledge and vision thus: ‘Whether I am walking or standing or sleeping or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and uninterruptedly present to me.’ When I asked him a question about the past (*pūrvāntaṃ*), he prevaricated, led the talk aside, and showed anger, hate, and bitterness. Then the memory of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) arose within me: ‘Ah, the Blessed One! Ah, the One Well-Gone (*sugata*)—who surely is well-skilled in these matters.’“

“But, Udayin, who was it that claimed to be omniscient and all-seeing…yet when asked a question by you about the past (*pūrvāntaṃ*), prevaricated, led the talk aside, and showed anger, hate, and bitterness?”

‘Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, venerable sir.’

“Udayin, if someone should recollect his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births…thus, with their aspects and particulars, should he recollect his manifold past lives, then either he might ask me a question about the past (*pūrvāntaṃ*) or I might ask him a question about the past (*pūrvāntaṃ*), and he might satisfy my mind with his answer to my question or I might satisfy his mind with my answer to his question.

“Udayin, if someone with the divine eye (*divyena cakṣunā*), which is purified and surpasses the human, should see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate… and understand how beings pass on according to their actions (*yathākammūpage*), then either he might ask me a question about the future (*aparantam*) or I might ask him a question about the future (*aparantam*), and he might satisfy my mind with his answer to my question or I might satisfy his mind with my answer to his question.

“But let be the past (*pūrvāntaṃ*), Udayin, let be the future (*aparantam*). I shall teach you the Dharma (*dhamma*): When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.”

“Venerable sir, I am not even able to recollect in detail what I have experienced in this present existence (*attabhāva*), how then could I recollect manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births…thus with their aspects and particulars I recollect my manifold past lives, like the Blessed One (*bhagavat*)? Venerable sir, I cannot even see a dust-demon now, how then could I see with the divine eye (*divyena cakkhunā*), which is purified and surpasses the human, beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate… and understand how beings pass on according to their actions (*yathākammūpage*), like the Blessed One (*bhagavat*)? But, venerable sir, when the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) told me: ‘But let be the past (*pūrvāntaṃ*), Udayin, let be the future (*aparantam*). I shall teach you the Dharma (*dhamma*): When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases’ - that is even more unclear to me. Perhaps, venerable sir, I might satisfy the Blessed One’s (*bhagavato*) mind by answering a question about our own teachers’ doctrine.”
commentary_pali:
271.Taṃyevettha paṭibhātūti sace dhammaṃ sotukāmo, tuyhevettha eko pañho ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ upaṭṭhātu. Yathā maṃ paṭibhāseyyāti yena kāraṇena mama dhammadesanā upaṭṭhaheyya, etena hi kāraṇena kathāya samuṭṭhitāya sukhaṃ dhammaṃ desetunti dīpeti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhanteti so kira taṃ disvā – ‘‘sace bhagavā idha abhavissā, ayametassa bhāsitassa atthoti dīpasahassaṃ viya ujjalāpetvā ajja me pākaṭaṃ akarissā’’ti dasabalaṃyeva anussari. Tasmā tassa mayhaṃ, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha aho nūnāti anussaraṇatthe nipātadvayaṃ. Tena tassa bhagavantaṃ anussarantassa etadahosi ‘‘aho nūna bhagavā aho nūna sugato’’ti. Yo imesanti yo imesaṃ dhammānaṃ. Sukusaloti suṭṭhu kusalo nipuṇo cheko. So bhagavā aho nūna katheyya, so sugato aho nūna katheyya, tassa hi bhagavato pubbenivāsañāṇassa anekāni kappakoṭisahassāni ekaṅgaṇāni pākaṭānīti, ayamettha adhippāyo.

Tassa vāhaṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbhāti yo hi lābhī hoti, so ‘‘pubbe tvaṃ khattiyo ahosi, brāhmaṇo ahosī’’ti vutte jānanto sakkaccaṃ sussūsati. Alābhī pana – ‘‘evaṃ bhavissati evaṃ bhavissatī’’ti sīsakampamettameva dasseti. Tasmā evamāha – ‘‘tassa vāhaṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbha pañhassa veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ ārādheyya’’nti.

Tassa vāhaṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbhā

So vā maṃ aparantanti dibbacakkhulābhino hi anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ ijjhati, tasmā evamāha. Itaraṃ pubbe vuttanayameva.

So vā maṃ aparanta

Dhammaṃte desessāmīti ayaṃ kira atīte desiyamānepi na bujjhissati, anāgate desiyamānepi na bujjhissati. Athassa bhagavā saṇhasukhumaṃ paccayākāraṃ desetukāmo evamāha. Kiṃ pana taṃ bujjhissatīti? Etaṃ pageva na bujjhissati, anāgate panassa vāsanāya paccayo bhavissatīti disvā bhagavā evamāha.

Dhammaṃ te desessāmī

Paṃsupisācakanti asuciṭṭhāne nibbattapisācaṃ. So hi ekaṃ mūlaṃ gahetvā adissamānakāyo hoti. Tatridaṃ vatthu – ekā kira yakkhinī dve dārake thūpārāmadvāre nisīdāpetvā āhārapariyesanatthaṃ nagaraṃ gatā. Dārakā ekaṃ piṇḍapātikattheraṃ disvā āhaṃsu, – ‘‘bhante, amhākaṃ mātā anto nagaraṃ paviṭṭhā, tassā vadeyyātha ‘yaṃ vā taṃ vā laddhakaṃ, gahetvā sīghaṃ gaccha, dārakā te jighacchitaṃ sandhāretuṃ na sakkontī’’’ti. Tamahaṃ kathaṃ passissāmīti? Idaṃ, bhante, gaṇhathāti ekaṃ mūlakhaṇḍaṃ adaṃsu. Therassa anekāni yakkhasahassāni paññāyiṃsu, so dārakehi dinnasaññāṇena taṃ yakkhiniṃ addasa virūpaṃ bībhacchaṃ kevalaṃ vīthiyaṃ gabbhamalaṃ paccāsīsamānaṃ. Disvā tamatthaṃ kathesi . Kathaṃ maṃ tvaṃ passasīti vutte mūlakhaṇḍaṃ dassesi, sā acchinditvā gaṇhi. Evaṃ paṃsupisācakā ekaṃ mūlaṃ gahetvā adissamānakāyā honti. Taṃ sandhāyesa ‘‘paṃsupisācakampi na passāmī’’ti āha. Na pakkhāyatīti na dissati na upaṭṭhāti.

Paṃsupisācaka Na pakkhāyatī
commentary_english:
271. “*Taṃyevettha paṭibhātū*ti”: If you are desirous of hearing the Dharma, a single question and a single cause should arise for you here.

“*Yathā maṃ paṭibhāseyyā*ti”: The explanation shows that he teaches the Dharma happily, so that a teaching of the Dharma might arise for me through whatever cause, by that cause, with the arising of speech.

“*Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante*ti”: It seems that he, having seen that, recalling only the one with the ten powers, thought, "If the Blessed One were here, he would have made this meaning of the spoken word clear to me today by illuminating it like a thousand lamps."

Therefore, he said, "*Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante*ti," and so forth.

There, "*Aho nūnā*ti" is a pair of particles in the sense of recollection.

By that, to him recollecting the Blessed One, it occurred, "Oh, surely the Blessed One, oh, surely the Well-gone One!"

"*Yo imesa*nti": That is, of these *dharmas*.

"*Sukusalo*ti": Very skillful, expert, clever.

That Blessed One, oh, surely he would speak; that Well-gone One, oh, surely he would speak. For the Blessed One’s gnosis of former abodes, many hundreds of thousands of eons, are manifestly single-grounded. This is the meaning here.

"*Tassa vāhaṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbhā*ti": For indeed, one who is a gainer respectfully listens, knowing that he was a *kṣatriya* in the past, that he was a *brāhmaṇa*.

But one who is not a gainer only shows a mere shaking of the head, saying, "It will be thus, it will be thus."

Therefore, he said thus: "Having begun with the former end for him, may I please his mind with an explanation of the question."

*Tassa vāhaṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbhā*.

"*So vā maṃ aparanta*nti": For indeed, to one possessing the divine eye, knowledge of the future succeeds; therefore, he said thus.

The other is just as was said before.

*So vā maṃ aparanta* *dhammaṃ* *te desessāmī*ti: It seems that this one will not understand even when taught in the past, nor will he understand when taught in the future.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to teach him the causal mode that is gentle and subtle, said thus.

What then will he understand? He will not understand this even today, but the Blessed One, having seen that in the future a cause for his disposition will come to be, said thus.

*Dhammaṃ* *te desessāmī* *paṃsupisācaka*nti: A goblin born in an impure place.

For he, having taken a root, has an invisible body.

There, this is the story: A certain *yakṣiṇī*, having made two children sit at the gate of the *thūpārāma*, went into the city to seek food.

The children, having seen a certain *piṇḍapātika* *tthera*, said, "Venerable sir, our mother has entered into the city. You should say to her, 'Having taken whatever gain there is, go quickly, for the children are not able to endure their hunger.'"

"How will I see her?" "Venerable sir, take this!" They gave him a piece of root.

Thousands of *yakṣas* appeared to the *tthera*. He saw that *yakṣiṇī* with the sign given by the children, deformed, repulsive, desiring only the filth of the womb in the street.

Having seen that meaning, he told it.

When she said, "How do you see me?", he showed her the piece of root. She snatched it away and took it.

Thus, the *paṃsupisācakas*, having taken a root, have invisible bodies.

With reference to that, he said, "I do not see even a *paṃsupisācaka*."

*Na pakkhāyatī*ti: He is not seen, he does not appear.

*Paṃsupisācaka* *na pakkhāyatī*.

mula_pali:
272. ‘‘Kinti pana te, udāyi, sake ācariyake hotī’’ti? ‘‘Amhākaṃ, bhante, sake ācariyake evaṃ hoti – ‘ayaṃ paramo vaṇṇo, ayaṃ paramo vaṇṇo’’’ti.

‘‘Yaṃ pana te etaṃ, udāyi, sake ācariyake evaṃ hoti – ‘ayaṃ paramo vaṇṇo, ayaṃ paramo vaṇṇo’ti, katamo so paramo vaṇṇo’’ti? ‘‘Yasmā, bhante, vaṇṇā añño vaṇṇo uttaritaro vā paṇītataro vā natthi so paramo vaṇṇo’’ti.

‘‘Katamo pana so paramo vaṇṇo yasmā vaṇṇā añño vaṇṇo uttaritaro vā paṇītataro vā natthī’’ti? ‘‘Yasmā , bhante, vaṇṇā añño vaṇṇo uttaritaro vā paṇītataro vā natthi so paramo vaṇṇo’’ti.

‘‘Dīghāpi kho te esā, udāyi, phareyya – ‘yasmā, bhante, vaṇṇā añño vaṇṇo uttaritaro vā paṇītataro vā natthi so paramo vaṇṇo’ti vadesi, tañca vaṇṇaṃ na paññapesi. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, puriso evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ yā imasmiṃ janapade janapadakalyāṇī taṃ icchāmi, taṃ kāmemī’ti. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ambho purisa, yaṃ tvaṃ janapadakalyāṇiṃ icchasi kāmesi, jānāsi taṃ janapadakalyāṇiṃ – khattiyī vā brāhmaṇī vā vessī vā suddī vā’’ti? Iti puṭṭho ‘no’ti vadeyya. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ambho purisa, yaṃ tvaṃ janapadakalyāṇiṃ icchasi kāmesi, jānāsi taṃ janapadakalyāṇiṃ – evaṃnāmā evaṃgottāti vāti…pe… dīghā vā rassā vā majjhimā vā kāḷī vā sāmā vā maṅguracchavī vāti… amukasmiṃ gāme vā nigame vā nagare vā’ti? Iti puṭṭho ‘no’ti vadeyya. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ambho purisa, yaṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi, taṃ tvaṃ icchasi kāmesī’’’ti? Iti puṭṭho ‘āmā’ti vadeyya.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi – nanu evaṃ sante, tassa purisassa appāṭihīrakataṃ bhāsitaṃ sampajjatī’’ti? ‘‘Addhā kho, bhante, evaṃ sante tassa purisassa appāṭihīrakataṃ bhāsitaṃ sampajjatī’’ti.

‘‘Evameva kho tvaṃ, udāyi, ‘yasmā, bhante, vaṇṇā añño vaṇṇo uttaritaro vā paṇītataro vā natthi so paramo vaṇṇo’ti vadesi, tañca vaṇṇaṃ na paññapesī’’ti.

‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhante, maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato paṇḍukambale nikkhitto bhāsate ca tapate ca virocati ca, evaṃ vaṇṇo attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā’’ti.
mula_english:
272. "What is it like with your teacher, Udayin?" "Venerable sir, with our teacher it is like this: 'This is the supreme splendour, this is the supreme splendour.'"

"But what is this, Udayin? With your teacher it is like this: 'This is the supreme splendour, this is the supreme splendour.' Which is that supreme splendour?" "Venerable sir, that splendour is the supreme splendour which is unsurpassed by any other splendour higher or more sublime."

"But what is that supreme splendour which is unsurpassed by any other splendour higher or more sublime?" "Venerable sir, that splendour is the supreme splendour which is unsurpassed by any other splendour higher or more sublime."

"Udayin, you might continue for a long time in this way. You say: 'Venerable sir, that splendour is the perfect splendour which is unsurpassed by any other splendour higher or more sublime,' yet you do not indicate what that splendour is. Suppose a man were to say: 'I am in love with the most beautiful girl in this country.' And other people were to say to him, 'Well, my good man, this most beautiful woman in this country with whom you are in love: do you know if she’s of the warrior caste, the *brāhmaṇa* caste, the merchant caste, or the laborer caste?' If he were asked this, he would say, 'No.' They might say to him, 'Well then, do you know her name or clan name? Whether she’s tall, short, or of medium height? Whether she’s dark, fair, or ruddy-skinned? Do you know what village or town or city she’s from?' If he were asked this, he would say, 'No.' And they might say: “Well then, you don’t know or see the one you seek for and desire?” If he were asked this, he would say, 'Yes.'"

"What do you think, Udayin? Surely, in that case, the speech of that man is unrealized?" "Certainly, venerable sir, in that case, the speech of that man is unrealized."

"But in the same way, Udayin, you say thus: 'Venerable sir, that splendour is the perfect splendour which is unsurpassed by any other splendour higher or more sublime,' yet you do not indicate what that splendour is."

"Suppose, venerable sir, there was a beryl gem, beautiful, genuine, eight-faceted, well-cut, placed on a woolen blanket. It would shine, glow, and radiate. Even so, the self is a healthy splendour after death."
commentary_pali:
272.Dīghāpi kho te esāti udāyi esā tava vācā dīghāpi bhaveyya, evaṃ vadantassa vassasatampi vassasahassampi pavatteyya, na ca atthaṃ dīpeyyāti adhippāyo. Appāṭihīrakatanti aniyyānikaṃ amūlakaṃ niratthakaṃ sampajjatīti attho.

Idāni taṃ vaṇṇaṃ dassento seyyathāpi, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha paṇḍukambale nikkhittoti visabhāgavaṇṇe rattakambale ṭhapito. Evaṃvaṇṇo attā hotīti idaṃ so subhakiṇhadevaloke nibbattakkhandhe sandhāya – ‘‘amhākaṃ matakāle attā subhakiṇhadevaloke khandhā viya jotetī’’ti vadati.

seyyathāpi, bhante paṇḍukambale nikkhitto Evaṃvaṇṇo attā hotī
commentary_english:
272. It is said that even if your speech is lengthy, even if someone speaking in this way continues for a hundred or a thousand years, the meaning will not be revealed, this is the idea.

"Unrefuted" means that it becomes unconvincing, groundless, and meaningless.

Now, showing that quality, he says, "Just as, O venerable one," and so forth.

There, "placed on a pale blanket" means placed on a red blanket of dissimilar color.

"The self is of such a color" means that he refers to the aggregates produced in the realm of the gods of steady radiance, saying, "At the time of our death, the self, like the aggregates, shines in the realm of the gods of steady radiance."

Just as, O venerable one, placed on a pale blanket, the self is of such a color.

mula_pali:
273. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yo vā maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato paṇḍukambale nikkhitto bhāsate ca tapate ca virocati ca, yo vā rattandhakāratimisāya kimi khajjopanako – imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ katamo vaṇṇo abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti? ‘‘Yvāyaṃ, bhante, rattandhakāratimisāya kimi khajjopanako – ayaṃ imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yo vā rattandhakāratimisāya kimi khajjopanako, yo vā rattandhakāratimisāya telappadīpo – imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ katamo vaṇṇo abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti? ‘‘Yvāyaṃ, bhante, rattandhakāratimisāya telappadīpo – ayaṃ imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yo vā rattandhakāratimisāya telappadīpo, yo vā rattandhakāratimisāya mahāaggikkhandho – imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ katamo vaṇṇo abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti? ‘‘Yvāyaṃ, bhante, rattandhakāratimisāya mahāaggikkhandho – ayaṃ imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yo vā rattandhakāratimisāya mahāaggikkhandho, yā vā rattiyā paccūsasamayaṃ viddhe vigatavalāhake deve osadhitārakā – imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ katamo vaṇṇo abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti? ‘‘Yvāyaṃ, bhante, rattiyā paccūsasamayaṃ viddhe vigatavalāhake deve osadhitārakā – ayaṃ imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yā vā rattiyā paccūsasamayaṃ viddhe vigatavalāhake deve osadhitārakā, yo vā tadahuposathe pannarase viddhe vigatavalāhake deve abhido abhide (ka. sī.), abhidosaṃ (ka.) abhidoti abhisaddena samānatthanipātapadaṃ (chakkaṅguttaraṭīkā mahāvagga aṭṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā) aḍḍharattasamayaṃ cando – imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ katamo vaṇṇo abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti? ‘‘Yvāyaṃ, bhante, tadahuposathe pannarase viddhe vigatavalāhake deve abhido aḍḍharattasamayaṃ cando – ayaṃ imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti.

abhide (ka. sī.), abhidosaṃ (ka.) abhidoti abhisaddena samānatthanipātapadaṃ (chakkaṅguttaraṭīkā mahāvagga aṭṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā)

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yo vā tadahuposathe pannarase viddhe vigatavalāhake deve abhido aḍḍharattasamayaṃ cando, yo vā vassānaṃ pacchime māse saradasamaye viddhe vigatavalāhake deve abhido majjhanhikasamayaṃ sūriyo – imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ katamo vaṇṇo abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti? ‘‘Yvāyaṃ, bhante, vassānaṃ pacchime māse saradasamaye viddhe vigatavalāhake deve abhido majjhanhikasamayaṃ sūriyo – ayaṃ imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’ti.

‘‘Ato kho te, udāyi, bahū hi bahutarā devā ye imesaṃ candimasūriyānaṃ ābhā nānubhonti, tyāhaṃ pajānāmi. Atha ca panāhaṃ na vadāmi – ‘yasmā vaṇṇā añño vaṇṇo uttaritaro vā paṇītataro vā natthī’ti. Atha ca pana tvaṃ, udāyi, ‘yvāyaṃ vaṇṇo kiminā khajjopanakena nihīnataro hīnataro (sī. pī.) ca patikiṭṭhataro ca so paramo vaṇṇo’ti vadesi, tañca vaṇṇaṃ na paññapesī’’ti. ‘‘Acchidaṃ acchira (ka.), acchida (?) bhagavā kathaṃ, acchidaṃ sugato katha’’nti!

hīnataro (sī. pī.) acchira (ka.), acchida (?)

‘‘Kiṃ pana tvaṃ, udāyi, evaṃ vadesi – ‘acchidaṃ bhagavā kathaṃ, acchidaṃ sugato kathaṃ’’’ti? ‘‘Amhākaṃ, bhante, sake ācariyake evaṃ hoti – ‘ayaṃ paramo vaṇṇo, ayaṃ paramo vaṇṇo’ti. Te mayaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā sake ācariyake samanuyuñjiyamānā samanuggāhiyamānā samanubhāsiyamānā rittā tucchā aparaddhā’’ti.
mula_english:
273. "What do you think, Udayin? Which of these two is more excellent and sublime: a beryl gem, beautiful, of good quality, eight-faceted, well-cut, placed on red brocade, which glows, radiates, and shines; or a glowworm in the thick darkness of the night?"

"Venerable sir, this glowworm in the thick darkness of the night is the more excellent and sublime of these two."

"What do you think, Udayin? Which of these two is more excellent and sublime: a glowworm in the thick darkness of the night, or an oil lamp in the thick darkness of the night?"

"Venerable sir, this oil lamp in the thick darkness of the night is the more excellent and sublime of these two."

"What do you think, Udayin? Which of these two is more excellent and sublime: an oil lamp in the thick darkness of the night, or a great bonfire in the thick darkness of the night?"

"Venerable sir, this great bonfire in the thick darkness of the night is the more excellent and sublime of these two."

"What do you think, Udayin? Which of these two is more excellent and sublime: a great bonfire in the thick darkness of the night, or the morning star towards dawn in a clear cloudless sky?"

"Venerable sir, the morning star towards dawn in a clear cloudless sky is the more excellent and sublime of these two."

"What do you think, Udayin? Which of these two is more excellent and sublime: the morning star towards dawn in a clear cloudless sky, or the full moon at midnight in a clear cloudless sky on the *uposatha* day of the fifteenth?"

"Venerable sir, the full moon at midnight in a clear cloudless sky on the *uposatha* day of the fifteenth is the more excellent and sublime of these two."

"What do you think, Udayin? Which of these two is more excellent and sublime: the full moon at midnight in a clear cloudless sky on the *uposatha* day of the fifteenth, or the full disk of the sun at midday in a clear cloudless sky in autumn in the last month of the rainy season?"

"Venerable sir, the full disk of the sun at midday in a clear cloudless sky in autumn in the last month of the rainy season is the more excellent and sublime of these two."

“Therefore, Udayin, there are many, far more gods who do not experience the splendor of these suns and moons, and I know them.

Yet I do not say, ‘There is no other splendor higher or more sublime than this splendor.’

But you, Udayin, say of that splendor which is lower and meaner than a glowworm’s: ‘This is the perfect splendor,’ yet you do not indicate what that splendor is.”

“Is the *Bhagavān* without divisions? Is the *Sugata* without divisions?”

“What do you think, Udayin? Do you say thus: ‘Is the *Bhagavān* without divisions? Is the *Sugata* without divisions?’”

“Venerable sir, this is what we have from our own teachers: ‘This is the supreme splendor, this is the supreme splendor.’

When we are pressed, questioned, and cross-questioned about our own teachers’ doctrine by the *Bhagavān*, we are found empty, hollow, and mistaken.”
commentary_pali:
273.Ayaṃimesaṃ ubhinnanti so kira yasmā maṇissa bahi ābhā na niccharati, khajjopanakassa aṅguladvaṅgulacaturaṅgulamattaṃ niccharati, mahākhajjopanakassa pana khaḷamaṇḍalamattampi niccharatiyeva, tasmā evamāha.

Viddheti ubbiddhe, meghavigamena dūrībhūteti attho. Vigatavalāhaketi apagatameghe. Deveti ākāse. Osadhitārakāti sukkatārakā. Sā hi yasmā tassā udayato paṭṭhāya tena saññāṇena osadhāni gaṇhantipi pivantipi, tasmā ‘‘osadhitārakā’’ti vuccati. Abhido aḍḍharattasamayanti abhinne aḍḍharattasamaye. Iminā gaganamajjhe ṭhitacandaṃ dasseti. Abhido majjhanhikepi eseva nayo.

Viddhe Vigatavalāhake Deve Osadhitārakā Abhido aḍḍharattasamaya

Ato khoti ye anubhonti, tehi bahutarā, bahū ceva bahutarā cāti attho. Ābhā nānubhontīti obhāsaṃ na vaḷañjanti, attano sarīrobhāseneva ālokaṃ pharitvā viharanti.

Ato kho Ābhā nānubhontī
commentary_english:
273.
*Ayaṃ imesaṃ ubhinna* means because, indeed, external light does not come out of a jewel ( *maṇi* ), [but] it comes out from a firefly to the extent of two, three, or four fingers, and from a large firefly it comes out even to the extent of a winnowing basket. Therefore, he said thus.

*Viddhe* means *ubbiddhe*, the meaning is: it is far away by the passing of clouds (*meghavigamena dūrībhūta*).
*Vigatavalāhake* means *apagatameghe*.
*Deve* means in the sky (*ākāśe*).
*Osadhitārakā* means Venus (*sukratārakā*).
Because she (*sā*) from the time of her rising (*udayato paṭṭhāya*) with that perception (*saññāṇena*) grasps and drinks medicinal herbs (*osadhāni gaṇhanti pi pivanti pi*), therefore she is called "herbal star" (*osadhitārakā iti vuccati*).
*Abhido aḍḍharattasamaya* means at different midnight times (*abhinne aḍḍharattasamaye*).
By this, he shows the moon standing in the middle of the sky (*gaganamajjhe ṭhitacandaṃ dasseti*).
Also for *abhido majjhanhikepi*, this is the same method (*nayo*).

*Viddhe vigatavalāhake deve osadhitārakā abhido aḍḍharattasamaya* *ato kho* means those who experience it (*ye anubhonti*), [are] more numerous than them, the meaning is: they are many and more numerous (*bahū ceva bahutarā cāti attho*).
*Ābhā nānubhontī* means they do not grasp the light (*obhāsaṃ na vaḷañjanti*), they live pervading the light with the light of their own body (*attano śarīrobhāsen’eva ālokaṃ pharitvā viharanti*).

*Ato kho ābhā nānubhontī*

mula_pali:
274. ‘‘Kiṃ panudāyi, atthi ekantasukho loko, atthi ākāravatī paṭipadā ekantasukhassa lokassa sacchikiriyāyā’’ti? ‘‘Amhākaṃ, bhante, sake ācariyake evaṃ hoti – ‘atthi ekantasukho loko, atthi ākāravatī paṭipadā ekantasukhassa lokassa sacchikiriyāyā’’’ti.

‘‘Katamā pana sā, udāyi, ākāravatī paṭipadā ekantasukhassa lokassa sacchikiriyāyā’’ti? ‘‘Idha, bhante, ekacco pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, adinnādānaṃ pahāya adinnādānā paṭivirato hoti, kāmesumicchācāraṃ pahāya kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato hoti, musāvādaṃ pahāya musāvādā paṭivirato hoti, aññataraṃ vā pana tapoguṇaṃ samādāya vattati. Ayaṃ kho sā, bhante, ākāravatī paṭipadā ekantasukhassa lokassa sacchikiriyāyā’’ti.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yasmiṃ samaye pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, ekantasukhī vā tasmiṃ samaye attā hoti sukhadukkhī vā’’ti? ‘‘Sukhadukkhī, bhante’’.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yasmiṃ samaye adinnādānaṃ pahāya adinnādānā paṭivirato hoti, ekantasukhī vā tasmiṃ samaye attā hoti sukhadukkhī vā’’ti? ‘‘Sukhadukkhī, bhante’’.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yasmiṃ samaye kāmesumicchācāraṃ pahāya kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato hoti, ekantasukhī vā tasmiṃ samaye attā hoti sukhadukkhī vā’’ti? ‘‘Sukhadukkhī, bhante’’.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yasmiṃ samaye musāvādaṃ pahāya musāvādā paṭivirato hoti, ekantasukhī vā tasmiṃ samaye attā hoti sukhadukkhī vā’’ti? ‘‘Sukhadukkhī, bhante’’.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, yasmiṃ samaye aññataraṃ tapoguṇaṃ samādāya vattati, ekantasukhī vā tasmiṃ samaye attā hoti sukhadukkhī vā’’ti? ‘‘Sukhadukkhī, bhante’’.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, api nu kho vokiṇṇasukhadukkhaṃ paṭipadaṃ āgamma ekantasukhassa lokassa sacchikiriyā hotī’’ti sacchikiriyāyāti (ka.)? ‘‘Acchidaṃ bhagavā kathaṃ, acchidaṃ sugato katha’’nti!

sacchikiriyāyāti (ka.)

‘‘Kiṃ pana tvaṃ, udāyi, vadesi – ‘acchidaṃ bhagavā kathaṃ, acchidaṃ sugato kathaṃ’’’ti? ‘‘Amhākaṃ, bhante, sake ācariyake evaṃ hoti – ‘atthi ekantasukho loko, atthi ākāravatī paṭipadā ekantasukhassa lokassa sacchikiriyāyā’ti. Te mayaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā sake ācariyake samanuyuñjiyamānā samanuggāhiyamānā samanubhāsiyamānā rittā tucchā aparaddhā’’ti aparaddhā (sī.), aparaddhāpi (syā. kaṃ. pī.).

aparaddhā (sī.), aparaddhāpi (syā. kaṃ. pī.)
mula_english:
274. “How is it, Udayin, is there an entirely pleasant world? Is there a practical way to realise an entirely pleasant world?” “Venerable sir, it is taught in our own teachers’ doctrine: “There is an entirely pleasant world; there is a practical way to realise an entirely pleasant world.’”

“But what, Udayin, is that practical way to realise an entirely pleasant world?” “Here, venerable sir, abandoning the killing of living beings, someone abstains from killing living beings; abandoning the taking of what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; abandoning misconduct in sensual pleasures, he abstains from misconduct in sensual pleasures; abandoning false speech, he abstains from false speech; or else he undertakes and practises some kind of asceticism. This is the practical way to realise an entirely pleasant world.”

“What do you think, Udayin? On an occasion when he abandons the killing of living beings and abstains from killing living beings, does his self then feel only pleasure or both pleasure and pain?” “Both pleasure and pain, venerable sir.”

“What do you think, Udayin? On an occasion when he abandons the taking of what is not given and abstains from taking what is not given, does his self then feel only pleasure or both pleasure and pain?” “Both pleasure and pain, venerable sir.”

“What do you think, Udayin? On an occasion when he abandons misconduct in sensual pleasures and abstains from misconduct in sensual pleasures, does his self then feel only pleasure or both pleasure and pain?” “Both pleasure and pain, venerable sir.”

“What do you think, Udayin? On an occasion when he abandons false speech and abstains from false speech, does his self then feel only pleasure or both pleasure and pain?” “Both pleasure and pain, venerable sir.”

“What do you think, Udayin? On an occasion when he under takes and practises some kind of asceticism, does his self then feel only pleasure or both pleasure and pain?” “Both pleasure and pain, venerable sir.”

“What do you think, Udayin? Is it possible, by following a path mixed with both pleasure and pain, to realise an entirely pleasant world?” “How is it that the Blessed One is without flaws? How is it that the *Sugata* is without flaws?”
