313. Then, Ānanda, Śakka, the ruler of the gods, knowing King Nimi's acceptance, just as quickly as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, vanished in the presence of King Nimi and appeared among the gods of the Thirty-three.

Then, Ānanda, Śakka, the ruler of the gods, addressed the charioteer Mātali: ‘Come, good Mātali, prepare a chariot harnessed to a thousand thoroughbreds, and having approached King Nimi, say this: “This chariot harnessed to a thousand thoroughbreds has been sent to you, great king, by Śakka, the ruler of the gods; mount it, great king, the divine vehicle, without misgiving.”’

‘Very good, Lord’, Ānanda, Mātali the charioteer replied to Śakka, the ruler of the gods, and having prepared a chariot harnessed to a thousand thoroughbreds, approached King Nimi, and said this: ‘This chariot harnessed to a thousand thoroughbreds has been sent to you, great king, by Śakka, the ruler of the gods; mount it, great king, the divine vehicle, without misgiving.

Furthermore, great king, by which *nemi* do evil-doers experience the result of evil deeds, and by which do virtuous-doers experience the result of virtuous deeds?’ ‘By both, Mātali, lead me!’

Mātali, the charioteer, then brought King Nimi to the Sudharma Assembly, Ānanda.

Śakka, the ruler of the gods, saw King Nimi coming from afar, Ānanda.

Having seen King Nimi, he said this: ‘Come, great king!

Welcome, great king!

The gods of the Thirty-three, great king, wanting to see you, are seated in the Sudharma Assembly, their forms expressing praise: “It is a gain, indeed, sirs, for the Videhans, a great gain, indeed, sirs, for the Videhans, that their King Nimi is a righteous king, a *dharma*-king, a great king established in the *dharma*; he conducts himself according to the *dharma* among brahmins and householders, among townspeople and country people; and he observes the *uposatha*, fasting on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight.”’

The gods of the Thirty-three, great king, want to see you.

Enjoy yourself, great king, among the gods with divine power!’

‘Enough, good sir. Let the charioteer drive me back to Mithilā.

There I will conduct myself according to the *dharma* among brahmins and householders, among townspeople and country people; and there I will observe the *uposatha*, fasting on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight.’
commentary_pali:
313.Evaṃ bhaddantavāti evaṃ hotu bhaddakaṃ tava vacananti vatvā. Yojetvāti ekasmiṃyeva yuge sahassaassājānīye yojetvā. Tesaṃ pana pāṭiyekkaṃ yojanakiccaṃ natthi, manaṃ āgamma yuttāyeva honti. So pana dibbaratho diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko hoti, naddhito paṭṭhāya rathasīsaṃ paññāsayojanāni, akkhabandho paṇṇāsayojanāni, akkhabandhato paṭṭhāya pacchābhāgo paṇṇāsayojanāni, sabbo sattavaṇṇaratanamayo. Devaloko nāma uddhaṃ, manussaloko adho, tasmā heṭṭhāmukhaṃ rathaṃ pesesīti na sallakkhetabbaṃ. Yathā pana pakatimaggaṃ peseti, evameva manussānaṃ sāyamāsabhatte niṭṭhite candena saddhiṃ yuganaddhaṃ katvā pesesi, yamakacandā uṭṭhitā viya ahesuṃ. Mahājano disvā ‘‘yamakacandā uggatā’’ti āha. Āgacchante āgacchante na yamakacandā, ekaṃ vimānaṃ, na vimānaṃ, eko rathoti. Rathopi āgacchanto āgacchanto pakatirathappamāṇova, assāpi pakatiassappamāṇāva ahesuṃ. Evaṃ rathaṃ āharitvā rañño pāsādaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pācīnasīhapañjaraṭṭhāne rathaṃ nivattetvā āgatamaggābhimukhaṃ katvā sīhapañjare ṭhatvāva ārohanasajjaṃ ṭhapesi.

Abhiruha mahārājāti rājā – ‘‘dibbayānaṃ me laddha’’nti na tāvadeva abhiruhi, nāgarānaṃ pana ovādaṃ adāsi ‘‘passatha tātā, yaṃ me sakkena devaraññā dibbaratho pesito, so ca kho na jātigottaṃ vā kulappadesaṃ vā paṭicca pesito, mayhaṃ pana sīlācāraguṇe pasīditvā pesito. Sace tumhepi sīlaṃ rakkhissatha, tumhākampi pesessati, evaṃ rakkhituṃ yuttaṃ nāmetaṃ sīlaṃ. Nāhaṃ devalokaṃ gantvā cirāyissāmi, appamattā hothā’’ti mahājanaṃ ovaditvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā rathaṃ abhiruhi. Tato mātali saṅgāhako ‘‘ahampi mahārājassa mamānucchavikaṃ karissāmī’’ti ākāsamhi dve magge dassetvā apica mahārājātiādimāha.

Abhiruha mahārājā apica mahārājā

Tattha katamenāti, mahārāja, imesu maggesu eko nirayaṃ gacchati, eko devalokaṃ, tesu taṃ katamena nemi. Yenāti yena maggena gantvā yattha pāpakammantā pāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvediyanti, taṃ ṭhānaṃ sakkā hoti passitunti attho. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Jātakepi –

katamenā Yenā

‘‘Kena taṃ nemi maggena, rājaseṭṭha disampati;

Yena vā pāpakammantā, puññakammā ca ye narā’’ti. (jā. 2.22.450) –

Gāthāya ayamevattho. Tenevāha –

‘‘Niraye tāva passāmi, āvāse pāpakamminaṃ;

Ṭhānāni luddakammānaṃ, dussīlānañca yā gatī’’ti. (jā. 2.22.451);

Ubhayeneva maṃ mātali nehīti mātali dvīhi maggehi maṃ nehi, ahaṃ nirayaṃ passitukāmo devalokampīti. Paṭhamaṃ katamena nemīti. Paṭhamaṃ nirayamaggena nehīti. Tato mātali attano ānubhāvena rājānaṃ pañcadasa mahāniraye dassesi. Vitthārakathā panettha –

Ubhayeneva maṃ mātali nehī

‘‘Dassesi mātali rañño, duggaṃ vetaraṇiṃ nadiṃ;

Kuthitaṃ khārasaṃyuttaṃ, tattaṃ aggisikhūpama’’nti. (jā. 2.22.452) –

Jātake vuttanayena veditabbā. Nirayaṃ dassetvā rathaṃ nivattetvā devalokābhimukhaṃ gantvā bīraṇīdevadhītāya soṇadinnadevaputtassa gaṇadevaputtānañca vimānāni dassento devalokaṃ nesi. Tatrāpi vitthārakathā –

‘‘Yadi te sutā bīraṇī jīvaloke,

Āmāyadāsī ahu brāhmaṇassa;

Sā pattakāle atithiṃ viditvā,

Mātāva puttaṃ sakimābhinandī;

Saṃyamā saṃvibhāgā ca,

Sā vimānasmi modatī’’ti. (jā. 2.22.507) –

Jātake vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Evaṃ gacchato pana tassa rathanemi vaṭṭiyā cittakūṭadvārakoṭṭhakassa ummāre pahatamatteva devanagare kolāhalaṃ ahosi. Sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ ekakaṃyeva ohāya devasaṅgho mahāsattaṃ paccuggamanamakāsi, taṃ devatānaṃ ādaraṃ disvā sakko cittaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto – ‘‘abhirama, mahārāja, devesu devānubhāvenā’’ti āha. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – ‘‘ayaṃ rājā ajja āgantvā ekadivaseneva devagaṇaṃ attano abhimukhamakāsi. Sace ekaṃ dve divase vasissati, na maṃ devā olokessantī’’ti. So usūyamāno, ‘‘mahārāja, tuyhaṃ imasmiṃ devaloke vasituṃ puññaṃ natthi, aññesaṃ puññena vasāhī’’ti iminā adhippāyena evamāha. Bodhisatto – ‘‘nāsakkhi jarasakko manaṃ sandhāretuṃ, paraṃ nissāya laddhaṃ kho pana yācitvā laddhabhaṇḍakaṃ viya hotī’’ti paṭikkhipanto alaṃ mārisātiādimāha. Jātakepi vuttaṃ –

alaṃ mārisā

‘‘Yathā yācitakaṃ yānaṃ, yathā yācitakaṃ dhanaṃ;

Evaṃsampadameve taṃ, yaṃ parato dānapaccayā;

Na cāhametamicchāmi, yaṃ parato dānapaccayā’’ti. (jā. 2.22.585-586) –

Sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ. Bodhisatto pana manussattabhāvena kativāre devalokaṃ gatoti. Cattāro – mandhāturājakāle sādhinarājakāle guttilavīṇāvādakakāle nimimahārājakāleti. So mandhātukāle devaloke asaṅkhyeyyaṃ kālaṃ vasi, tasmiñhi vasamāneyeva chattiṃsa sakkā caviṃsu. Sādhinarājakāle sattāhaṃ vasi, manussagaṇanāya satta vassasatāni honti. Guttilavīṇāvādakakāle ca nimirājakāle ca muhuttamattaṃ vasi, manussagaṇanāya satta divasāni honti.
commentary_english:
313. "Thus, the Blessed One," means saying, "Thus, may good fortune be yours!"

"Having yoked" means having yoked a thousand thoroughbreds in a single *yuga*, having yoked [them].

However, for them, there is no individual yoking task; they are proper simply by having come to mind.

That celestial chariot was one and a half *yojanas* in length, from the axle to the chariot's head was fifty *yojanas*, the axle-band was fifty *yojanas*, from the axle-band to the rear was fifty *yojanas*; the whole was made of seven-jeweled colors.

The world of the gods is above, the world of humans is below; therefore, one should not consider that he sent the chariot face-down.

Just as he sends it on a natural path, just so, when the evening meal of humans was finished, he sent it having made a pair yoked together with the moon; they were as if twin moons had risen.

The multitude, having seen [it], said, "Twin moons have risen!"

Coming and coming, they were not twin moons, [but] one celestial mansion; not a celestial mansion, [but] one chariot.

The chariot, also, coming and coming, was just the size of a natural chariot; the horses, also, were just the size of natural horses.

Having thus brought the chariot, and having circumambulated the king's palace, and having turned the chariot at the eastern lion-cage location, and having made [it] facing the road from which it had come, he placed [it] in the lion-cage, just standing, ready for mounting.

"Ascend, great king!" the king [thought], "I have obtained a divine vehicle," but he did not ascend just then; however, he gave counsel to the townspeople, "See, fathers, this divine chariot has been sent to me by Śakra, king of the gods, but it has not been sent paying attention to birth or lineage or family origin, but rather, it has been sent being pleased with my virtue, conduct, and qualities.

If you, also, will protect virtue, he will send [one] to you, also; thus, it is proper to protect this virtue.

I will not go to the world of the gods and stay for long; be diligent!" Having thus advised the multitude, and having established [them] in the five precepts, he ascended the chariot.

Then Mātalī, the charioteer, thinking, "I, also, will do what is fitting for the great king," having shown two paths in the sky, spoke, beginning with, "Moreover, great king!"

"Ascend, great king!" "Moreover, great king!" There, "By which?" [he asked]. Great king, of these paths, one goes to hell, one to the world of the gods; by which of those do you lead?

"By which?" means, by which path having gone, to where beings experience the result of evil actions, that place it is possible to see, is the meaning.

The same method [applies] in the second line, also.

In the Jātaka, also—

"By which? By which path do you lead, O best of kings, lord of the directions; or by which [path] do beings of evil deeds, and those who perform meritorious deeds [go]?"

(Jā. 2.22.450)—

This is just the meaning of the verse.

Therefore, he said—

"In hell, indeed, I see the dwellings of those who have done evil deeds; the places of those of cruel deeds, and what is the fate of the immoral?"

(Jā. 2.22.451);

"Lead me, Mātalī, by both!" means, Mātalī, lead me by both paths, for I wish to see hell, and also the world of the gods.

First, by which do you lead?

First, lead by the path to hell!

Then Mātalī, by his own power, showed the king the fifteen great hells.

The detailed account is here—

"Lead me, Mātalī, by both!" "Mātalī showed the king the difficult-to-cross Vaitaraṇī River;"

It should be understood according to the method stated in the *Jātaka*.
Having shown hell, having turned back the chariot, having gone towards the heavenly realm, showing the palaces to Bīraṇīdevadhītā, Soṇadinnadevaputta, and Gaṇadevaputtas, he led [them] to the heavenly realm.
There also [is] an extensive talk–

‘‘If your daughter Bīraṇī [is] in the world of the living,
[she] became a servant afflicted by illness of a *brāhmaṇa*;
she, having known the guest at the proper time,
like a mother, rejoiced once the son;

Through restraint and sharing,
she rejoices in the palace.’’
(Jā.
2.
22.
507) –

It should be understood just according to the method stated in the *Jātaka*.

Thus, while going, just when the wheel-rim of his chariot struck the lintel of the gate-chamber of Cittakūṭadvāra, there was an uproar in the city of the gods.
Having abandoned Śakka, the king of the gods, alone, the assembly of gods paid homage to the great being, seeing that respect of the gods, Śakka, unable to restrain his mind, said: ‘‘Delight, great king, in the gods through the power of the gods.’’
Thus, it occurred to him: ‘‘This king, having come today, has turned the host of gods towards himself in one day.
If he lives for one or two days, the gods will not look at me.’’
Being envious, he said thus with this intention: ‘‘Great king, you do not have merit to live in this heavenly world; live by the merit of others.’’
The *bodhisattva*– ‘‘Old Śakka was not able to restrain his mind; a borrowed item obtained by begging is like a [weapon],’’ rejecting, said, beginning with "Enough, friend."
It was also said in the *Jātaka*–

Enough friend!
‘‘Just as a borrowed vehicle, just as borrowed wealth;
just that attainment [is] like that which [comes] from the alms of another;
I do not want that which [comes] from the alms of another.’’
(Jā.
2.
22.
585-586) –

Everything should be spoken.
How many times has the *bodhisattva* gone to the heavenly world in human form?
Four–in the time of King Mandhātu, in the time of King Sādhina, in the time of Guttilavīṇāvādaka, and in the time of King Nimi Mahārāja.
He lived in the heavenly world for an *asaṃkhyeyya* period in the time of Mandhātu, indeed, while he was living there, thirty-six Śakkas passed away.
He lived for a week in the time of King Sādhina; according to human reckoning, it is seven hundred years.
He lived for just a moment in the time of Guttilavīṇāvādaka and in the time of King Nimi; according to human reckoning, it is seven days.

mula_pali: 314. ‘‘Atha kho, ānanda, sakko devānamindo mātaliṃ saṅgāhakaṃ āmantesi – ‘ehi tvaṃ, samma mātali, sahassayuttaṃ ājaññarathaṃ yojetvā nimiṃ rājānaṃ tattheva mithilaṃ paṭinehī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bhaddantavā’ti kho, ānanda, mātali saṅgāhako sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā sahassayuttaṃ ājaññarathaṃ yojetvā nimiṃ rājānaṃ tattheva mithilaṃ paṭinesi. Tatra sudaṃ, ānanda, nimi rājā dhammaṃ carati brāhmaṇagahapatikesu negamesu ceva jānapadesu ca, uposathañca upavasati cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ aṭṭhamiñca pakkhassāti. Atha kho, ānanda, nimi rājā bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasatānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasahassānaṃ accayena kappakaṃ āmantesi – ‘yadā me, samma kappaka, passeyyāsi sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni, atha me āroceyyāsī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, ānanda, kappako nimissa rañño paccassosi. Addasā kho, ānanda, kappako bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasatānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasahassānaṃ accayena nimissa rañño sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni. Disvāna nimiṃ rājānaṃ etadavoca – ‘pātubhūtā kho devassa devadūtā; dissanti sirasmiṃ palitāni jātānī’ti. ‘Tena hi, samma kappaka, tāni palitāni sādhukaṃ saṇḍāsena uddharitvā mama añjalismiṃ patiṭṭhāpehī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, ānanda, kappako nimissa rañño paṭissutvā tāni palitāni sādhukaṃ saṇḍāsena uddharitvā nimissa rañño añjalismiṃ patiṭṭhāpesi. Atha kho, ānanda, nimi rājā kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ āmantāpetvā etadavoca – ‘pātubhūtā kho me, tāta kumāra, devadūtā; dissanti sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni; bhuttā kho pana me mānusakā kāmā; samayo dibbe kāme pariyesituṃ. Ehi tvaṃ, tāta kumāra, imaṃ rajjaṃ paṭipajja. Ahaṃ pana kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmi. Tena hi, tāta kumāra, yadā tvampi passeyyāsi sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni, atha kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ sādhukaṃ rajje samanusāsitvā kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyyāsi. Yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyāsi, mā kho me tvaṃ antimapuriso ahosi. Yasmiṃ kho, tāta kumāra, purisayuge vattamāne evarūpassa kalyāṇassa vattassa samucchedo hoti so tesaṃ antimapuriso hoti. Taṃ tāhaṃ, tāta kumāra, evaṃ vadāmi – ‘yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyāsi, mā kho me tvaṃ antimapuriso ahosī’ti.
mula_english:
314. Then, Ānanda, Sakka, the ruler of the gods, addressed the charioteer Mātali, "Come, good Mātali, prepare a chariot harnessed to a thousand thoroughbreds, and take King Nimi right back to Mithilā."

"May your words be held sacred," replied the charioteer Mātali. And having prepared the chariot harnessed to a thousand thoroughbreds, he drove King Nimi right back to Mithilā.

And there, indeed, Ānanda, King Nimi conducted himself by the *dharma* among *brāhmaṇas* and householders, among town-dwellers and countryfolk; and there he observed the *uposatha* days on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight.

Then, Ānanda, King Nimi, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, addressed his barber, "Good barber, when you see grey hairs appearing on my head, then inform me."

"Yes, sire," replied the barber to King Nimi.

After the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, the barber saw grey hairs appearing on King Nimi's head.

Seeing them, he said to King Nimi, "The divine messengers have appeared, sire; grey hairs are visible on your head."

"Then, good barber, carefully pluck out those grey hairs with tweezers and place them in my cupped hands."

"Yes, sire," replied the barber to King Nimi. Carefully plucking out those grey hairs with tweezers, he placed them in King Nimi's cupped hands.

Then, Ānanda, King Nimi gave the best village to the barber, and summoning his eldest son, the prince, said to him, "The divine messengers have appeared, dear prince; grey hairs are visible on my head. I have enjoyed human sensual pleasures; now is the time to seek divine sensual pleasures.

Come, dear prince, take over this kingship.

I, however, will shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the house life into homelessness."

"Therefore, dear prince, when you too see grey hairs appearing on your head, then, after giving the best village to the barber and properly instructing the prince, your eldest son, in the kingship, shave off your hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the house life into homelessness.

Continue this good practice instituted by me, so that you may not be the last man.

Dear prince, in whatever generation of men this good practice is discontinued, he is the last man among them.

Therefore, dear prince, I say to you: ‘Continue this good practice instituted by me, so that you may not be the last man.’"
commentary_pali: 314.Tatthevamithilaṃ paṭinesīti paṭinetvā pakatisirigabbheyeva patiṭṭhāpesi.
commentary_english: Just as he had brought her to Mithila, he brought her back and established her in the natural auspicious chamber.

mula_pali: 315. ‘‘Atha kho, ānanda, nimi rājā kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ sādhukaṃ rajje samanusāsitvā imasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbaji. So mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihāsi, tathā dutiyaṃ , tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā vihāsi. Karuṇāsahagatena cetasā… muditāsahagatena cetasā… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihāsi, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā vihāsi. Nimi kho, panānanda, rājā caturāsītivassasahassāni kumārakīḷitaṃ kīḷi, caturāsītivassasahassāni oparajjaṃ kāresi, caturāsītivassasahassāni rajjaṃ kāresi, caturāsītivassasahassāni imasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito brahmacariyamacari. So cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā brahmalokūpago ahosi. Nimissa kho panānananda , rañño kaḷārajanako nāma putto ahosi. Na so agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbaji. So taṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ samucchindi. So tesaṃ antimapuriso ahosi.
mula_english:
315. Then, Ānanda, King Nimi, after giving the best township to his barber and after carefully instructing the prince, his eldest son, in kingship, in the Maghadeva Mango Grove, shaved off his hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.

He abided pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness ( *maitrī*), likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, around, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he abided pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility and without ill will.

He abided pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion ( *karuṇā*)…with a mind imbued with appreciative joy ( *muditā*)…with a mind imbued with equanimity ( *upekṣā*), likewise the second, likewise’ the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, around, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he abided pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind imbued with equanimity, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility and without ill will.

Nimi, Ānanda, for eighty-four thousand years the king played childish games; for eighty-four thousand years he acted as viceregent; for eighty-four thousand years he governed the kingdom; for eighty-four thousand years in this very Maghadeva Mango Grove he went forth from the home life into homelessness and practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

By developing the four divine abodes ( *brahmavihāra*), on the dissolution of the body, after death, he passed on to the Brahma-world.

Nimi's son was a youth called Kalarajanaka.

He did not go forth from the home life into homelessness.

He broke that good practice.

He was the last man among them.
commentary_pali: 315.Kaḷārajanakoti tassa nāmaṃ. Kaḷāradantatāya pana kaḷārajanakoti vutto. Na so agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajīti ettakamattameva na akāsi, sesaṃ sabbaṃ pākatikameva ahosi.
commentary_english:
315. His name was *kaḷārajanako*.

Because of his black teeth, he was called *kaḷārajanaka*.

"He did not go forth from the household life into homelessness," he did not do only this much, but the rest was just natural.

mula_pali:
316. ‘‘Siyā kho pana te, ānanda, evamassa – ‘añño nūna tena samayena rājā maghadevo ahosi, yena taṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihita’nti yo taṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihinīti (sī.). Na kho panetaṃ, ānanda, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ahaṃ tena samayena rājā maghadevo ahosiṃ. (Ahaṃ taṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihiniṃ,) ( ) natthi (ka.) mayā taṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ; pacchimā janatā anuppavattesi. Taṃ kho panānanda, kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ na nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva brahmalokūpapattiyā. Idaṃ kho panānanda, etarahi mayā kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati. Katamañcānanda, etarahi mayā kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo , sammāsati, sammāsamādhi. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etarahi mayā kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati. Taṃ vo ahaṃ, ānanda, evaṃ vadāmi – ‘yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyātha, mā kho me tumhe antimapurisā ahuvattha’. Yasmiṃ kho, ānanda, purisayuge vattamāne evarūpassa kalyāṇassa vattassa samucchedo hoti so tesaṃ antimapuriso hoti. Taṃ vo ahaṃ, ānanda, evaṃ vadāmi – ‘yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyātha, mā kho me tumhe antimapurisā ahuvatthā’’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā ānando bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

Maghadevasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.
mula_english:
“Now, Ānanda, it may be that you think thus: ‘Certainly, someone else was King Maghadeva at that time, by whom that beautiful practice was established,’” do not view it in that way, Ānanda. I was King Maghadeva at that time. By me that beautiful practice was established; the later generations continued that good practice.

But that beautiful practice, Ānanda, does not lead to disenchantment (*nirbidā*), to dispassion (*virāga*), to cessation (*nirodha*), to peace (*upaśamā*), to direct knowledge (*abhijñāya*), to enlightenment (*saṃbodhāya*), to *Nibbāna* (*nirvāṇa*), but only to reappearance in the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*).

This good practice (*kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ*), Ānanda, instituted by me now, leads to complete disenchantment (*ekantanibbidāya*), to dispassion (*virāgāya*), to cessation (*nirodhāya*), to peace (*upasamāya*), to direct knowledge (*abhijñāya*), to enlightenment (*saṃbodhāya*), to *Nibbāna* (*nirvāṇa*).

And what, Ānanda, is the good practice (*kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ*) established by me now, which leads to complete disenchantment (*ekantanibbidāya*), to dispassion (*virāgāya*), to cessation (*nirodhāya*), to peace (*upasamāya*), to direct knowledge (*abhijñāya*), to enlightenment (*saṃbodhāya*), to *Nibbāna* (*nirvāṇa*)? It is just this noble eightfold path (*ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo*), that is to say: right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), right intention (*sammāsaṅkappo*), right speech (*sammāvācā*), right action (*sammākammanto*), right livelihood (*sammāājīvo*), right effort (*sammāvāyāmo*), right mindfulness (*sammāsati*), right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*).

This good practice (*kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ*), Ānanda, instituted by me now, leads to complete disenchantment (*ekantanibbidāya*), to dispassion (*virāgāya*), to cessation (*nirodhāya*), to peace (*upasamāya*), to direct knowledge (*abhijñāya*), to enlightenment (*saṃbodhāya*), to *Nibbāna* (*nirvāṇa*).

Ānanda, I say this to you: may you continue this good practice (*kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ*) established by me, may you not be the last men.

Ānanda, in whatever generation of men, while this kind of beautiful practice is in place, there is utter destruction, he is the last of them.

Ānanda, I say this to you: may you continue this good practice (*kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ*) established by me, may you not be the last men.’”

Thus spoke the Blessed One (*bhagavā*). The venerable Ānanda, delighted, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

The Maghadeva Sutta, the third, is finished.
commentary_pali:
316.Samucchedo hotīti ettha kalyāṇavattaṃ ko samucchindati, kena samucchinnaṃ, ko pavatteti, kena pavattitaṃ nāma hotīti ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Tattha sīlavā bhikkhu ‘‘na sakkā mayā arahattaṃ laddhu’’nti vīriyaṃ akaronto samucchindati. Dussīlena samucchinnaṃ nāma hoti. Satta sekhā pavattenti. Khīṇāsavena pavattitaṃ nāma hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Maghadevasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
Here, "utter destruction occurs," who completely cuts off the practice of virtue? By whom is it completely cut off? Who sets it in motion? By whom is it set in motion? This distinction should be understood. There, a virtuous *bhikṣu* (monk), not generating *vīrya* (energy) thinking, " It is not possible for me to attain *arhattva* (arahantship)," completely cuts it off. It is said to be completely cut off by immorality. The seven learners set it in motion. It is said to be set in motion by one with destroyed *āsrava* (influxes). The rest is clear throughout.

The commentary on the *Maghadevasutta* is finished.

mula_pali: 317. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā mahākaccāno madhurāyaṃ viharati gundāvane. Assosi kho rājā mādhuro avantiputto – ‘‘samaṇo khalu, bho, kaccāno madhurāyaṃ mathurāyaṃ (ṭīkā) viharati gundāvane. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ kaccānaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – ‘paṇḍito viyatto medhāvī bahussuto cittakathī kalyāṇapaṭibhāno vuddho ceva arahā ca’. Sādhu kho pana tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ dassanaṃ hotī’’ti. Atha kho rājā mādhuro avantiputto bhadrāni bhadrāni yānāni yojāpetvā bhadraṃ yānaṃ abhiruhitvā bhadrehi bhadrehi yānehi madhurāya niyyāsi mahaccarājānubhāvena āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ dassanāya. Yāvatikā yānassa bhūmi yānena gantvā yānā paccorohitvā pattikova yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā mahākaccānena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho rājā mādhuro avantiputto āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘brāhmaṇā, bho kaccāna, evamāhaṃsu – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇova sukko vaṇṇo, kaṇho añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇāva sujjhanti, no abrāhmaṇā; brāhmaṇāva brahmuno puttā orasā mukhato jātā brahmajā brahmanimmitā brahmadāyādā’ti. Idha bhavaṃ kaccāno kimakkhāyī’’ti? ‘‘Ghosoyeva kho eso, mahārāja, lokasmiṃ – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇova sukko vaṇṇo, kaṇho añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇāva sujjhanti, no abrāhmaṇā; brāhmaṇāva brahmuno puttā orasā mukhato jātā brahmajā brahmanimmitā brahmadāyādā’ti. Tadamināpetaṃ, mahārāja, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā ghosoyeveso lokasmiṃ – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’’’ti.
mula_english:
317
Thus have I heard. On one occasion the venerable Mahākaccāna was living at Madhurā in the Gunda Grove.

King Mādhurā Avantiputta heard: “The recluse Kaccāna is living at Madhurā in the Gunda Grove.”

Now a good report of Master Kaccāna has been spread to this effect: ‘He is wise, discerning, sagacious, learned, articulate, and perspicacious; he is aged and he is an *arhat* (arahā ca).’

“It is good to see such a worthy one.”

Then King Mādhurā Avantiputta had a number of state carriages made ready, and mounting a state carriage, he drove out from Madhurā with the full pomp of royalty in order to see the venerable Mahākaccāna.

He went thus as far as the road was passable for carriages, and then he got down from his carriage and went forward on foot to the venerable Mahākaccāna; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the venerable Mahākaccāna.

When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side.

Having sat down to one side, King Mādhurā Avantiputta said to the venerable Mahākaccāna: “The *brahmins* (brāhmaṇā), Master Kaccāna, say thus: ‘*Brahmins* (brāhmaṇā) are the highest caste (*varṇa*), those of any other caste are inferior; *brahmins* (brāhmaṇā) are the fairest caste, those of any other caste are dark; only *brahmins* (brāhmaṇā) are purified, not non-*brahmins* (abrāhmaṇā); *brahmins* (brāhmaṇā) alone are the sons of *Brahmā*, the offspring of *Brahmā*, born of his mouth, born of *Brahmā*, created by *Brahmā*, heirs of *Brahmā*.’

What do you say about this?”

“It is just a saying in the world, great king, that ‘*Brahmins* (brāhmaṇā) are the highest caste (*varṇa*), those of any other caste are inferior; *brahmins* (brāhmaṇā) are the fairest caste, those of any other caste are dark; only *brahmins* (brāhmaṇā) are purified, not non-*brahmins* (abrāhmaṇā); *brahmins* (brāhmaṇā) alone are the sons of *Brahmā*, the offspring of *Brahmā*, born of his mouth, born of *Brahmā*, created by *Brahmā*, heirs of *Brahmā*.’

And there is a way whereby it can be understood how that statement of the *brahmins* (brāhmaṇā) is just a saying in the world.
commentary_pali: 317.Evaṃme sutanti madhurasuttaṃ. Tattha mahākaccānoti gihikāle ujjenikarañño purohitaputto abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ca. Madhurāyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Gundāvaneti kaṇhakagundāvane . Avantiputtoti avantiraṭṭhe rañño dhītāya putto. Vuddho ceva arahā cāti daharaṃ arahantampi na tathā sambhāventi yathā mahallakaṃ, thero pana vuddho ceva ahosi arahā ca. Brāhmaṇā, bho kaccānāti so kira rājā brāhmaṇaladdhiko, tasmā evamāha. Brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇotiādīsu jātigottādīnaṃ paññāpanaṭṭhāne brāhmaṇāva seṭṭhāti dasseti. Hīno añño vaṇṇoti itare tayo vaṇṇā hīnā lāmakāti vadati. Sukkoti paṇḍaro. Kaṇhoti kāḷako. Sujjhantīti jātigottādipaññāpanaṭṭhānesu sujjhanti. Brahmuno puttāti mahābrahmuno puttā. Orasā mukhato jātāti ure vasitvā mukhato nikkhantā, ure katvā saṃvaddhitāti vā orasā. Brahmajāti brahmato nibbattā. Brahmanimmitāti brahmunā nimmitā. Brahmadāyādāti brahmuno dāyādā. Ghosoyeva kho esoti vohāramattamevetaṃ.
commentary_english:
317. Thus, I heard, [is] the Madhura Sutta.

There, Mahākaccāna means, in the householder period, the son of the chaplain of Ujjeni King, handsome, beautiful, pleasing, golden-colored, and.

Madhurā means in a city of that name.

Gundāvana means in Kaṇhakagundāvana.

Avantiputta means the son of the daughter of the king in the Avanti country.

Vuddha and Arahā means they do not honor a young Arahant as much as an old man; but a Thera was old and an Arahant.

Brāhmaṇas, bho Kaccānā means that king was one who obtained [his position] from Brahmins, therefore he spoke thus.

Brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, etc., means that in the designation of jāti, gotta, etc., he shows that only the brāhmaṇas are the best.

Hīno añño vaṇṇo means the other three *vaṇṇas* are low and wretched, he says.

Sukko means paṇḍaro.

Kaṇho means kāḷako.

Sujjhantī means in the designation of *jāti*, *gotta*, etc., they are purified.

Brahmuno puttā means the sons of Mahābrahmā.

Orasā mukhato jātā means having lived in the breast, having emerged from the mouth, or having made [him] in [his] breast, he was raised, or [they are] *orasa*.

Brahmajā means born from Brahmā.

Brahmanimmitā means created by Brahmā.

Brahmadāyādā means the heirs of Brahmā.

Ghosoyeva kho eso means it is merely a convention.

mula_pali:
318. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, khattiyassa cepi ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā khattiyopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… brāhmaṇopissāssa… vessopissāssa… suddopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī’’ti? ‘‘Khattiyassa cepi, bho kaccāna, ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā khattiyopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… brāhmaṇopissāssa… vessopissāssa… suddopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī’’ti.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, brāhmaṇassa cepi ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā brāhmaṇopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… vessopissāssa… suddopissāssa … khattiyopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī’’ti? ‘‘Brāhmaṇassa cepi, bho kaccāna, ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā brāhmaṇopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… vessopissāssa… suddopissāssa … khattiyopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī’’ti.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, vessassa cepi ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā vessopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… suddopissāssa… khattiyopissāssa… brāhmaṇopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī’’ti? ‘‘Vessassa cepi, bho kaccāna, ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā vessopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… suddopissāssa… khattiyopissāssa… brāhmaṇopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī’’ti.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, suddassa cepi ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā suddopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… khattiyopissāssa… brāhmaṇopissāssa… vessopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī’’ti? ‘‘Suddassa cepi, bho kaccāna, ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā suddopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādīti… khattiyopissāssa… brāhmaṇopissāssa… vessopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī’’ti.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, yadi evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti no vā? Kathaṃ vā te ettha hotī’’ti? ‘‘Addhā kho, bho kaccāna, evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti. Nesaṃ nāsaṃ (sī.), nāhaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) ettha kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ samanupassāmī’’ti. ‘‘Imināpi kho etaṃ, mahārāja, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā ghoso yeveso lokasmiṃ – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’’’ti.

nāsaṃ (sī.), nāhaṃ (syā. kaṃ.)
mula_english:
318. “What do you think, great king? If a noble (*kṣatriya*) prospers in wealth (*dhana*), grain (*dhānya*), silver (*rajata*), or gold (*jātarūpa*), will there be nobles who rise before him and retire after him, who are eager to serve him, who seek to please him and speak sweetly to him, and will there also be brahmins (*brāhmaṇa*), merchants (*vaiśya*), and workers (*śūdra*) who do likewise?”

“What do you think, great king? If a brahmin prospers in wealth, grain, silver, or gold, will there be brahmins who rise before him and retire after him, who are eager to serve him, who seek to please him and speak sweetly to him, and will there also be merchants, workers, and nobles who do likewise?”

“What do you think, great king? If a merchant prospers in wealth, grain, silver, or gold, will there be merchants who rise before him and retire after him, who are eager to serve him, who seek to please him and speak sweetly to him, and will there also be workers, nobles, and brahmins who do likewise?”

“What do you think, great king? If a worker prospers in wealth, grain, silver, or gold, will there be workers who rise before him and retire after him, who are eager to serve him, who seek to please him and speak sweetly to him, and will there also be nobles, brahmins, and merchants who do likewise?”

commentary_pali: 318.Ijjheyyāti samijjheyya, yattakāni dhanādīni pattheyya, tattakehissa manoratho pūreyyāti attho. Khattiyopissāssāti khattiyopi assa issariyasampattassa pubbuṭṭhāyī assa. Nesaṃ ettha kiñcīti na etesaṃ ettha kiñci.
commentary_english:
"Ijjheyyā" means may be successful, whatever wealth etc. is desired, in that way may his wish be fulfilled, is the meaning.

"Khattiyopissāssā" means even a noble may be an early riser in the attainment of sovereignty.

"Nesaṃ ettha kiñcī" means nothing of theirs is here.

319. “What do you think, great king? Suppose a noble (*kṣatriya*) were to kill living beings (*prāṇātipātī*), take what is not given (*adinnādāyī*), misconduct himself in sensual pleasures (*kāmesumicchācārī*), speak falsely (*musāvādī*), speak maliciously (*pisuṇavāco*), speak harshly (*pharusavāco*), gossip (*samphappalāpī*), be covetous (*abhijjhālu*), have a mind of ill will (*byāpannacitto*), and hold wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*). On the dissolution of the body (*kāyassa bhedā*), after death (*paraṃ maraṇā*), would he be likely to reappear in a state of deprivation (*apāyaṃ*), in an unhappy destination (*duggatiṃ*), in perdition (*vinipātaṃ*), even in hell (*nirayaṃ*), or not? How does it appear to you in this case?”

“Whether it be a noble (*kṣatriyo*), Master Kaccāna, who kills living beings (*prāṇātipātī*), takes what is not given (*adinnādāyī*), misconducts himself in sensual pleasures (*kāmesumicchācārī*), speaks falsely (*musāvādī*), speaks maliciously (*pisuṇavāco*), speaks harshly (*pharusavāco*), gossips (*samphappalāpī*), is covetous (*abhijjhālu*), has a mind of ill will (*byāpannacitto*), and holds wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), on the dissolution of the body (*kāyassa bhedā*), after death (*paraṃ maraṇā*), he is likely to reappear in a state of deprivation (*apāyaṃ*), in an unhappy destination (*duggatiṃ*), in perdition (*vinipātaṃ*), even in hell (*nirayaṃ*). That is how it appears to me in this case, and thus I have heard from the arahants.”

“Excellent, excellent, great king! It is good that this appears to you thus, great king, and good that you have heard this from the arahants. What do you think, great king? Suppose a Brahmin…a merchant… a worker were to kill living beings, take what is not given…and hold wrong view. On the dissolution of the body, after death, would he be likely to reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell, or not? How does it appear to you in this case?”

“Whether it be a worker (*śūddo*), Master Kaccāna, who kills living beings (*prāṇātipātī*), takes what is not given (*adinnādāyī*)…and holds wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), on the dissolution of the body (*kāyassa bhedā*), after death (*paraṃ maraṇā*), he is likely to reappear in a state of deprivation (*apāyaṃ*), in an unhappy destination (*duggatiṃ*), in perdition (*vinipātaṃ*), even in hell (*nirayaṃ*). 320. “What do you think, great king? On the dissolution of the body (*kāyassa bhedā*), after death (*paraṃ maraṇā*), would he be likely to reappear in a happy destination (*sugatiṃ*), even in the heavenly world (*saggaṃ lokaṃ*), or not (*upapajjeyya no vā*)? What do you think about this?”

“Even a noble (*khattiyopi hi*), venerable Kaccāna, who abstains from killing living beings (*pāṇātipātā paṭivirato*), abstains from taking what is not given (*adinnādānā paṭivirato*), abstains from misconduct in sensual pleasures (*kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato*), abstains from false speech (*musāvādā paṭivirato*), abstains from malicious speech (*pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato*), abstains from harsh speech (*pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato*), abstains from gossip (*samphappalāpā paṭivirato*), is uncovetous (*anabhijjhālu*), has a mind without ill will (*abyāpannacitto*), and holds right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), on the dissolution of the body (*kāyassa bhedā*), after death (*paraṃ maraṇā*), is likely to reappear in a happy destination (*sugatiṃ*), even in the heavenly world (*saggaṃ lokaṃ*). “Excellent (*sādhu*)! Excellent (*sādhu*), great king (*mahārāja*)! What do you think about this?”

“Even a worker (*śūdra*), venerable Kaccāna, who abstains from killing living beings (*pāṇātipātā paṭivirato*), abstains from taking what is not given (*adinnādānā paṭivirato*)… and holds right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), on the dissolution of the body (*kāyassa bhedā*), after death (*paraṃ maraṇā*), is likely to reappear in a happy destination (*sugatiṃ*), even in the heavenly world (*saggaṃ lokaṃ*). Thus it appears to me here, and thus I have heard from the worthy ones (*arahataṃ sutaṃ*).”

mula_english:
321. “What do you think, great king? Suppose a noble (*kṣatriya*) were to break into houses (*sandhiṃ chindeyya*), plunder wealth (*nillopaṃ hareyya*), commit burglary (*ekāgārikaṃ kareyya*), ambush highways (*paripanthe vā tiṭṭheyya*), or seduce another’s wife (*paradāraṃ vā gaccheyya*), and if your men arrested him and produced him, saying: ‘Sire, this is the culprit; this is a criminal (*coro āgucārī*).
Command what punishment you wish for him (*imassa yaṃ icchasi taṃ daṇḍaṃ paṇehī’ti*).’ What would you do to him?” “We would have him executed (*ghāteyyāma*), Master Kaccāna, or we would have him fined (*jāpeyyāma*), or we would have him exiled (*pabbājeyyāma*), or we would do with him as he deserved (*yathāpaccayaṃ vā kareyyāma*).
What is the reason for that (*taṃ kissa hetu*)? Because his former designation ‘noble’ (*khattiyo’ti samaññā*) would have disappeared (*antarahitā*); he would simply go by the name of thief (*corotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatī’’ti*).”

“What do you think, great king? Suppose a brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*), a merchant (*vessa*), a worker (*śūddo*) were to break into houses, plunder wealth, commit burglary, ambush highways, or seduce another’s wife, and if your men arrested him and produced him, saying: ‘Sire, this is the culprit; this is a criminal.

There is no difference between them at all that I see (*nesaṃ ettha kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ samanupassāmī’’ti*).”

mula_english:
322. “What do you think, great king? Suppose a noble (kṣatriya) here shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness, abstaining from killing living beings (prāṇātipātā), abstaining from taking what is not given (adinnādānā), abstaining from false speech (musāvādā), refraining from nocturnal meals, eating only one meal a day, living a life of chastity (brahmacārī), virtuous (śīlavā), and of good character (kalyāṇadhammo). What would you do for him?” “We would bow down to him, Master Kāccāna, or rise up to greet him, or offer him a seat, or invite him to accept robes, alms-food, lodgings, or medicinal requisites for curing illness; or we would arrange for him lawful guarding, defense, and protection. Why is that? Because his former designation, ‘a noble,’ has vanished; he is simply reckoned as a renunciate (śramaṇa).”

Why is that? Because his former designation, ‘a worker,’ has vanished; he is simply reckoned as a renunciate (śramaṇa).”

“What do you think, great king? If that is so, then are these four castes (varṇā) all the same, or are they not? How do you see it?” “Indeed, Master Kāccāna, if that is so, then these four castes (varṇā) are all the same. I see no difference between them at all.”

“That is also a way, great king, whereby it can be understood how that statement in the world is just a saying: ‘The Brahmin (brāhmaṇa) is the highest caste (varṇa), other castes (varṇa) are inferior; the Brahmin (brāhmaṇa) is the fair caste (varṇa), other castes (varṇa) are dark; only Brahmins (brāhmaṇā) are purified, not non-Brahmins; Brahmins (brāhmaṇā) are the legitimate sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, offspring of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, heirs of Brahmā."
commentary_pali:
322.Āsanena vā nimanteyyāmāti nisinnāsanaṃ papphoṭetvā idha nisīdāti vadeyyāma. Abhinimanteyyāmapi nanti abhiharitvā taṃ nimanteyyāma. Tattha duvidho abhihāro vācāya ceva kāyena ca. ‘‘Tumhākaṃ icchiticchitakkhaṇe mamaṃ cīvarādīhi vadeyyātha yenattho’’ti vadanto hi vācāya abhiharitvā nimanteti nāma. Cīvarādivekallaṃ sallakkhetvā ‘‘idaṃ gaṇhathā’’ti tāni dento pana kāyena abhiharitvā nimanteti nāma. Tadubhayampi sandhāya ‘‘abhinimanteyyāmapi na’’nti āha. Rakkhāvaraṇaguttinti rakkhāsaṅkhātañceva āvaraṇasaṅkhātañca guttiṃ. Yā panesā āvudhahatthe purise ṭhapentena rakkhā, sā dhammikā nāma saṃvihitā na hoti. Yathā pana avelāya kaṭṭhahārikāpaṇṇahārikādayo vihāraṃ na pavisanti, migaluddakādayo vihārasīmāya mige vā macche vā na gaṇhanti, evaṃ saṃvidahantena dhammikā nāma saṃvihitā hoti. Taṃ sandhāyāha ‘‘dhammika’’nti.

Evaṃsanteti evaṃ catunnampi vaṇṇānaṃ pabbajitānaṃ pabbajitasakkārena same samāne. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Evaṃ sante

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Madhurasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
322. "Should we invite [him] with a seat?" Saying this, having snapped the prepared seat, one should say, "Sit here."
"Even if we over-invite [him], no," [meaning] having brought it near, we should invite him.
There, the bringing near is twofold: by speech and by body.
"At whatever moment you desire, you should speak to me with robes etc., by which there is a purpose," thus, speaking, indeed, by speech, he invites, it is said.
Having considered the lack of robes etc., "Take this," giving those, however, by body, he invites, it is said.
Having considered both of these, he said, "Even if we over-invite [him], no."
*rakṣāvaraṇagutti* means protection, guarding, and preservation, namely, something that is counted as protection and something that is counted as guarding.
That protection by which a person is stationed with a weapon in hand, that is not called a *dhārmikā* (righteous) arrangement.
Just as, however, at the wrong time, firewood carriers, leaf carriers, etc., do not enter the monastery, hunters etc., do not seize deer or fish within the boundary of the monastery, thus, by arranging, it is called a *dhārmikā* arrangement.
Having considered that, he said, "*dhārmikā*."

"Thus, while it exists," thus, in this way, for all four castes, for those who have gone forth, with the honor of those who have gone forth, it is the same, equal.
The rest is clear throughout.

Thus, while it exists, the *Papañcasūdanī* commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*, the *Madhurasuttavaṇṇanā*, is finished.

mula_pali:
323. Evaṃ vutte, rājā mādhuro avantiputto āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘abhikkantaṃ, bho kaccāna, abhikkantaṃ, bho kaccāna! Seyyathāpi, bho kaccāna, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya – ‘cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī’ti; evamevaṃ bhotā kaccānena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ bhavantaṃ kaccānaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca . Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ kaccāno dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata’’nti. ‘‘Mā kho maṃ tvaṃ, mahārāja, saraṇaṃ agamāsi. Tameva tvaṃ tametaṃ tvaṃ (syā. kaṃ.), tametaṃ (ka.) bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gaccha yamahaṃ saraṇaṃ gato’’ti. ‘‘Kahaṃ pana, bho kaccāna, etarahi so bhagavā viharati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho’’ti? ‘‘Parinibbuto kho, mahārāja, etarahi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho’’ti. ‘‘Sacepi mayaṃ, bho kaccāna, suṇeyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ dasasu yojanesu, dasapi mayaṃ yojanāni gaccheyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ. Sacepi mayaṃ, bho kaccāna, suṇeyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ vīsatiyā yojanesu, tiṃsāya yojanesu, cattārīsāya yojanesu, paññāsāya yojanesu, paññāsampi mayaṃ yojanāni gaccheyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ. Yojanasate cepi mayaṃ bho kaccāna, suṇeyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ, yojanasatampi mayaṃ gaccheyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ. Yato ca, bho kaccāna, parinibbuto so bhagavā, parinibbutampi mayaṃ bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāma dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ kaccāno dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata’’nti.

Madhurasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.
mula_english:
When this was said, King Avantiputta of Madhura said to the venerable Mahā-Kaccāna: “Magnificent, Master Kaccāna! Magnificent, Master Kaccāna! Just as, Master Kaccāna, one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or point out the path to one who was lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the dark, so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been revealed in many ways by Master Kaccāna.

I go to Master Kaccāna for refuge, and to the Dharma, and to the monastic community ( *bhikkhusaṃgha* ). May Master Kaccāna regard me as a lay follower ( *upāsaka* ) who, from this day forward, has gone for refuge for life.”

“Do not go to me for refuge, great king. Go to the Blessed One ( *bhagavant* ) for refuge, to whom I have gone for refuge.”

“But where, Master Kaccāna, does that Blessed One ( *bhagavā* ), the worthy one, the fully enlightened one, reside now?”

“That Blessed One ( *bhagavā* ), great king, the worthy one, the fully enlightened one, has attained final *parinirvāṇa*.”

“If we were to hear, Master Kaccāna, that that Blessed One ( *bhagavant* ) was within ten *yojanas*, we would go ten *yojanas* in order to see that Blessed One ( *bhagavant* ), the worthy one, the fully enlightened one. If we were to hear, Master Kaccāna, that that Blessed One ( *bhagavant* ) was within twenty *yojanas*…thirty *yojanas*…forty *yojanas*…fifty *yojanas*, we would go fifty *yojanas* in order to see that Blessed One ( *bhagavant* ), the worthy one, the fully enlightened one. If we were to hear, Master Kaccāna, that that Blessed One ( *bhagavant* ) was within a hundred *yojanas*, we would go a hundred *yojanas* in order to see that Blessed One ( *bhagavant* ), the worthy one, the fully enlightened one.

And since, Master Kaccāna, that Blessed One ( *bhagavā* ) has attained final *parinirvāṇa*, we go to that Blessed One ( *bhagavant* ) for refuge, and to the Dharma, and to the monastic community ( *bhikkhusaṃgha* ). May Master Kaccāna regard me as a lay follower ( *upāsaka* ) who, from this day forward, has gone for refuge for life.”

The Madhura Sutta, the fourth, is finished.

mula_pali: 324. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā bhaggesu viharati susumāragire bhesakaḷāvane migadāye. Tena kho pana samayena bodhissa rājakumārassa kokanado kokanudo (syā. kaṃ. ka.) nāma pāsādo acirakārito hoti anajjhāvuṭṭho samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā kenaci vā manussabhūtena. Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro sañjikāputtaṃ māṇavaṃ āmantesi – ‘‘ehi tvaṃ, samma sañjikāputta, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vanda, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ puccha – ‘bodhi, bhante, rājakumāro bhagavato pāde sirasā vandati, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchatī’ti. Evañca vadehi – ‘adhivāsetu kira, bhante, bhagavā bodhissa rājakumārassa svātanāya bhattaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā’’’ti. ‘‘Evaṃ, bho’’ti kho sañjikāputto māṇavo bodhissa rājakumārassa paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho sañjikāputto māṇavo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘bodhi kho bodhi bho gotama (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) rājakumāro bhoto gotamassa pāde sirasā vandati, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchati. Evañca vadeti – ‘adhivāsetu kira bhavaṃ gotamo bodhissa rājakumārassa svātanāya bhattaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā’’’ti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena. Atha kho sañjikāputto māṇavo bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ viditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā yena bodhi rājakumāro tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bodhiṃ rājakumāraṃ etadavoca – ‘‘avocumha bhoto vacanena taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ – ‘bodhi kho rājakumāro bhoto gotamassa pāde sirasā vandati, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchati. Evañca vadeti – adhivāsetu kira bhavaṃ gotamo bodhissa rājakumārassa svātanāya bhattaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā’ti. Adhivuṭṭhañca pana samaṇena gotamenā’’ti.
mula_english:
324. Thus I have heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas in Susumāragiri in the Bhesakala Grove, the deer park.

Now on that occasion a palace named Kokanada had recently been built for Prince Bodhi, and it had not yet been inhabited by any recluse (*śramaṇa*) or *brāhmaṇa* or any human being at all.

Then Prince Bodhi addressed the *brāhmaṇa* student Sanjikaputta thus: “Come, my dear Sanjikaputta, go to the Blessed One and pay homage in my name with your head at his feet, and ask whether he is free from illness and affliction and is healthy, strong, and abiding in comfort, saying: ‘Venerable sir (*bhante*), Prince Bodhi pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and he asks whether the Blessed One is free from illness…and abiding in comfort.’

Then say this: ‘Venerable sir (*bhante*), let the Blessed One together with the *saṃgha* of *bhikkhus* consent to accept tomorrow’s meal from Prince Bodhi.’“

“Yes, sir (*bho*),” Sanjikaputta replied, and he went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.

When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side.

Sitting at one side, Sanjikaputta said to the Blessed One: “Prince Bodhi pays homage with his head at Master Gotama’s feet and asks whether he is free from illness…and abiding in comfort.

And he says this: ‘Let Master Gotama together with the *saṃgha* of *bhikkhus* consent to accept tomorrow’s meal from Prince Bodhi.’“

The Blessed One consented by maintaining silence (*tuṇhībhāvena*).

Then, knowing that the Blessed One had consented, Sanjikaputta rose from his seat, went to Prince Bodhi, and told him what had happened, adding:

“I told Master Gotama in your words: ‘Prince Bodhi pays homage with his head at Master Gotama’s feet and asks whether he is free from sickness, free from illness, in good health, and living comfortably.

And he says this: ‘Let Master Gotama together with the *saṃgha* of *bhikkhus* consent to accept tomorrow’s meal from Prince Bodhi.’“

“And the recluse Gotama has consented.”
commentary_pali: 324.Evaṃme sutanti bodhirājakumārasuttaṃ. Tattha kokanadoti kokanadaṃ vuccati padumaṃ. So ca maṅgalapāsādo olokanakapadumaṃ dassetvā kato, tasmā kokanadoti saṅkhaṃ labhi.
commentary_english:
Thus, the *Bodhirājakumārasūtra*, "[regarding] what was heard by me."

There, *kokanada* means *paduma*, the lotus.

And that auspicious palace (*maṅgalapāsāda*) was made displaying the *olokanaka paduma*; therefore it obtained the designation *kokanada*.

mula_pali: 325. Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro tassā rattiyā accayena sake nivesane paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā, kokanadañca pāsādaṃ odātehi dussehi santharāpetvā yāva pacchimasopānakaḷevarā kaḷebarā (sī.), sañjikāputtaṃ māṇavaṃ āmantesi – ‘‘ehi tvaṃ, samma sañjikāputta, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavato kālaṃ ārocehi – ‘kālo, bhante, niṭṭhitaṃ bhatta’’’nti. ‘‘Evaṃ, bho’’ti kho sañjikāputto māṇavo bodhissa rājakumārassa paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavato kālaṃ ārocesi – ‘‘kālo, bho gotama, niṭṭhitaṃ bhatta’’nti. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena bodhissa rājakumārassa nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkami. Tena kho pana samayena bodhi rājakumāro bahidvārakoṭṭhake ṭhito hoti bhagavantaṃ āgamayamāno. Addasā kho bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna paccuggantvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā purakkhatvā yena kokanado pāsādo tenupasaṅkami. Atha kho bhagavā pacchimaṃ sopānakaḷevaraṃ nissāya aṭṭhāsi. Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘abhiruhatu abhirūhatu (syā. kaṃ. pī.) akkamatu (cūḷava. 268), bhante, bhagavā dussāni, abhiruhatu sugato dussāni; yaṃ mama assa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā’’ti. Evaṃ vutte, bhagavā tuṇhī ahosi. Dutiyampi kho…pe… tatiyampi kho bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘abhiruhatu, bhante, bhagavā. Dussāni, abhiruhatu sugato dussāni; yaṃ mama assa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā’’ti.
mula_english:
325.
Then, when the night had passed, Prince Bodhi, having had prepared fine food, both खादनिय *khādanīya* and भोजनीय *bhojanīya*, in his own residence, and having had the Kokanada Palace spread with white cloths as far as the last step of the staircase, addressed the brahmin student Sañjikaputta thus: “Come, my dear Sañjikaputta, go to the Blessed One *bhagavā* and announce that it is time thus: ‘It is time, venerable sir *bhante*, the meal is ready.’”

“Yes, sir,” Sañjikaputta replied, and he went to the Blessed One *bhagavā* and announced that it was time thus: “It is time, Master Gotama, the meal is ready.”

Then the Blessed One *bhagavā*, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, went to Prince Bodhi's residence.

Now at that time Prince Bodhi was standing in the outer gatehouse, waiting for the Blessed One *bhagavantaṃ*.

Prince Bodhi saw the Blessed One *bhagavantaṃ* coming from afar.

Having seen him, he went out to meet him and, having paid homage to the Blessed One *bhagavantaṃ*, and respectfully leading him, he went to the Kokanada Palace.

Then the Blessed One *bhagavā* stood near the last step of the staircase.

Then Prince Bodhi said this to the Blessed One *bhagavantaṃ*: “Venerable sir *bhante*, may the Blessed One *bhagavā* step on the cloths; may the Well-Gone *sugata* step on the cloths, that it may be for my long-term benefit and happiness.”

When this was said, the Blessed One *bhagavā* was silent.

A second time… A third time Prince Bodhi said this to the Blessed One *bhagavantaṃ*: “Venerable sir *bhante*, may the Blessed One *bhagavā* step on the cloths; may the Well-Gone *sugata* step on the cloths, that it may be for my long-term benefit and happiness.”
commentary_pali:
325.Yāva pacchimasopānakaḷevarāti ettha pacchimasopānakaḷevaranti paṭhamaṃ sopānaphalakaṃ vuttaṃ. Addasākhoti olokanatthaṃyeva dvārakoṭṭhake ṭhito addasa. Bhagavā tuṇhī ahosīti ‘‘kissa nu kho atthāya rājakumārena ayaṃ mahāsakkāro kato’’ti āvajjanto puttapatthanāya katabhāvaṃ aññāsi. So hi rājakumāro aputtako, sutañcānena ahosi – ‘‘buddhānaṃ kira adhikāraṃ katvā manasā icchitaṃ labhantī’’ti. So – ‘‘sacāhaṃ puttaṃ labhissāmi, sammāsambuddho mama celappaṭikaṃ akkamissati. No ce labhissāmi, na akkamissatī’’ti patthanaṃ katvā santharāpesi. Atha bhagavā ‘‘nibbattissati nu kho etassa putto’’ti āvajjetvā ‘‘na nibbattissatī’’ti addasa.

Pubbe kira so ekasmiṃ dīpe vasamāno samacchandena sakuṇapotake khādi. Sacassa mātugāmo aññova bhaveyya, puttaṃ labheyya. Ubhohi pana samānacchandehi hutvā pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, tenassa putto na nibbattissatīti aññāsi. Dusse pana akkante – ‘‘buddhānaṃ adhikāraṃ katvā patthitapatthitaṃ labhantīti loke anussavo, mayā ca mahāabhinīhāro kato, na ca puttaṃ labhāmi, tucchaṃ idaṃ vacana’’nti micchāgahaṇaṃ gaṇheyya. Titthiyāpi – ‘‘natthi samaṇānaṃ akattabbaṃ nāma, celappaṭikaṃ maddantā āhiṇḍantī’’ti ujjhāyeyyuṃ . Etarahi ca akkamantesu bahū bhikkhū paracittaviduno, te bhabbaṃ jānitvā akkamissanti, abhabbaṃ jānitvā na akkamissanti. Anāgate pana upanissayo mando bhavissati, anāgataṃ na jānissanti. Tesu akkamantesu sace patthitaṃ ijjhissati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ . No ce ijjhissati, – ‘‘pubbe bhikkhusaṅghassa abhinīhāraṃ katvā icchiticchitaṃ labhanti, taṃ idāni na labhanti . Teyeva maññe bhikkhū paṭipattipūrakā ahesuṃ, ime paṭipattiṃ pūretuṃ na sakkontī’’ti manussā vippaṭisārino bhavissantīti imehi kāraṇehi bhagavā akkamituṃ anicchanto tuṇhī ahosi. Sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi ‘‘na, bhikkhave, celappaṭikā akkamitabbā’’ti (cūḷava. 268). Maṅgalatthāya paññattaṃ anakkamantesu pana akkamanatthāya anupaññattiṃ ṭhapesi – ‘‘gihī, bhikkhave, maṅgalikā, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gihīnaṃ maṅgalatthāyā’’ti (cūḷava. 268).
commentary_english:
325. "Yāva pacchimasopāṇakaḷevarā ti ettha pacchimasopāṇakaḷevara" means the first step-plank is stated.

addasā kho ti: He saw, standing at the doorway, just for the sake of looking.

bhagavā tuṇhī ahosī ti: The Blessed One was silent, thinking, "For what purpose has this great honor been done by the prince?" he understood it to be done for the sake of a son.

So hi rājakumāro aputtako, sutañcānena ahosi – "buddhānaṃ kira adhikāraṃ katvā manasā icchitaṃ labhantī"ti: For that prince was childless, and it had been heard by him that "by making an offering to the Buddhas, they obtain what is desired by the mind."

So – "sacāhaṃ puttaṃ labhissāmi, sammāsambuddho mama celappaṭikaṃ akkamissati. No ce labhissāmi, na akkamissatī"ti patthanaṃ katvā santharāpesi: He, thinking, "If I obtain a son, the Perfectly Enlightened One will step on my garment. If I do not obtain [one], he will not step," had a layer [of cloth] spread out.

Atha bhagavā ‘‘nibbattissati nu kho etassa putto’’ti āvajjetvā ‘‘na nibbattissatī’’ti addasa: Then the Blessed One, reflecting, "Will a son be born to him?", saw, "He will not be born."

Previously, it seems, while living on an island, he ate young birds with equal desire.

If there should be a different mother for him, he might obtain a son.

But having committed an evil deed with similar desire, he understood that a son will not be born to him.

If they step on the cloth, they might take up a wrong idea, thinking, "In the world it is heard that by making an offering to the Buddhas, they obtain whatever they desire, and a great effort has been made by me, but I do not obtain a son; this saying is empty."

Even the sectarians might criticize, saying, "There is nothing that these ascetics should not do; they wander about trampling on cloths."

And now, if they step on it, many monks are knowers of others' minds; knowing what is possible, they will step on it; knowing what is impossible, they will not step on it.

But in the future, the basis will be weak, and they will not know the future.

If, when they step on it, what is desired is achieved, that will be skillful.

If it is not achieved, people will become remorseful, thinking, "Formerly, by making an offering to the community of monks, they obtained whatever they desired; now they do not obtain [it]. Those monks, I think, were fulfillers of practice; these are not able to fulfill the practice." Because of these reasons, the Blessed One, not wanting to step on it, was silent.

He established a training rule, "Monks, garments should not be stepped on." (Cūḷava. 268)

Having established [that it is] for the sake of auspiciousness, when they do not step on it, he established a secondary rule for the sake of stepping on it, "Householders, monks, are auspicious; I allow, monks, [offerings] for the sake of auspiciousness for householders." (Cūḷava. 268)

mula_pali: 326. Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ apalokesi. Atha kho āyasmā ānando bodhiṃ rājakumāraṃ etadavoca – ‘‘saṃharatu, rājakumāra, dussāni; na bhagavā celapaṭikaṃ celapattikaṃ (sī. pī.) akkamissati. Pacchimaṃ janataṃ tathāgato anukampatī’’ti apaloketīti (sabbattha). Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro dussāni saṃharāpetvā uparikokanadapāsāde uparikokanade pāsāde (sī. pī. vinayeca), uparikokanade (syā. kaṃ.) āsanāni paññapesi. Atha kho bhagavā kokanadaṃ pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena sahatthā santappesi sampavāresi. Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ bhuttāviṃ onītapattapāṇiṃ aññataraṃ nīcaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘mayhaṃ kho, bhante, evaṃ hoti – ‘na kho sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, dukkhena kho sukhaṃ adhigantabba’’’nti.
mula_english:
Then, the Blessed One looked at venerable Ānanda.

Then venerable Ānanda said this to Prince Bodhi: "Prince, let the cloths be removed. The Blessed One will not step on a strip of cloth (celapaṭikaṃ). The *Tathāgata* looks with compassion on future generations."

Then Prince Bodhi had the cloths folded up and had seats prepared up in the upper Kokanada palace.

Then the Blessed One, having ascended to the Kokanada palace, sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*).

Then Prince Bodhi, with his own hands, served and satisfied the community of monks, with the Buddha at its head, with exquisite staple and non-staple food (khādanīyena bhojanīyena).

Then Prince Bodhi, after the Blessed One had eaten and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl (onītapattapāṇiṃ), took a low seat and sat down to one side.

Having sat down to one side, Prince Bodhi said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it occurs to me thus: 'Pleasure is not to be gained through pleasure; pleasure is to be gained through pain.'"
commentary_pali: 326.Pacchimaṃ janataṃ tathāgato anukampatīti idaṃ thero vuttesu kāraṇesu tatiyaṃ kāraṇaṃ sandhāyāha. Na kho sukhena sukhanti kasmā āha? Kāmasukhallikānuyogasaññī hutvā sammāsambuddho na akkami, tasmā ahampi satthārā samānacchando bhavissāmīti maññamāno evamāha.
commentary_english:
326. The phrase, "The *Tathāgata* has compassion for the later generations" refers to the third reason among the reasons stated by the elders.

Why is it said, "Bliss is not attained through bliss"? Because the perfectly enlightened Buddha did not proceed by adhering to sensual pleasures; therefore, thinking "I too will have the same inclination as the Teacher," he spoke thus.

mula_pali:
327. ‘‘Mayhampi kho, rājakumāra, pubbeva sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato etadahosi – ‘na kho sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, dukkhena kho sukhaṃ adhigantabba’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, aparena samayena daharova samāno susukāḷakeso bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato paṭhamena vayasā akāmakānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ assumukhānaṃ rudantānaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajiṃ. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno kiṃkusalagavesī kiṃkusalaṃgavesī (ka.) anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso kālāma, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu’nti. Evaṃ vutte, rājakumāra, āḷāro kālāmo maṃ etadavoca – ‘viharatāyasmā, tādiso ayaṃ dhammo yattha viññū puriso nacirasseva sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇiṃ. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, tāvatakeneva oṭṭhapahatamattena lapitalāpanamattena ñāṇavādañca vadāmi, theravādañca jānāmi passāmīti ca paṭijānāmi, ahañceva aññe ca. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘na kho āḷāro kālāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti; addhā āḷāro kālāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ viharatī’ti.

‘‘Atha khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā no, āvuso kālāma, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesī’ti upasampajja pavedesīti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)? Evaṃ vutte, rājakumāra, āḷāro kālāmo ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi saddhā, mayhaṃpatthi saddhā; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi vīriyaṃ…pe… sati… samādhi… paññā, mayhaṃpatthi paññā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ āḷāro kālāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya padaheyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Atha khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘ettāvatā no, āvuso kālāma, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti? ‘Ettāvatā kho ahaṃ, āvuso, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemī’ti. ‘Ahampi kho, āvuso, ettāvatā imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī’ti. ‘Lābhā no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ no, āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma . Iti yāhaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemi, taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi. Yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi, tamahaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemi. Iti yāhaṃ dhammaṃ jānāmi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi; yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi tamahaṃ dhammaṃ jānāmi. Iti yādiso ahaṃ, tādiso tuvaṃ; yādiso tuvaṃ tādiso ahaṃ. Ehi dāni, āvuso, ubhova santā imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharāmā’ti. Iti kho, rājakumāra, āḷāro kālāmo ācariyo me samāno (attano) ( ) natthi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) antevāsiṃ maṃ samānaṃ attanā attano (sī. pī.) samasamaṃ ṭhapesi, uḷārāya ca maṃ pūjāya pūjesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva ākiñcaññāyatanūpapattiyā’ti . So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, taṃ dhammaṃ analaṅkaritvā tasmā dhammā nibbijja apakkamiṃ.

upasampajja pavedesīti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) ( ) natthi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) attano (sī. pī.)
mula_english:
327. “To me also, Prince, before the Awakening, while I was still only an unenlightened Bodhisatta, it occurred to me: ‘Pleasure is not to be gained through pleasure; pleasure is to be gained through pain.’

Later, while still young, a black-haired young man endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, though my mother and father wished otherwise and wept with tearful faces, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.

So, having gone forth in this way, seeking what is skillful, searching for the unsurpassed peaceful state, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma; having gone to him, I said to Āḷāra Kālāma: ‘I wish, friend Kālāma, to lead the holy life in this *dharma* and *vinaya*.’

When this was said, Prince, Āḷāra Kālāma said to me: ‘The venerable one may stay here. This *dharma* is such that a wise man can soon enter upon and abide in it, realising for himself through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.’

I soon quickly learned that *dharma*.

As far as mere lip-reciting and rehearsal of his teaching went, I could speak with knowledge and assurance, and I claimed, ‘I know and see’—and there were others who did likewise.

I considered: ‘It is not through mere faith alone that Āḷāra Kālāma declares: “By realising for myself with direct knowledge, I enter upon and abide in this *dharma*.” Certainly Āḷāra Kālāma abides knowing and seeing this *dharma*.’

Then I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and asked him: ‘Friend Kālāma, in what way do you declare that by realising for yourself with direct knowledge you enter upon and abide in this *dharma*?’
Āḷāra Kālāma declared the Sphere of Nothingness.

I considered: ‘Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has faith, *vīrya* (energy), *sati* (mindfulness), *samādhi* (concentration), and *prajñā* (wisdom). I too have faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

Suppose I endeavour to realise the *dharma* that Āḷāra Kālāma declares he enters upon and abides in by realising for himself with direct knowledge?’

I soon quickly entered upon and abided in that *dharma* by realising for myself with direct knowledge.

Then I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and asked him: ‘Friend Kālāma, is it in this way that you declare that you enter upon and abide in this *dharma* by realising for yourself with direct knowledge?’
‘That is the way, friend.’

‘I too, friend, enter upon and abide in this *dharma* by realising for myself with direct knowledge.’

‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great gain for us that we have such a venerable one for our companion in the holy life.

So the *dharma* that I declare I enter upon and abide in by realising for myself with direct knowledge is the *dharma* that you enter upon and abide in by realising for yourself with direct knowledge.

And the *dharma* that you enter upon and abide in by realising for yourself with direct knowledge is the *dharma* that I declare I enter upon and abide in by realising for myself with direct knowledge.

So you know the *dharma* that I know and I know the *dharma* that you know.

As I am, so are you; as you are, so am I.

Come, friend, let us now lead this community together.’

Thus Āḷāra Kālāma, my teacher, placed me, his pupil, on an equal footing with himself and awarded me the highest honour.

But it occurred to me: ‘This *dharma* does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge (*abhijñā*), to enlightenment (*sambodha*), to *Nibbāna*, but only to reappearance in the base of nothingness.
So I, O prince, not being satisfied with that *dharma*, being disappointed with that *dharma*, I left.

commentary_pali: 327.So kho ahantiādi ‘‘yāva rattiyā pacchime yāme’’ti tāva mahāsaccake (ma. ni. 1.364 ādayo) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Tato paraṃ yāva pañcavaggiyānaṃ āsavakkhayā pāsarāsisutte (ma. ni. 1.272 ādayo) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.
commentary_english:
327. So kho aha, etc., "until the last watch of the night," so much should be understood according to the method stated in Mahāsaccaka (Ma. Ni. 1.364 ādayo).

Furthermore, until the destruction of intoxicants of the group of five monks in the Pāsarāsi Sutta (Ma. Ni. 1.272 ādayo), [it] should be understood according to the method stated.

mula_pali:
328. ‘‘So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, kiṃkusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno yena udako uddako (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso āvuso rāma (sī. syā. kaṃ. ka.) passa ma. ni. 1.278 pāsarāsisutte, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu’nti. Evaṃ vutte, rājakumāra, udako rāmaputto maṃ etadavoca – ‘viharatāyasmā, tādiso ayaṃ dhammo yattha viññū puriso nacirasseva sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇiṃ. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, tāvatakeneva oṭṭhapahatamattena lapitalāpanamattena ñāṇavādañca vadāmi, theravādañca jānāmi passāmīti ca paṭijānāmi, ahañceva aññe ca. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘na kho rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesi; addhā rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ vihāsī’ti. Atha khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā no, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesī’ti? Evaṃ vutte, rājakumāra, udako rāmaputto nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘na kho rāmasseva ahosi saddhā, mayhaṃpatthi saddhā; na kho rāmasseva ahosi vīriyaṃ…pe… sati… samādhi… paññā, mayhaṃpatthi paññā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya padaheyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsiṃ.

‘‘Atha khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘ettāvatā no, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti? ‘Ettāvatā kho, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti. ‘Ahampi kho, āvuso, ettāvatā imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī’ti. ‘Lābhā no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ no, āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma. Iti yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi. Yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi taṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesi. Iti yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo abhiññāsi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi; yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi taṃ dhammaṃ rāmo abhiññāsi. Iti yādiso rāmo ahosi tādiso tuvaṃ, yādiso tuvaṃ tādiso rāmo ahosi. Ehi dāni, āvuso, tuvaṃ imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharā’ti. Iti kho, rājakumāra, udako rāmaputto sabrahmacārī me samāno ācariyaṭṭhāne maṃ ṭhapesi, uḷārāya ca maṃ pūjāya pūjesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpapattiyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, taṃ dhammaṃ analaṅkaritvā tasmā dhammā nibbijja apakkamiṃ.
mula_english:
328. “So, O prince, seeking what is skillful, searching for the unsurpassed state of peace, I went to Udaka Rāmaputta. Having gone, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘I wish, friend, to practice the holy life in this Dharma and discipline.’

When this was said, Udaka Rāmaputta said this to me: ‘The venerable one may stay here. This *dharma* is such that a wise man can soon realize his own teacher’s doctrine through direct knowledge and abide in it, having attained it.’

So, O prince, in no long time, I quickly mastered that *dharma*.

So, O prince, I speak with knowledge and assurance as far as mere lip-reciting and rehearsal of his teaching goes, and I claim, ‘I know and see’—and there were others who did likewise.

It occurred to me: ‘It was not through mere faith alone that Rāma declared: “By realizing for myself with direct knowledge, I enter upon and abide in this *dharma*.” Certainly Rāma abided knowing and seeing this *dharma*.’

Then, O prince, I went to Udaka Rāmaputta. Having gone, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘In what way did Rāma declare that by realizing for himself with direct knowledge he entered upon and abided in this *dharma*?’ When this was said, Udaka Rāmaputta declared the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

It occurred to me: ‘It was not Rāma alone who had faith; I too have faith. It was not Rāma alone who had energy… *pe*… mindfulness… *samādhi*… wisdom; I too have wisdom.

Suppose I endeavor to realize the *dharma* that Rāma declared he entered upon and abided in by realizing for himself with direct knowledge.’

So, O prince, in no long time, I quickly entered upon and abided in that *dharma* by realizing it for myself with direct knowledge.”

“Then, O prince, I went to Udaka Rāmaputta. Having gone, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘Is it in this way that Rāma declared that he entered upon and abided in this *dharma* by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge?’ ‘It is in this way, friend, that Rāma declared that he entered upon and abided in this *dharma* by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge.’ ‘I too, friend, enter upon and abide in this *dharma* in this way by realizing it for myself with direct knowledge.’ ‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great gain for us that we have such a venerable one for our companion in the holy life. So the *dharma* that Rāma declared he entered upon and abided in by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge is the *dharma* that you enter upon and abide in by realizing it for yourself with direct knowledge. And the *dharma* that you enter upon and abide in by realizing it for yourself with direct knowledge is the *dharma* that Rāma declared he entered upon and abided in by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge. So you know the *dharma* that Rāma knew; and the *dharma* you know is the *dharma* Rāma knew. Thus as Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma. Come, friend, now lead this community.’

Thus, O prince, Udaka Rāmaputta, my companion in the holy life, placed me in the position of a teacher and accorded me the highest honor.

It occurred to me: ‘This *dharma* does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to *Nibbāna*, but only to reappearance in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’
