Imehi kho, bho, so bhavaṃ gotamoti, bho ācariya, imehi dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi so bhavaṃ gotamo samannāgato devanagare samussitaratanavicittaṃ suvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viya yojanasatubbedho sabbapāliphullo pāricchattako viya selantaramhi supupphitasālarukkho viya tārāgaṇapaṭimaṇḍitagaganatalamiva ca attano sirivibhavena lokaṃ ālokaṃ kurumāno viya caratīti imatthampi dīpetvā kiriyācāraṃ ācikkhituṃ gacchanto kho panātiādimāha.

Imehi kho, bho, so bhavaṃ gotamo gacchanto kho panā
commentary_english:
386. Therein, *suppatiṭṭhitapāda* means: Just as when others place their foot on the ground, either the ball of the foot, or the heel, or the side touches first, or there is an empty space in the middle, or when they lift it up, only one part of the ball of the foot, etc., rises up first, it is not like that for him. For him, however, like the sole of a golden slipper, the entire sole of the foot touches the ground with a single impact, and rises up from the ground. Therefore, he says, "The venerable Gotama has well-planted feet."

Herein, this is [the meaning] of the Blessed One's well-planted feet: Even if the Blessed One extends his foot intending to step into a hell with hundreds of men, as soon as he does so, the low-lying ground rises up like a bellows filled with wind and becomes level with the earth, and even the high ground sinks down. When he extends his foot intending to step far away, even a mountain the size of Mount Sineru bends down and comes near his foot like a freshly cut cane shoot. Thus, when he performed the Twin Miracle and extended his foot intending to step onto Mount Yugandhara, the mountain bent down and came near his foot, and he stepped on it and then stepped with his second foot into the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Indeed, a place that should be established with the wheel mark cannot become uneven. Thorns, splinters, gravel, urine, feces, phlegm, snot, and other such things go away beforehand, and sink into the earth right there. For the Tathāgata, due to the power of moral virtue, the power of wisdom, the power of Dhamma, and the power of the ten perfections (*pāramī*), this great earth is level, soft, and strewn with flowers. There, the Tathāgata places his foot evenly, lifts it up evenly, and touches the ground with all the edges of his sole.

*Cakkāni* means two wheels on two feet. Their spokes, rims, and hubs have already been mentioned in the Pāli. *Sabbākāraparipūrāni* means: Herein, this distinction should be understood: It is said that in the middle of the sole of those wheels, a hub is visible, a circular line encircling the hub is visible, a band surrounding the hub is visible, the mouth of the nave is visible, the spokes are visible, circular lines are visible on the spokes, the rims are visible, and the rim jewels are visible. This much, indeed, has come in the Pāli itself.

However, the many kinds of [wheel marks] that have not yet come [in the Pāli] should be seen like this: a spear (*śakti*), prosperity (*śrī*), a calf (*vatsa*), delight (*nandi*), a swastika (*sovattika*), an ear ornament (*vaṭaṃsaka*), an increment (*vaḍḍhamānakaṃ*), a pair of fish (*maccayugalaṃ*), a Bhadda seat (*bhaddapīṭhaṃ*), a hook (*aṅkuśaṃ*), a javelin (*tomara*), a palace (*pāsāda*), an archway (*toraṇaṃ*), a white umbrella (*setacchattaṃ*), a sword (*khaggo*), a palm fan (*tālavaṇṭaṃ*), a peacock feather fan (*morahatthako*), a Valabi fan (*vāḷabījanī*), a turban (*uṇhīsaṃ*), a bowl (*patto*), a jewel (*maṇi*), a garland of flowers (*kusumadāmaṃ*), a blue lotus (*nīluppalaṃ*), a red lotus (*rattuppalaṃ*), a white lotus (*setuppalaṃ*), a lotus (*padumaṃ*), a white lotus (*puṇḍarīkaṃ*), a full pot (*puṇṇaghaṭo*), a full bowl (*puṇṇapāti*), the ocean (*samuddo*), the *cakkavāḷa* mountains, the Himalayas (*himavā*), Mount Sineru (*sineru*), the moon and the sun (*candimasūriyā*), the constellations (*nakkhattāni*), the four great continents (*cattāro mahādīpā*), the two thousand minor continents (*dveparittadīpasahassāni*), and lastly, including the retinue of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattirañño parisaṃ*), all this is the entourage of the wheel mark itself.

*Āyatapaṇhī* means long heels (*dīghapaṇhi*), it means having full heels (*paripuṇṇapaṇhi*). Just as for others the ball of the foot is long, the shin is established at the top of the heel, and the heel is like something carved and placed there, it is not like that for the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata, however, two parts out of four parts are the ball of the foot, the shin is established in the third part, and the heel in the fourth part is like a red blanket, round like a ball made by means of an awl.

*Dīghaṅgulī* means: Just as for others some fingers are long and some are short, it is not like that for the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata, however, like a monkey's, the fingers and toes are long, thick at the base, gradually tapering towards the tip, and like green orpiment sticks that have been kneaded with oil and rounded. Therefore, it is said, "long fingers."

*Mudutalunahatthapādo* means soft and tender hands and feet. Soft like a layer of cotton that has been beaten a hundred times and placed after dipping it in clarified butter, and because his hands and feet are always tender like those of a newly born child, [he has] soft and tender hands and feet.

*Jālahatthapādo* means: the space between the fingers is not connected by skin. Someone with such webbed hands does not even receive ordination, being afflicted by a defect of a man. For the Tathāgata, however, the four fingers of the hand and the five toes of the foot are of equal length, and because they are of equal length, the barley mark stands piercing each other. Moreover, his hands and feet are like latticed windows joined by a skilled carpenter. Therefore, it is said, "webbed hands and feet."
<hi rend="bold">Jālahatthapādo</hi>: [He] has webbed hands and feet.

<hi rend="bodytext">Uddhaṃ patiṭṭhitagopphakattā ussaṅkhā pādā assāti</hi> <pb ed="p" n="3.0377"/><hi rend="bold">ussaṅkhapādo</hi>: Because his ankles are set high, his feet are raised; therefore, he is called "ussaṅkhapādo". For others, the ankles are on the back of their feet. Because of that, their feet are stiff, as if bound with a cord; they do not turn easily, and the soles of their feet are not visible when they walk. But for the Tathāgata, the ankles are set high, above. Because of that, from his navel upwards, his body is still, like a golden statue placed on a boat; only the lower part of his body moves. His feet turn easily. The soles of his feet are visible to those standing in front, behind, and on both sides, not only from behind like elephants.

<pb ed="p" n="3.0377"/> <hi rend="bold">Ussaṅkhapādo</hi> <pb ed="m" n="3.0259"/> <hi rend="bodytext"><hi rend="bold">Eṇijaṅgho</hi>ti</hi> eṇimigasadisajaṅgho maṃsussadena paripuṇṇajaṅgho, na ekato baddhapiṇḍikamaṃso <pb ed="v" n="3.0268"/>, samantato samasaṇṭhitena maṃsena parikkhittāhi suvaṭṭitāhi sāligabbhasadisāhi jaṅghāhi samannāgatoti attho: <hi rend="bold">Eṇijaṅgho</hi> means [he] has shanks like those of a gazelle, [his] shanks are full and rounded with muscle, not with the muscle massed in one lump, <pb ed="v" n="3.0268"/> [but] possessed of shanks that are well-rounded, surrounded by evenly distributed muscle, like the inside of a rice stalk; this is the meaning.

<hi rend="bold">Eṇijaṅgho</hi> <pb ed="v" n="3.0268"/> <hi rend="bodytext"><hi rend="bold">Anonamanto</hi>ti</hi> anamanto: <hi rend="bold">Anonamanto</hi> means not bending down.

<hi rend="bodytext">Etenassa akhujjaavāmanabhāvo dīpito</hi>: By this, his state of not being hunchbacked or dwarfish is indicated. For other people are either hunchbacked or dwarfish. For hunchbacks, the upper part of their body is incomplete; for dwarfs, the lower part of their body. Because they have incomplete bodies, they are unable to rub their knees without bending down. But the Tathāgata is able to because he has a complete body.

<hi rend="bold">Anonamanto</hi>: <hi rend="bodytext">Usabhavāraṇādīnaṃ viya suvaṇṇapadumakaṇṇikasadise kose ohitaṃ paṭicchannaṃ vatthaguyhaṃ assāti</hi> <hi rend="bold">kosohitavatthaguyho</hi>: Because his genitals are hidden and concealed in a sheath like the golden lotus pistil of a bull or elephant, [he is called] “kosohitavatthaguyho”.

<hi rend="bold">Vatthaguyha</hi>nti vatthena gūhitabbaṃ aṅgajātaṃ vuccati: <hi rend="bold">Vatthaguyha</hi> means it is called the part of the body that should be hidden by clothing.

<hi rend="bold">Kosohitavatthaguyho. Vatthaguyha</hi> <hi rend="bodytext"><hi rend="bold">Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo</hi>ti</hi> jātihiṅgulakena majjitvā dīpidāṭhāya ghaṃsitvā gerukaparikammaṃ katvā ṭhapitaghanasuvaṇṇarūpakasadisoti attho: <hi rend="bold">Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo</hi> means like a solid gold statue that has been soaked in real vermillion, rubbed with a leopard’s tusk, and treated with red ochre.

<hi rend="bodytext">Etenassa ghanasiniddhasaṇhasarīrataṃ dassetvā chavivaṇṇadassanatthaṃ</hi> <hi rend="bold">kañcanasannibhattaco</hi>ti vuttaṃ, purimassa vā vevacanameva etaṃ: By this, having shown the solidity, smoothness, and tenderness of his body, in order to show the color of his skin, it is said [he] has <hi rend="bold">kañcanasannibhattaco</hi> [skin the color of gold]; or this is simply a synonym of the former.

<hi rend="bold">Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo Kañcanasannibhattaco</hi> <hi rend="bodytext"><hi rend="bold">Rajojalla</hi>nti</hi> <pb ed="p" n="3.0378"/> rajo vā malaṃ vā: <hi rend="bold">Rajojalla</hi> means either dust or dirt.

<hi rend="bold">Na upalimpatī</hi>ti na laggati, padumapalāsato udakabindu viya vivaṭṭati: <hi rend="bold">Na upalimpatī</hi> means it does not stick, [but] rolls off like a drop of water from a lotus leaf.

<hi rend="bodytext">Hatthadhovanapādadhovanādīni pana utuggahaṇatthāya ceva dāyakānaṃ puññaphalatthāya ca buddhā karonti, vattasīsenāpi ca karontiyeva</hi>: But the Buddhas perform washing of hands and washing of feet etc. for the sake of veneration and for the sake of the merit of the donors, and they certainly do so in accordance with custom.

<hi rend="bodytext">Senāsanaṃ pavisantena hi bhikkhunā pāde dhovitvā pavisitabbanti vuttametaṃ</hi>: For it is said that a monk entering a dwelling should enter after washing his feet.

<hi rend="bold">Rajojalla</hi> <pb ed="p" n="3.0378"/> <hi rend="bold">Na upalimpatī</hi> <hi rend="bodytext"><hi rend="bold">Uddhaggalomo</hi>ti</hi> āvaṭṭapariyosāne uddhaggāni hutvā mukhasobhaṃ ullokayamānāni viya ṭhitāni lomāni assāti uddhaggalomo: <hi rend="bold">Uddhaggalomo</hi> means [he] has hairs that stand erect, with the tips turned upwards at the end of the whorls, standing as if looking up at the beauty of [his] face; therefore, [he is called] “uddhaggalomo”.

<hi rend="bold">Uddhaggalomo</hi> <hi rend="bodytext"><hi rend="bold">Brahmūjugatto</hi>ti</hi> <pb ed="m" n="3.0260"/> brahmā viya ujugatto, ujumeva uggatadīghasarīro: <hi rend="bold">Brahmūjugatto</hi> means [he] has an upright body like Brahmā, [his] long body has grown straight up.

<hi rend="bodytext">Yebhuyyena hi sattā khandhe kaṭiyaṃ jāṇūsūti tīsu ṭhānesu namanti</hi>: For most beings bend in three places: in the shoulders, at the waist, and at the knees.

<hi rend="bodytext">Te kaṭiyaṃ namantā pacchato namanti, itaresu dvīsu ṭhānesu purato</hi>: Those who bend at the waist bend backward, [and] in the other two places, forward.

<hi rend="bodytext">Dīghasarīrā paneke passavaṅkā honti, eke mukhaṃ unnāmetvā nakkhattāni gaṇayantā</hi> <pb ed="v" n="3.0269"/> viya caranti, eke appamaṃsalohitā sūlasadisā honti, pavedhamānā gacchanti: But some who have long bodies are bent to the side; some walk around with their faces raised, as if counting the stars; <pb ed="v" n="3.0269"/> some have little flesh and blood [and] are like stakes, going along trembling.

<hi rend="bodytext">Tathāgato pana ujumeva uggantvā dīghappamāṇo devanagare ussitasuvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viya hoti</hi>: But the Tathāgata, having grown straight up, being of great stature, is like a golden arch raised up in a city of the gods.

<hi rend="bold">Brahmūjugatto</hi> <pb ed="m" n="3.0260"/> <pb ed="v" n="3.
"Having seven prominences" means that he has full, rounded flesh in seven places, namely, two on the backs of the hands, two on the backs of the feet, two on the shoulders, and one on the torso.

For others, networks of veins are visible on the backs of the hands and feet, and bony points on the shoulders and torso; they appear like human ghosts, not like a Tathāgata.

But the Tathāgata, because he has full, rounded flesh in seven places, with the backs of his hands and so on having concealed networks of veins, and with a torso like a golden lingam that has been rounded and put in place, appears like a stone statue or like a painted image.

"Having the front part of a lion's body" means that his body is like the front part of a lion's body.

For a lion, only the front part of its body is full and rounded; the back part of its body is not full and rounded.

But for the Tathāgata, his entire body is full and rounded like the front part of a lion's body.

And it is like a lion's, not unsightly or deformed in that it is uneven with depressions and protrusions; but where it is fitting to be long, it is long, and in places where it is fitting to be short, thin, thick, or round, it is just that way.

It was said thus:

"Monks, when a pleasing result of karma presents itself, the parts with which it is beautiful to be long remain long.

The parts with which it is beautiful to be short remain short.

The parts with which it is beautiful to be thick remain thick.

The parts with which it is beautiful to be thin remain thin.

The parts with which it is beautiful to be round remain round."

Thus, the Tathāgata's being, fashioned with various virtuous thoughts and adorned with the ten perfections, cannot be imitated even by all the artisans or powerful beings in the world.

"Having a filled-in interscapular region" means that the interscapular region, which is called the space between the two shoulder blades, is full in his case; hence, he has a filled-in interscapular region.

For others, that place is sunken, and the two shoulder blades are separately visible.

But for the Tathāgata, a layer of flesh extends from the waist up to the shoulders, covering the back and remaining in place like an elevated golden slab.

"Having the পরিমণ্ডল (parimaṇḍala) of a banyan tree" means परिমণ্ডল (parimaṇḍala) like a banyan tree.

Just as a banyan tree with a trunk and branches of equal size, whether fifty or a hundred হাত (hattha)s tall, is the same measure in both height and width, so too is he the same measure in both body and arms' length.

For others, either the body is long or the arms' length is, but not in his case, where they are of unequal measure; this is the meaning.

Therefore, it was said, "As great as is his body," and so on.

There, "as great as" is *yāvatakvassa*.

"Having a well-rounded neck" means having a well-rounded neck.

For some, like herons, cranes, or boars, have long necks, crooked necks, or thick necks, and when they speak, a network of veins is visible and a weak sound comes out; but not so with him.

But the Tathāgata has a neck like a well-rounded golden lingam; when he speaks, a network of veins is not visible, and his voice is great, like a cloud rumbling.

"Having taste-conducting veins at the top" means that in this case, *rasaggasā* means taste-conducting veins (rasaharaṇīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ), and he has them at the top (tā aggā assāti rasaggasaggī).

For the Tathāgata has seven thousand taste-conducting veins that run upwards and are attached at the neck.

Even a sesame seed's worth of food placed on the tip of his tongue spreads throughout his entire body; therefore, even when he was practicing the great exertion, his body was sustained by one grain of rice and so on, or by a hundred measures of black bean soup.

But for others, because they do not have that, nourishment does not spread throughout their entire body; therefore, they have many ailments.

This characteristic becomes evident by way of the непреходящ (nissanda) result reckoned as few illnesses.
hanu assāti *sīhahanu*.
That is, *hanu* means "lion's jaw."
There, the lion's lower jaw is very complete, not the upper.
For the Tathāgata, both jaws are as complete and as beautiful as the moon on the twelfth day of the month.

*sīhahanu*
In [*cattālīsadanto*], twenty teeth are positioned in the upper jaw, and twenty in the lower, thus, forty teeth constitute *cattālīsadanto*.
For others, those with complete teeth have thirty-two teeth, but the Tathāgata has forty.

*cattālīsadanto*
For others, some teeth are high, some are low, so they are uneven, but for the Tathāgata, they are even like an iron plate covering a conch shell.

For others, the teeth are sparse like those of a *kumbhīla*, the space between the teeth is filled when eating fish and meat etc.
For the Tathāgata, the teeth are not sparse, like a row of diamonds placed on a golden vine, appearing as if their outlines were shown by a brush.

*susukkadāṭho*
For others, decayed teeth arise, thus some canine teeth are black or discolored.
The Tathāgata has very white canine teeth, surpassing even the osadhitāraka, endowed with radiant light, thus it is said "very white canine teeth" (*susukkadāṭho*).

*susukkadāṭho*
*pahūtajivho*: For others, the tongue is thick, thin, short, stiff, or uneven, but for the Tathāgata, it is soft, long, broad, and possesses excellent color.
To dispel the doubts of those who have come to seek that characteristic, due to its softness, he rolls that tongue like a hard needle and touches both nostrils; due to its length, he touches both ear holes; due to its breadth, he completely covers even the forehead up to the end of the hairline.
Thus, revealing the softness, length, and breadth of that tongue, he dispels doubt.
Thus, referring to the tongue endowed with three characteristics, it is said "possessing a large tongue" (*pahūtajivho*).

*pahūtajivho*
*brahmassaro*: For others, the voice is broken, distorted, or like a crow, but the Tathāgata is endowed with a voice like the sound of Mahābrahmā.
For Mahābrahmā, the sound is pure because it is free from bile and phlegm.
Even by the Tathāgata, the material which is the basis of speech is purified; because the material is pure, the voice, arising from the navel, is pure and arises only endowed with eight qualities.
karaviko viya bhaṇatīti *karavikabhāṇī*, mattakaravikarutamañjughosoti attho.
He speaks like a *karavika*, therefore he is *karavikabhāṇī*; that is, his sound is delightful like the sound of a joyful *karavika* bird.

*brahmassaro* *karavikabhāṇī*
Here, the delight of the sound of the *karavika* bird is described: it is said that the *karavika* bird, having struck a ripe mango with its beak, tastes the dripping juice, and then, giving a beat with its wings, it begins to play, singing, as if intoxicated, with the four-footed animals etc.
Even the four-footed animals, intent on grazing, leave the grass in their mouths and listen to that sound; the wild animals, chasing small animals, stand without lifting the raised foot, even the pursued animals stand having abandoned the fear of death, the birds flying in the sky stand spreading their wings, even the fish in the water stand flapping their ear fins, listening to that sound.
Thus, the *karavika* bird is delightful.

asandhimittāpi dhammāsokassa devī – ‘‘atthi nu kho, bhante, buddhasaddena sadiso kassaci saddo’’ti saṅghaṃ pucchi.
Even Asandhimittā, the queen of Dharmāśoka, asked the Saṃgha: "Is there, venerable sirs, any sound similar to the sound of the Buddha?"
"There is, it is like the sound of a *karavika* bird."
"Where, venerable sir, is the bird?" "In the Himalayas."
She said to the king, "O king, I want to see the *karavika* bird."
The king released a golden cage, saying, "Let the *karavika* bird come, sitting in this cage!"
The cage went and stood before one *karavika* bird.
It thought, "The cage has come by order of the king, it is not possible not to go," and sat there.
The cage, having come, stood before the king.
They are not able to make the *karavika* bird sound.

Then the king said, "How is it that these make a sound?" Seeing relatives, he thought it was a god.

Then the king had him surrounded with mirrors.

Seeing his own reflection, thinking, "My relatives have come," he clapped his wings, and like one playing a jeweled flute with a sweet voice, he sang.

In the entire city, people behaved as if drunk.

Asandhimittā thought: "Even this animal has such a sweet sound, how much more so would it be for the Blessed One, who has attained the glory of omniscience and wisdom?" Generating joy, and not abandoning that joy, together with seven hundred women, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*).

Thus, the *karavika*'s sound is sweet.

Therefore, the Tathāgata's sound is a hundred times, a thousand times sweeter. However, in the world, since there is no sweeter sound than the *karavika*, he is said to be "*karavikabhāṇī*" (one who speaks like a *karavika* bird).

*Abhinīlanetto* (having very blue eyes): he does not have entirely blue eyes. However, in the places where blue should be, he has eyes endowed with an exceedingly pure blue color, like an *umā* flower.

In the places where yellow should be, [they are endowed] with a yellow color like a *kaṇikāra* flower; in the places where red should be, [they are endowed] with a red color like a *bandhujīvaka* flower; in the places where white should be, [they are endowed] with a white color like an *osadhitāraka* star; in the places where black should be, [they are endowed] with a black color like an *addāriṭṭhaka* jewel. They appear like jeweled lion cages opened in a golden mansion.

*Abhinīlanetto* (having very blue eyes)

*Gopakhumo*: here, *pakhuma* means the entire eye structure is intended.

That [eye structure] of a black calf is dense, of a red calf, it is clear. The meaning is: the eye structure is like that of a red calf just born.

For others, the eye structures are incomplete. [The eyes] of elephants, mice, crows, etc., are endowed with protruding, deep eyes similar to their own.

However, the Tathāgata has eyes filled with soft, smooth, blue, delicate lashes, like jeweled marbles that have been washed and polished.

*Gopakhumo* (having eyelashes like a cow) *pakhuma* (eyelash)

*Uṇṇā* means an *uṇṇā* hair.

*Bhamukantare* (between the eyebrows): it is born in the middle of the two eyebrows, right on the bridge of the nose.

But having emerged, it is born in the middle of the forehead.

*Odātā* (white): perfectly pure, the color of an *osadhitāraka* star.

*Mudū* (soft): like a layer of cotton that has been dipped in clarified butter and kept there a hundred times.

*Tūlasannibhā* (like cotton): similar to *simbali* cotton or *latā* cotton, this is a simile for its whiteness.

But this one, when grasped at the tip and pulled, is about half a cubit long. When released, it turns in a clockwise direction and stands upright. It shines with an exceedingly lovely radiance, like silver filaments placed in the middle of a golden plate, like a stream of milk coming out of a golden pot, and like an *osadhitāraka* star on a path tinged with the light of dawn.

*Uṇṇā* (urna hair) *bhamukantare* (between the eyebrows)

*Odātā* (white) *mudū* (soft) *tūlasannibhā* (like cotton)

*Uṇhīsasīso*: this is said with reference to two meanings: having a perfectly formed forehead and having a perfectly formed head.

For the Tathāgata, a layer of flesh rises from the top of the right ear, covering and filling the entire forehead, and settles on the top of the left ear. It shines like the headdress worn by a king.

It is said that the Bodhisattvas in their last existence knew this mark and made headdresses for kings. This is one meaning.

Other people, however, have incomplete heads: some have pot-shaped heads, some have fruit-shaped heads, some have bone-shaped heads, some have gourd-shaped heads, some have cave-shaped heads.

However, the Tathāgata has a perfectly formed head, like a water bubble that has been rounded with a tool.

Therefore, according to the first meaning, *uṇhīsasīso* is like a head wrapped with a turban (*uṇhīsa*).

According to the second meaning, *uṇhīsasīso* means a head that is round everywhere, like a turban (*uṇhīsa*).
These, however, are the characteristics of a great man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*): action, the likeness of action, characteristics, the benefits of characteristics. These four sections are well explained, having shown them in each characteristic.

Therefore, these actions and so on, which are stated by the Blessed One in the Characteristics Discourse (*lakkhaṇasutta*) (Dī.

Thus, sir, teacher, that venerable Gotama is endowed with these thirty-two characteristics of a great man (*dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇa*), like a golden archway, adorned with rising jewels in a city of gods, with a hundred *yojanas* in height, fully blooming with all kinds of flowers, like a *pāricchattaka* tree, like a well-bloomed *sāla* tree in a mountain range, and as if adorning the surface of the sky with a group of stars. He walks as if illuminating the world with his own glory and majesty. Having illuminated even this meaning, to explain proper conduct, he said, "Indeed, when going..." and so on.

"Indeed, sir, that venerable Gotama..." "Indeed, when going..."

mula_pali:
387. ‘‘Gacchanto kho pana so bhavaṃ gotamo dakkhiṇeneva pādena paṭhamaṃ pakkamati. So nātidūre pādaṃ uddharati, nāccāsanne pādaṃ nikkhipati; so nātisīghaṃ gacchati, nātisaṇikaṃ gacchati; na ca adduvena adduvaṃ saṅghaṭṭento gacchati, na ca gopphakena gopphakaṃ saṅghaṭṭento gacchati. So gacchanto na satthiṃ unnāmeti, na satthiṃ onāmeti; na satthiṃ sannāmeti, na satthiṃ vināmeti. Gacchato kho pana tassa bhoto gotamassa adharakāyova aḍḍhakāyova (ka.), āraddhakāyova (syā. kaṃ.) iñjati, na ca kāyabalena gacchati. Apalokento kho pana so bhavaṃ gotamo sabbakāyeneva apaloketi; so na uddhaṃ ulloketi, na adho oloketi; na ca vipekkhamāno gacchati, yugamattañca pekkhati; tato cassa uttari anāvaṭaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ bhavati. So antaragharaṃ pavisanto na kāyaṃ unnāmeti , na kāyaṃ onāmeti; na kāyaṃ sannāmeti, na kāyaṃ vināmeti. So nātidūre nāccāsanne āsanassa parivattati, na ca pāṇinā ālambitvā āsane nisīdati, na ca āsanasmiṃ kāyaṃ pakkhipati. So antaraghare nisinno samāno na hatthakukkuccaṃ āpajjati, na pādakukkuccaṃ āpajjati; na adduvena adduvaṃ āropetvā nisīdati; na ca gopphakena gopphakaṃ āropetvā nisīdati; na ca pāṇinā hanukaṃ upadahitvā upādiyitvā (sī. pī.) nisīdati. So antaraghare nisinno samāno na chambhati na kampati na vedhati na paritassati. So achambhī akampī avedhī aparitassī vigatalomahaṃso. Vivekavatto ca so bhavaṃ gotamo antaraghare nisinno hoti. So pattodakaṃ paṭiggaṇhanto na pattaṃ unnāmeti, na pattaṃ onāmeti; na pattaṃ sannāmeti, na pattaṃ vināmeti. So pattodakaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti nātithokaṃ nātibahuṃ. So na khulukhulukārakaṃ bulubulukārakaṃ (sī.) pattaṃ dhovati, na samparivattakaṃ pattaṃ dhovati, na pattaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipitvā hatthe dhovati; hatthesu dhotesu patto dhoto hoti, patte dhote hatthā dhotā honti. So pattodakaṃ chaḍḍeti nātidūre nāccāsanne, na ca vicchaḍḍayamāno. So odanaṃ paṭiggaṇhanto na pattaṃ unnāmeti, na pattaṃ onāmeti; na pattaṃ sannāmeti, na pattaṃ vināmeti. So odanaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti nātithokaṃ nātibahuṃ. Byañjanaṃ kho pana bhavaṃ gotamo byañjanamattāya āhāreti, na ca byañjanena ālopaṃ atināmeti. Dvattikkhattuṃ kho bhavaṃ gotamo mukhe ālopaṃ samparivattetvā ajjhoharati; na cassa kāci odanamiñjā asambhinnā kāyaṃ pavisati, na cassa kāci odanamiñjā mukhe avasiṭṭhā hoti; athāparaṃ ālopaṃ upanāmeti. Rasapaṭisaṃvedī kho pana so bhavaṃ gotamo āhāraṃ āhāreti, no ca rasarāgapaṭisaṃvedī.

‘‘Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato (ka.) kho pana so bhavaṃ gotamo āhāraṃ āhāreti – neva davāya, na madāya na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya, yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāya, vihiṃsūparatiyā brahmacariyānuggahāya – ‘iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmi, yātrā ca me bhavissati anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cā’ti . So bhuttāvī pattodakaṃ paṭiggaṇhanto na pattaṃ unnāmeti, na pattaṃ onāmeti; na pattaṃ sannāmeti, na pattaṃ vināmeti. So pattodakaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti nātithokaṃ nātibahuṃ. So na khulukhulukārakaṃ pattaṃ dhovati, na samparivattakaṃ pattaṃ dhovati, na pattaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipitvā hatthe dhovati; hatthesu dhotesu patto dhoto hoti, patte dhote hatthā dhotā honti. So pattodakaṃ chaḍḍeti nātidūre nāccāsanne, na ca vicchaḍḍayamāno. So bhuttāvī na pattaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipati nātidūre nāccāsanne, na ca anatthiko pattena hoti, na ca ativelānurakkhī pattasmiṃ. So bhuttāvī muhuttaṃ tuṇhī nisīdati, na ca anumodanassa kālamatināmeti. So bhuttāvī anumodati, na taṃ bhattaṃ garahati, na aññaṃ bhattaṃ paṭikaṅkhati; aññadatthu dhammiyā kathāya taṃ parisaṃ sandasseti samādapeti samuttejeti sampahaṃseti. So taṃ parisaṃ dhammiyā kathāya sandassetvā samādapetvā samuttejetvā sampahaṃsetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamati. So nātisīghaṃ gacchati, nātisaṇikaṃ gacchati, na ca muccitukāmo gacchati; na ca tassa bhoto gotamassa kāye cīvaraṃ accukkaṭṭhaṃ hoti na ca accokkaṭṭhaṃ, na ca kāyasmiṃ allīnaṃ na ca kāyasmā apakaṭṭhaṃ; na ca tassa bhoto gotamassa kāyamhā vāto cīvaraṃ apavahati; na ca tassa bhoto gotamassa kāye rajojallaṃ upalimpati . So ārāmagato nisīdati paññatte āsane. Nisajja pāde pakkhāleti; na ca so bhavaṃ gotamo pādamaṇḍanānuyogamanuyutto viharati. So pāde pakkhāletvā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So neva attabyābādhāya ceteti, na parabyābādhāya ceteti, na ubhayabyābādhāya ceteti; attahitaparahitaubhayahitasabbalokahitameva so bhavaṃ gotamo cintento nisinno hoti. So ārāmagato parisati dhammaṃ deseti, na taṃ parisaṃ ussādeti, na taṃ parisaṃ apasādeti; aññadatthu dhammiyā kathāya taṃ parisaṃ sandasseti samādapeti samuttejeti sampahaṃseti.

aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato (ka.)

‘‘Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato kho panassa bhoto gotamassa mukhato ghoso niccharati – vissaṭṭho ca, viññeyyo ca, mañju ca, savanīyo ca, bindu ca, avisārī ca, gambhīro ca, ninnādī ca. Yathāparisaṃ kho pana so bhavaṃ gotamo sarena viññāpeti, na cassa bahiddhā parisāya ghoso niccharati. Te tena bhotā gotamena dhammiyā kathāya sandassitā samādapitā samuttejitā sampahaṃsitā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamanti avalokayamānāyeva apalokayamānāyeva (sī. ka.) avijahitattā avijahantābhāvena (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Addasāma kho mayaṃ, bho, taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ gacchantaṃ, addasāma ṭhitaṃ, addasāma antaragharaṃ pavisantaṃ, addasāma antaraghare nisinnaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ, addasāma antaraghare bhuñjantaṃ, addasāma bhuttāviṃ nisinnaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ, addasāma bhuttāviṃ anumodantaṃ, addasāma ārāmaṃ gacchantaṃ, addasāma ārāmagataṃ nisinnaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ, addasāma ārāmagataṃ parisati dhammaṃ desentaṃ. Ediso ca ediso ca so bhavaṃ gotamo, tato ca bhiyyo’’ti.

apalokayamānāyeva (sī. ka.) avijahantābhāvena (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)
mula_english:
387. “When the venerable Gotama walks, he steps out with the right foot first.

He does not lift his foot too far, nor does he place his foot too near; he walks neither too quickly nor too slowly; he walks without his knees knocking together; he walks without his ankles knocking together.

When he walks, he does not raise his thighs, nor does he lower his thighs; he does not bend his thighs forwards, nor does he bend his thighs back.

When the venerable Gotama walks, only the lower part of his body oscillates, and he does not walk with bodily effort.

When the venerable Gotama turns to look, he does so with his whole body; he does not look straight up; he does not look straight down; he does not walk looking about; he looks a plough-yoke’s length before him; beyond that he has unhindered knowledge and vision.

When he goes indoors, he does not raise his body, nor does he lower his body; he does not bend his body forwards, nor does he bend his body back.

He does not turn round too far from the seat nor too near it, and he does not lean on the seat with his hand; he does not throw his body onto the seat.

When seated indoors, he does not fidget with his hands; he does not fidget with his feet; he does not sit with his knees crossed; he does not sit with his ankles crossed; he does not sit with his hand holding his chin.

When seated indoors he is not afraid, he does not shiver and tremble, he is not nervous.

He is without fear, without wavering, without quaking, without trembling, his hair does not stand on end.

The venerable Gotama dwells in seclusion when seated indoors.

When receiving water for the bowl, he does not raise the bowl, nor does he lower the bowl; he does not bend the bowl forwards, nor does he bend the bowl back.

He receives neither too little nor too much water for the bowl.

He washes the bowl without making a splashing noise, he washes the bowl without turning it round, he does not put the bowl on the ground to wash his hands; when his hands are washed, the bowl is washed, and when the bowl is washed, his hands are washed.

He pours the water for the bowl neither too far nor too near, and he does not pour it about.

When receiving rice, he does not raise the bowl, nor does he lower the bowl; he does not bend the bowl forwards, nor does he bend the bowl back.

He receives neither too little rice nor too much rice.

The venerable Gotama takes sauces in the right proportion; he does not exceed the right amount of sauce in the mouthful.

The venerable Gotama turns the mouthful over two or three times in his mouth and then swallows it, and no rice kernel enters his body unchewed, and no rice kernel remains in his mouth; then he takes another mouthful.

The venerable Gotama takes his food experiencing the taste, though not experiencing greed for the taste.

“The food the venerable Gotama takes has eight factors: it is neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for the sake of physical beauty and attractiveness, but only for the endurance and continuance of his body, for the ending of discomfort, and for assisting the holy life; he considers: “Thus I shall terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings and I shall be healthy and blameless and shall live in comfort.”

After eating, when taking water in the bowl, he does not bend the bowl upwards, without bending the bowl downwards;

He receives neither too little nor too much water for the bowl.

He washes the bowl without making a splashing noise, he washes the bowl without turning it round, he does not put the bowl on the floor to wash his hands: when his hands are washed, the bowl is washed; and when the bowl is washed, his hands are washed.
He discards the bowl water neither too far nor too near, without throwing it about.
When he has eaten, he puts the bowl on the floor neither too far nor too near; and he is neither careless of the bowl nor over-solicitous about it.
When he has eaten, he sits in silence for a while, but he does not let the time for the blessing go by.
When he has eaten and gives the blessing, he does not do so criticising the meal or expecting another meal; he instructs, urges, rouses, and encourages that audience with talk purely on the Dhamma.
When he has done so, he rises from his seat and departs.
He walks neither too fast nor too slow, and he does not go as one who wants to get away. His robe is worn neither too high nor too low on his body, nor too tight against his body, nor too loose on his body, nor does the wind blow his robe away from his body. Dust and dirt do not soil his body.
When he has gone to the monastery, he sits down on a seat made ready.
Having sat down, he washes his feet, though he does not concern himself with grooming his feet.
Having washed his feet, he seats himself cross-legged, sets his body erect, and establishes mindfulness in front of him.
He intends neither his own affliction, nor the affliction of others, nor the affliction of both; the Blessed Gotama sits thinking only of the benefit of himself, the benefit of others, the benefit of both, the benefit of the whole world.
When he has gone to the monastery, he teaches the Dhamma to an audience. He neither flatters nor berates that audience; he instructs, urges, rouses, and encourages it with talk purely on the Dhamma.

The speech that issues from his mouth has eight qualities: it is distinct, intelligible, melodious, audible, ringing, euphonious, deep, and sonorous.
But while his voice is intelligible as far as the audience extends, his speech does not issue out beyond the audience.
When the people have been instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged by him, they rise from their seats and depart looking only at him and concerned with nothing else.
“We have seen Master Gotama walking, sir, we have seen him standing, we have seen him entering indoors, we have seen him indoors seated in silence after eating, we have seen him giving the blessing after eating, we have seen him going to the monastery in silence, we have seen him in the monastery teaching the Dhamma to an audience.
Such is the Master Gotama; such he is, and more than that.”
pī.

commentary_pali:
387.Dakkhiṇenāti buddhānañhi ṭhatvā vā nisīditvā vā nipajjitvā vā gamanaṃ abhinīharantānaṃ dakkhiṇapādova purato hoti. Satatapāṭihāriyaṃ kiretaṃ. Nātidūrepādaṃ uddharatīti taṃ dakkhiṇapādaṃ na atidūre ṭhapessāmīti uddharati. Atidūrañhi abhihariyamāne dakkhiṇapādena vāmapādo ākaḍḍhiyamāno gaccheyya, dakkhiṇapādopi dūraṃ gantuṃ na sakkuṇeyya, āsanneyeva patiṭṭhaheyya, evaṃ sati padavicchedo nāma hoti. Dakkhiṇapāde pana pamāṇeneva uddhate vāmapādopi pamāṇeneva uddhariyati, pamāṇena uddhato patiṭṭhahantopi pamāṇeyeva patiṭṭhāti. Evamanena tathāgatassa dakkhiṇapādakiccaṃ vāmapādena niyamitaṃ, vāmapādakiccaṃ dakkhiṇapādena niyamitanti veditabbaṃ.

Nātisīghanti divā vihārabhattatthāya gacchanto bhikkhu viya na atisīghaṃ gacchati. Nātisaṇikanti yathā pacchato āgacchanto okāsaṃ na labhati, evaṃ na atisaṇikaṃ gacchati. Adduvena adduvanti jaṇṇukena jaṇṇukaṃ, nasatthiṃ unnāmetīti gambhīre udake gacchanto viya na ūruṃ unnāmeti. Na onāmetīti rukkhasākhāchedanadaṇḍaṅkusapādo viya na pacchato osakkāpeti. Na sannāmetīti obaddhānābaddhaṭṭhānehi pādaṃ koṭṭento viya na thaddhaṃ karoti. Navināmetīti yantarūpakaṃ kīḷāpento viya na ito cito ca cāleti. Adharakāyovāti heṭṭhimakāyova iñjati, uparimakāyo nāvāya ṭhapitasuvaṇṇapaṭimā viya niccalo hoti. Dūre ṭhatvā olokento hi buddhānaṃ ṭhitabhāvaṃ vā gamanabhāvaṃ vā na jānāti . Kāyabalenāti bāhā khipanto sarīrato sedehi muccantehi na kāyabalena gacchati. Sabbakāyenevāti gīvaṃ aparivattetvā rāhulovāde vuttanāgāpalokitavaseneva apaloketi.

Nātisīgha Nātisaṇika Adduvena adduva na satthiṃ unnāmetī Na onāmetī Na sannāmetī Na vināmetī Adharakāyovā Kāyabalenā Sabbakāyenevā

Na uddhantiādīsu nakkhattāni gaṇento viya na uddhaṃ ulloketi, naṭṭhaṃ kākaṇikaṃ vā māsakaṃ vā pariyesanto viya na adho oloketi, na hatthiassādayo passanto viya ito cito ca vipekkhamāno gacchati. Yugamattanti navavidatthimatte cakkhūni ṭhapetvā gacchanto yugamattaṃ pekkhati nāma, bhagavāpi yuge yutto sudantaājānīyo viya ettakaṃ passanto gacchati. Tato cassa uttarīti yugamattato paraṃ na passatīti na vattabbo. Na hi kuṭṭaṃ vā kavāṭaṃ vā gaccho vā latā vā āvarituṃ sakkoti, atha khvassa anāvaraṇañāṇassa anekāni cakkavāḷasahassāni ekaṅgaṇāneva honti. Antaragharanti heṭṭhā mahāsakuludāyisutte indakhīlato paṭṭhāya antaragharaṃ, idha gharaummārato paṭṭhāya veditabbaṃ. Nakāyantiādi pakatiiriyapatheneva pavisatīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Daliddamanussānaṃ nīcagharakaṃ pavisantepi hi tathāgate chadanaṃ vā uggacchati, pathavī vā ogacchati, bhagavā pana pakatigamaneneva gacchati. Nātidūreti atidūre parivattantena hi ekaṃ dve padavāre piṭṭhibhāgena gantvā nisīditabbaṃ hoti. Nāccāsanneti accāsanne parivattantena ekaṃ dve padavāre purato gantvā nisīditabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā yasmiṃ padavāre ṭhitena purato vā pacchato vā agantvā nisīditabbaṃ hoti, tattha parivattati.

Na uddha Yugamatta Tato cassa uttarī Antaraghara Na kāya Nāccāsanne

Pāṇināti kaṭivātābādhiko viya na āsanaṃ hatthehi gahetvā nisīdati. Pakkhipatīti yo kiñci kammaṃ katvā kīḷanto ṭhitakova patati, yopi orimaṃ aṅgaṃ nissāya nisinno ghaṃsanto yāva pārimaṅgā gacchati, pārimaṅgaṃ vā nissāya nisinno tatheva yāva orimaṅgā āgacchati, sabbo so āsane kāyaṃ pakkhipati nāma. Bhagavā pana evaṃ akatvā āsanassa majjhe olambakaṃ dhārento viya tūlapicuṃ ṭhapento viya saṇikaṃ nisīdati. Hatthakukkuccanti pattamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ udakabinduṭhapanaṃ makkhikabījaniyā paṇṇacchedanaphālanādi hatthena asaṃyatakaraṇaṃ. Pādakukkuccanti pādena bhūmighaṃsanādi asaṃyatakaraṇaṃ.

Pāṇinā Pakkhipatī Hatthakukkucca Pādakukkucca

Na chambhatīti na bhāyati. Na kampatīti na osīdati. Na vedhatīti na calati. Naparitassatīti bhayaparitassanāyapi taṇhāparitassanāyapi na paritassati. Ekacco hi dhammakathādīnaṃ atthāya āgantvā manussesu vanditvā ṭhitesu ‘‘sakkhissāmi nu kho tesaṃ cittaṃ gaṇhanto dhammaṃ vā kathetuṃ, pañhaṃ vā pucchito vissajjetuṃ, bhattānumodanaṃ vā kātu’’nti bhayaparitassanāya paritassati. Ekacco ‘‘manāpā nu kho me yāgu āgacchissati, manāpaṃ antarakhajjaka’’nti vā taṇhāparitassanāya paritassati. Tadubhayampi tassa natthīti na paritassati. Vivekāvaṭṭoti viveke nibbāne āvaṭṭamānaso hutvā. Vivekavattotipi pāṭho, vivekavattayutto hutvāti attho. Vivekavattaṃ nāma katabhattakiccassa bhikkhuno divāvihāre samathavipassanāvasena mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisīdanaṃ. Evaṃ nisinnassa hi iriyāpatho upasanto hoti.

Na chambhatī Na kampatī Na vedhatī Na paritassatī Vivekāvaṭṭo

Na pattaṃ unnāmetītiādīsu ekacco pattamukhavaṭṭiyā udakadānaṃ āharanto viya pattaṃ unnāmeti, eko pādapiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhapento viya onāmeti, eko baddhaṃ katvā gaṇhāti, eko ito cito ca phandāpeti, evaṃ akatvā ubhohi hatthehi gahetvā īsakaṃ nāmetvā udakaṃ paṭiggaṇhātīti attho. Na samparivattakanti parivattetvā paṭhamameva pattapiṭṭhiṃ na dhovati. Nātidūreti yathā nisinnāsanato dūre patati, na evaṃ chaḍḍeti. Nāccāsanneti pādamūleyeva na chaḍḍeti. Vicchaḍḍayamānoti vikiranto, yathā paṭiggāhako temati, na evaṃ chaḍḍeti.

Na pattaṃ unnāmetī Na samparivattaka Nāccāsanne Vicchaḍḍayamāno

Nātithokanti yathā ekacco pāpiccho appicchataṃ dassento muṭṭhimattameva gaṇhāti, na evaṃ. Atibahunti yāpanamattato atirekaṃ. Byañjanamattāyāti byañjanassa mattā nāma odanato catuttho bhāgo. Ekacco hi bhatte manāpe bhattaṃ bahuṃ gaṇhāti, byañjane manāpe byañjanaṃ bahuṃ. Satthā pana tathā na gaṇhāti. Na ca byañjanenāti amanāpañhi byañjanaṃ ṭhapetvā bhattameva bhuñjanto, bhattaṃ vā ṭhapetvā byañjanameva khādanto byañjanena ālopaṃ atināmeti nāma. Satthā ekantarikaṃ byañjanaṃ gaṇhāti, bhattampi byañjanampi ekatova niṭṭhanti. Dvattikkhattunti tathāgatassa hi puthujivhāya dantānaṃ upanītabhojanaṃ dvattikkhattuṃ dantehi phuṭṭhamattameva saṇhakaraṇīyapiṭṭhavilepanaṃ viya hoti, tasmā evamāha. Na mukhe avasiṭṭhāti pokkharapatte patitaudakabindu viya vinivattitvā paragalameva yāti, tasmā avasiṭṭhā na hoti. Rasapaṭisaṃvedīti madhuratittakadukādirasaṃ jānāti. Buddhānañhi antamaso pānīyepi dibbojā pakkhittāva hoti, tena nesaṃ sabbattheva raso pākaṭo hoti, rasagedho pana natthi.

Nātithoka Atibahu Byañjanamattāyā Na ca byañjanenā Dvattikkhattu Na mukhe avasiṭṭhā Rasapaṭisaṃvedī

Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatanti ‘‘neva davāyā’’ti vuttehi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ. Visuddhimagge panassa vinicchayo āgatoti sabbāsavasutte vuttametaṃ. Hatthesu dhotesūti satthā kiṃ karoti? Paṭhamaṃ pattassa gahaṇaṭṭhānaṃ dhovati. Tattha pattaṃ gahetvā sukhumajālahatthaṃ pesetvā dve vāre sañcāreti. Ettāvatā pokkharapatte patitaudakaṃ viya vinivattitvā gacchati. Na ca anatthikoti yathā ekacco pattaṃ ādhārake ṭhapetvā patte udakaṃ na puñchati, raje patante ajjhupekkhati, na evaṃ karoti. Na ca ativelānurakkhīti yathā ekacco pamāṇātikkantaṃ ārakkhaṃ ṭhapeti, bhuñjitvā vā patte udakaṃ puñchitvā cīvarabhogantaraṃ pavesetvā pattaṃ udarena akkamitvā gaṇhāti, na evaṃ karoti.

Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgata Visuddhimagge Hatthesu dhotesū Na ca anatthiko Na ca ativelānurakkhī

Na ca anumodanassāti yo hi bhuttamattova dārakesu bhattatthāya rodantesu chātajjhattesu manussesu bhuñjitvā anāgatesveva anumodanaṃ ārabhati, tato sabbakammāni chaḍḍetvā ekacce āgacchanti, ekacce anāgatāva honti, ayaṃ kālaṃ atināmeti. Yopi manussesu āgantvā anumodanatthāya vanditvā nisinnesu anumodanaṃ akatvāva ‘‘kathaṃ tissa, kathaṃ phussa, kathaṃ sumana, kathaṃ tisse, kathaṃ phusse, kathaṃ sumane, kaccittha arogā, sassaṃ sampanna’’ntiādiṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, ayaṃ anumodanassa kālaṃ atināmeti, manussānaṃ pana okāsaṃ ñatvā āyācitakāle karonto nātināmeti nāma, satthā tathā karoti.

Na ca anumodanassā

Na taṃ bhattanti kiṃ bhattaṃ nāmetaṃ uttaṇḍulaṃ atikilinnantiādīni vatvā na garahati. Naaññaṃ bhattanti svātanāya vā punadivasāya vā bhattaṃ uppādessāmīti hi anumodanaṃ karonto aññaṃ bhattaṃ paṭikaṅkhati. Yo vā – ‘‘yāva mātugāmānaṃ bhattaṃ paccati, tāva anumodanaṃ karissāmi, atha me anumodanāvasāne attano pakkabhattatopi thokaṃ dassantī’’ti anumodanaṃ vaḍḍheti, ayampi paṭikaṅkhati nāma. Satthā na evaṃ karoti. Na ca muccitukāmoti ekacco hi paṭisaṃmuñcitvā gacchati, vegena anubandhitabbo hoti. Satthā pana na evaṃ gacchati, parisāya majjhe ṭhitova gacchati. Accukkaṭṭhanti yo hi yāva hanukaṭṭhito ukkhipitvā pārupati, tassa accukkaṭṭhaṃ nāma hoti. Yo yāva gopphakā otāretvāva pārupati, tassa accukkaṭṭhaṃ hoti. Yopi ubhato ukkhipitvā udaraṃ vivaritvā yāti, tassapi accukkaṭṭhaṃ hoti. Yo ekaṃsaṃ katvā thanaṃ vivaritvā yāti, tassapi accukkaṭṭhaṃ. Satthā taṃ sabbaṃ na karoti.

Na taṃ bhatta Na aññaṃ bhatta Na ca muccitukāmo Accukkaṭṭha

Allīnanti yathā aññesaṃ sedena tintaṃ allīyati, na evaṃ satthu. Apakaṭṭhanti khalisāṭako viya kāyato muccitvāpi na tiṭṭhati. Vātoti verambhavātopi uṭṭhahitvā cāletuṃ na sakkoti. Pādamaṇḍanānuyoganti iṭṭhakāya ghaṃsanādīhi pādasobhānuyogaṃ. Pakkhāletvāti pādeneva pādaṃ dhovitvā. So neva attabyābādhāyātiādīni na pubbenivāsacetopariyañāṇānaṃ atthitāya vadati, iriyāpathasantataṃ pana disvā anumānena vadati. Dhammanti pariyattidhammaṃ. Na ussādetīti kiṃ mahāraṭṭhika, kiṃ mahākuṭumbikātiādīni vatvā gehassitavasena na ussādeti. Na apasādetīti ‘‘kiṃ, upāsaka, kathaṃ te vihāramaggo ñāto? Kiṃ bhayena nāgacchasi? Na hi bhikkhū kiñci acchinditvā gaṇhanti, mā bhāyī’’ti vā ‘‘kiṃ tuyhaṃ evaṃ macchariyajīvitaṃ nāmā’’ti vā ādīni vatvā gehassitapemena na apasādeti.

Allīna Apakaṭṭha Vāto Pādamaṇḍanānuyoga Pakkhāletvā So neva attabyābādhāyā Dhamma Na ussādetī Na apasādetī

Vissaṭṭhoti siniddho apalibuddho. Viññeyyoti viññāpanīyo pākaṭo, vissaṭṭhattāyeva cesa viññeyyo hoti. Mañjūti madhuro. Savanīyoti sotasukho, madhurattāyeva cesa savanīyo hoti. Bindūti sampiṇḍito. Avisārīti avisaṭo, binduttāyeva cesa avisārī hoti. Gambhīroti gambhīrasamuṭṭhito. Ninnādīti ninnādavā, gambhīrattāyeva cesa ninnādī hoti. Yathāparisanti cakkavāḷapariyantampi ekābaddhaparisaṃ viññāpeti. Bahiddhāti aṅgulimattampi parisato bahiddhā na gacchati. Tasmā? So evarūpo madhurassaro akāraṇā mā nassīti. Iti bhagavato ghoso parisāya matthakeneva carati.

Vissaṭṭho Viññeyyo Mañjū Savanīyo Bindū Avisārī Gambhīro Ninnādī Yathāparisa Bahiddhā

Avalokayamānāti sirasmiṃ añjaliṃ ṭhapetvā bhagavantaṃ olokentāva paccosakkitvā dassanavijahanaṭṭhāne vanditvā gacchanti. Avijahitattāti yo hi kathaṃ sutvā vuṭṭhito aññaṃ diṭṭhasutādikaṃ kathaṃ kathento gacchati, esa sabhāvena vijahati nāma. Yo pana sutadhammakathāya vaṇṇaṃ kathentova gacchati, ayaṃ na vijahati nāma, evaṃ avijahantabhāvena pakkamanti. Gacchantanti rajjuyantavasena ratanasattubbedhaṃ suvaṇṇagghikaṃ viya gacchantaṃ. Addasāma ṭhitanti samussitakañcanapabbataṃ viya ṭhitaṃ addasāma. Tato ca bhiyyoti vitthāretvā guṇe kathetuṃ asakkonto avasese guṇe saṃkhipitvā kalāpaṃ viya suttakabaddhaṃ viya ca katvā vissajjento evamāha. Ayamettha adhippāyo – mayā kathitaguṇehi akathitāva bahutarā. Mahāpathavimahāsamuddādayo viya hi tassa bhoto anantā appameyyā guṇā ākāsamiva vitthāritāti.

Avalokayamānā Avijahitattā Gacchanta Addasāma ṭhita addasāma. Tato ca bhiyyo
commentary_english:
387. *dakkhiṇenā* means: indeed, for the Buddhas, whether standing, sitting, or lying down, when setting forth, the right foot goes first. One should perform the continuous miracle ( *satatapāṭihāriyaṃ*). *nātidūre* *pādaṃ uddharatī* means: that right foot, [one] lifts it, not placing it too far away. For, if the right foot is moved too far, the left foot, being dragged, might slip, and the right foot, too, might not be able to go far; it would be established very near. Thus, there would be what is called a break in the sequence. But when the right foot has been raised with measure, the left foot too is raised with measure; having been raised with measure, even while being placed, it is placed with measure. Thus, by this, the function of the Tathāgata's right foot is regulated by the left foot, and it should be understood that the function of the left foot is regulated by the right foot. *nātisīgha* means: like a monk going for alms in the monastery during the day, [one] does not go too quickly. *nātisaṇika* means: just as one coming from behind does not get an opportunity, so too, [one] does not go too closely. *adduvena adduva* means: knee to knee; [one] does not *satthiṃ unnāmetī*, meaning, like one going in deep water, [one] does not raise the thigh. *na onāmetī* means: like the foot of a tool for cutting branches, [one] does not withdraw backwards. *na sannāmetī* means: like one stamping the foot with places bound and unbound, [one] does not make it stiff. *na vināmetī* means: like one playing a mechanical toy, [one] does not move it this way and that. *adharakāyovā* means: the lower body alone moves; the upper body is still, like a golden statue placed on a ship. For one looking from afar does not know the state of standing or the state of walking of the Buddhas . *kāyabalenā* means: flapping the arms, with sweat pouring from the body, [one] does not walk with bodily force. *sabbakāyenevā* means: without turning the neck, [one] looks around only with the turn of the Nāga described in the advice to Rāhula. *nātisīgha, nātisaṇika, adduvena adduva, na* *satthiṃ unnāmetī, na onāmetī, na sannāmetī, na* *vināmetī, adharakāyovā* *kāyabalenā, sabbakāyenevā* *na uddha* and so on, meaning: like one counting the constellations, [one] does not look upwards; like one searching for a lost *kākaṇika* or *māsaka*, [one] does not look downwards; like one seeing elephants, horses, etc., [one] does not walk looking this way and that. *yugamatta* means: placing the eyes at a distance of nine spans, [one] looks at a yoke's distance. Namely, the Blessed One, too, yoked to the *yuga*, like a well-trained thoroughbred, goes seeing that much. *tato cassa uttarī* means: [one] should not say that [he] does not see beyond the yoke's distance. For [one] is not able to be obstructed by a wall, or a door, or a tree, or a creeper; rather, for [one] whose knowledge is unobstructed, even thousands of world-systems are like a single courtyard. *antaraghara* means: below, in the *Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta*, *antaraghara* [means] starting from the *indakhīla*; here, it should be understood as starting from the door-lintel of the house. *na kāya* and so on, meaning: it was said to show that [one] enters only with the natural deportment. Even when entering a poor person's lowly house, for the Tathāgata, either the roof rises up or the earth sinks down; but the Blessed One goes only with a natural gait. *nātidūre* means: for one turning around too far, it would be necessary to go one or two steps with the back before sitting down. *nāccāsanne* means: for one turning around too near, it would be necessary to go one or two steps forward before sitting down. Therefore, in whatever step [one] is standing, without going forward or backward, it is necessary to sit down; there [one] turns around. *na uddha, yugamatta, tato cassa uttarī, antaraghara, na* *kāya, nāccāsanne* *pāṇinā* means: like one afflicted with stiffness in the back, [one] does not take hold of the seat with the hands and sit down. *pakkhipatī* means: whoever, having done some deed, falls down while playing, or whoever, relying on one side [of the seat], having sat down, slides until [he] reaches the other side, or, relying on the other side , having sat down, comes back just so far as this side, all of that is called "throwing the body onto the seat". But the Blessed One, without doing thus, sits down gently, as if holding a plumb-bob in the middle of the seat, as if placing a cotton-flower. *Hattha-kukkucca* means careless actions with the hands, such as putting drops of water on the mouth of a bowl, using a fly whisk, cutting leaves, splitting things, etc. *Pāda-kukkucca* means careless actions with the feet, such as rubbing the ground with the foot, etc. He throws [it] with his hand. 0267"/> *Hattha-kukkucca, Pāda-kukkucca*.

*Na chambhatī* means he is not afraid. *Na kampatī* means he does not sink down. *Na vedhatī* means he does not waver. *Na* 0390"/> *paritassatī* means he is not agitated either by the agitation of fear or by the agitation of craving. One person, having come to the assembly for the sake of a Dhamma talk, etc., having greeted the people and stood there, worries with the agitation of fear, thinking, "Will I be able to take hold of their minds and give a Dhamma talk, answer a question that is asked, or give a meal blessing?" One person worries with the agitation of craving, thinking, "Will agreeable rice-gruel come to me? [Will I get] agreeable side dishes?" For one who does not have both of those, there is no agitation. *Vivekāvaṭṭo* means having a mind turned towards *viveka*, *nirvāṇa*. *Vivekavattotipi* is also a reading, meaning associated with *vivekavatta*. *Vivekavatta* is the sitting of a monk who has finished his meal duties, having taken a root meditation subject in a day-retreat, folding his legs into the lotus position. For one sitting thus, his deportment is peaceful.

*Na chambhatī Na kampatī Na vedhatī Na* 0390"/> *paritassatī* 0276"/> *vivekāvaṭṭo*

*Na pattaṃ unnāmetī* among those beginning with "he does not raise the bowl," one person raises the bowl as if bringing water to the mouth of the bowl, one person lowers [the bowl] as if placing [it] on the footrest, one person takes [it] having made [it] firm, one person shakes [it] back and forth. Without doing thus, having taken [the bowl] with both hands, having bent [it] down slightly, he receives the water. This is the meaning. *Na samparivattaka* means not washing the surface of the bowl right away after turning [it over]. *Nātidūre* means he does not throw [the water] so that it falls far from the seat where he is sitting. *Nāccāsanne* means he does not throw [it] right at the base of the foot. *Vicchaḍḍayamāno* 0391"/> scattering [it], he does not throw [it] so that the receiver gets wet.

*Na pattaṃ unnāmetī Na samparivattaka Nāccāsanne Vicchaḍḍayamāno* 0391"/>

*Nātithoka* 0268"/> as one person, being of evil desires, showing [himself] to be of few desires, takes only a fistful, he does not do thus. *Atibahu* means more than the mere maintenance [of life]. *Byañjanamattāyā* means the measure of side dishes is called one-fourth of the rice. One person takes much rice when the rice is agreeable, [and takes] much side dish when the side dish is agreeable. But the teacher does not take thus. *Na ca byañjanenā* means, if a side dish is disagreeable, while eating only the rice after setting aside the side dish, or while eating only the side dish after setting aside the rice, he does not let a morsel pass with the side dish. The teacher takes a separated side dish; he finishes both the rice and the side dish at the same time. *Dvattikkhattu* means, for the Tathāgata, the food brought near to the teeth with his broad tongue touches [the teeth] only two or three times, just like a smooth face-powder. Therefore, he said thus. *Na mukhe avasiṭṭhā* means having turned back like a drop of water fallen on a lotus leaf, it goes right into the throat. Therefore, there is no remaining [food] in the mouth. *Rasapaṭisaṃvedī* means he knows the taste, such as sweet, bitter, sour, etc. For the Buddhas, even in water, celestial flavors are always put in. Therefore, for them, taste is manifest in all things, but there is no craving for taste.

*Nātithoka* 0268"/> *Atibahu Byañjanamattāyā Na ca byañjanenā Dvattikkhattu Na mukhe avasiṭṭhā Rasapaṭisaṃvedī*

*Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgata* 0392"/> "not even for heat," is complete with the eight factors that were said. *Visuddhimagga*: Moreover, the decision has come, as it is said in the *sabbāsavasutta*. *hatthesu dhotesū*: What does the teacher do when the hands have been washed? First, he washes the place where he holds the bowl. There, having taken the bowl, he sends forth a fine, net-like hand and moves it around twice. To that extent, like water falling on a lotus leaf, it turns away and goes. *na ca anatthiko*: He is not unconcerned, as when some person places the bowl on a support and does not wipe the water from the bowl, but is indifferent when dust falls on it; he does not do that. *na ca ativelānurakkhī*: He is not excessively protective, as when some person establishes a protection exceeding the measure, or having eaten, wipes the water from the bowl, puts the bowl inside the robe and presses the bowl against his stomach, he does not do that. *aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgata* *Visuddhimagga* *hatthesu dhotesū* *na ca anatthiko* *na ca ativelānurakkhī* *na ca anumodanassā*: Moreover, whoever, having just eaten, when the children are crying for food, when people are afflicted by hunger, having eaten, begins the rejoicing only in the future, then, abandoning all tasks, some come, some do not come, he spends the time. Whoever among people, having come to rejoice, having worshipped and sat down, without rejoicing, raises up individual talk, "How is Tissa, how is Phussa, how is Sumana, how is Tissa, how is Phussa, how is Sumana, are you healthy, is the harvest prosperous?", he spends the time of rejoicing, but knowing the opportunity of the people, doing it at the time of request, he does not spend the time, the teacher does that. *na ca anumodanassā* *na taṃ bhatta*: He does not disparage, saying "What kind of food is this, it is unsalted rice, it is excessively wet," etc. *aññaṃ bhatta*: Moreover, whoever, making rejoicing, thinks, "I will produce food for tomorrow or the day after tomorrow," he desires other food. Or whoever thinks, "As long as the food of the women of the household is cooking, so long will I rejoice, then at the end of my rejoicing, they will give me a little bit from their own cooked food," he increases the rejoicing, he also desires. The teacher does not do thus. *na ca muccitukāmo*: Moreover, whoever, having covered himself, goes away, he must be followed with speed. But the teacher does not go thus, he goes standing in the midst of the assembly. *accukkaṭṭha*: Moreover, whoever, having lifted it up as far as the chin, puts it on, that is called *accukkaṭṭha*. Whoever, having lowered it as far as the ankles, puts it on, that is *accukkaṭṭha*. Moreover, whoever, having lifted up both sides and opened his belly, goes, that is also *accukkaṭṭha*. Whoever, having made one shoulder and opened her breast, goes, that is also *accukkaṭṭha*. The teacher does not do all that. *na taṃ bhatta* *na* *aññaṃ bhatta* *na ca muccitukāmo* *accukkaṭṭha* *allīna*: Moreover, as when something sticks, wet with the sweat of others, the teacher is not like that. *apakaṭṭha*: Like a loose cloak, even having been released from the body, it does not stay. *vāto*: Moreover, even a *verambha* wind, having arisen, is not able to shake it. *pādamaṇḍanānuyoga*: Moreover, it is the practice of beautifying the feet with brick-rubbing, etc., it is the practice of beautifying the feet. *pakkhāletvā*: Moreover, having washed foot with foot. *so neva attabyābādhāyā*: Moreover, he does not speak those things because of the existence of knowledge of past lives and the minds of others, but having seen the continuous path, he speaks by inference. *dhamma*: Moreover, it is the teaching of the scriptures. *na ussādetī*: Moreover, he does not encourage by saying, "Are you a great landowner? Are you from a great family?", etc., on account of being attached to the household. *na apasādetī*: Moreover, he does not discourage by saying, "What, lay follower, how is the path to the monastery known to you? Why do you not come out of fear? Indeed, monks do not take anything by force, do not be afraid," or, "What, is your life such that you are stingy?", etc., on account of affection for the household. *allīna* *apakaṭṭha* *vāto* *pādamaṇḍanānuyoga* *pakkhāletvā* *so neva attabyābādhāyā* *dhamma* *na ussādetī* na apasādeti vissaṭṭho means smooth and not obstructed. viññeyyo means easily understood, manifest, because it is easily spread. mañjū means sweet. savanīyo means pleasing to the ear, because it is sweet. bindū means compacted. avisārī means not dispersed, because it is compacted. gambhīro means arising from depth. ninnādī means resonant, because it is deep. yathāparisa means it makes the entire assembly up to the limit of the *cakravāḷa* understand that it is a single, connected assembly. bahiddhā means not going outside the assembly even the length of a finger. Therefore? May that sweet sound of such a kind not perish without cause. Thus, the voice of the Blessed One moves through the assembly like [over] the head. vissaṭṭho viññeyyo mañjū savanīyo bindū avisārī gambhīro ninnādī yathāparisa bahiddhā avalokayamānā Having placed their joined hands on their heads, looking at the Blessed One, retreating backwards, bowing down in the place of abandoning sight, they depart. avijahitattā means someone who, having heard the Dharma talk, gets up and goes away talking about other things that are seen, heard, etc., abandons [the Dharma talk] by nature. But someone who goes away praising the virtue of the Dharma talk that has been heard, does not abandon it, thus they proceed with a mind that does not abandon it. gacchanta means going like a golden digger piercing a ratana-sattu jewel by means of a rope-device. addasāma ṭhita means we saw him standing like a raised mountain of gold, addasāma. tato ca bhiyyo means being unable to expound at length, he summarizes the remaining qualities, and having made them like a bundle, like something bound by a thread, he dismisses [them], thus he says. The meaning here is this – the qualities I have spoken of are far fewer than those not spoken of. The qualities of that Blessed One are infinite and immeasurable, like the great earth, the great ocean, etc.; they are spread out like the sky. avalokayamānā avijahitattā gacchanta addasāma ṭhita addasāma. tato ca bhiyyo

mula_pali:
388. Evaṃ vutte, brahmāyu brāhmaṇo uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā tikkhattuṃ udānaṃ udāneti –

‘‘Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

‘‘Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

‘‘Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassā’’ti.

‘‘Appeva nāma mayaṃ kadāci karahaci tena bhotā gotamena samāgaccheyyāma? Appeva nāma siyā kocideva kathāsallāpo’’ti!
mula_english:
When this was said, Brahmāyu the Brahmin rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and, with his joined hands raised toward the Blessed One, exclaimed three times:

“Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One (namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa).”

“Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One (namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa).”

“Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One (namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa)!”

“Perhaps sometime or other we might meet Master Gotama? Perhaps there might be some conversation.”

mula_pali:
389. Atha kho bhagavā videhesu anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena mithilā tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā mithilāyaṃ viharati maghadevambavane. Assosuṃ kho mithileyyakā methileyyakā (sī. pī.) brāhmaṇagahapatikā – ‘‘samaṇo khalu, bho, gotamo sakyaputto sakyakulā pabbajito videhesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi mithilaṃ anuppatto, mithilāyaṃ viharati maghadevambavane. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavāti. So imaṃ lokaṃ sadevakaṃ samārakaṃ sabrahmakaṃ sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajaṃ sadevamanussaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti . So dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti. Sādhu kho pana tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ dassanaṃ hotī’’’ti.

Atha kho mithileyyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā appekacce bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu; appekacce bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu, sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu; appekacce yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu; appekacce bhagavato santike nāmagottaṃ sāvetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu; appekacce tuṇhībhūtā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.
mula_english:
389. Then, the Blessed One, wandering gradually in the country of the Videhas, eventually arrived at Mithilā. There the Blessed One lived in Makhadeva’s Mango Grove.

The *brāhmaṇa* householders of Mithilā heard: “The *śramaṇa* Gotama, son of the Śākyas, who went forth from a Śākya clan, wandering in the country of the Videhas, has arrived at Mithilā with a large *bhikkhu-saṃgha*, with about five hundred *bhikkhus*, and is living in Makhadeva’s Mango Grove.

Now a good report of the esteemed Gotama has been spread to this effect: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One is an *arhat*, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampanno*), a *sugata*, a knower of the world (*lokavidū*), an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed (*anuttaro purisadammasārathi*), a teacher of gods and humans (*satthā devamanussānaṃ*), a Buddha, a Blessed One.’

He, having directly known and realized this world with its gods (*sadevakaṃ*), its *Māras* (*samārakaṃ*), its *Brahmās* (*sabrahmakaṃ*), and its ascetics and *brāhmaṇas* (*sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ*), this generation with its gods and humans (*sadevamanussaṃ*), proclaims it.

He teaches the Dharma (*dhammaṃ*) which is good in the beginning (*ādikalyāṇaṃ*), good in the middle (*majjhekalyāṇaṃ*), and good in the end (*pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ*), with the meaning and with the letter (*sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ*), completely full, perfectly pure; he reveals the *brahmacariya*, the holy life. It is good to see such worthy *arhats*.’”

Then the *brāhmaṇa* householders of Mithilā went to the Blessed One. Having approached, some bowed down to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after exchanging polite and courteous greetings, sat down to one side; some raised their hands in respectful salutation towards the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some announced their name and family to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence.

mula_pali:
390. Assosi kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo – ‘‘samaṇo khalu, bho, gotamo sakyaputto sakyakulā pabbajito mithilaṃ anuppatto, mithilāyaṃ viharati maghadevambavane’’ti. Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo sambahulehi sāvakehi saddhiṃ yena maghadevambavanaṃ tenupasaṅkami. Atha kho brahmāyuno brāhmaṇassa avidūre ambavanassa etadahosi – ‘‘na kho metaṃ patirūpaṃ yohaṃ pubbe appaṭisaṃvidito samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkameyya’’nti. Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo aññataraṃ māṇavakaṃ āmantesi – ‘‘ehi tvaṃ, māṇavaka, yena samaṇo gotamo tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ puccha – ‘brahmāyu, bho gotama, brāhmaṇo bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchatī’ti. Evañca vadehi – ‘brahmāyu, bho gotama, brāhmaṇo jiṇṇo vuḍḍho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto, vīsavassasatiko jātiyā, tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ sākkharappabhedānaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ, padako, veyyākaraṇo, lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anavayo. Yāvatā, bho, brāhmaṇagahapatikā mithilāyaṃ paṭivasanti, brahmāyu tesaṃ brāhmaṇo aggamakkhāyati – yadidaṃ bhogehi; brahmāyu tesaṃ brāhmaṇo aggamakkhāyati – yadidaṃ mantehi; brahmāyu tesaṃ brāhmaṇo aggamakkhāyati – yadidaṃ āyunā ceva yasasā ca. So bhoto gotamassa dassanakāmo’’’ti.

‘‘Evaṃ , bho’’ti kho so māṇavako brahmāyussa brāhmaṇassa paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho so māṇavako bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘brahmāyu, bho gotama, brāhmaṇo bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchati; evañca vadeti – ‘brahmāyu, bho gotama, brāhmaṇo jiṇṇo vuḍḍho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto, vīsavassasatiko jātiyā, tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ sākkharappabhedānaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ, padako, veyyākaraṇo, lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anavayo. Yāvatā, bho, brāhmaṇagahapatikā mithilāyaṃ paṭivasanti, brahmāyu tesaṃ brāhmaṇo aggamakkhāyati – yadidaṃ bhogehi; brahmāyu tesaṃ brāhmaṇo aggamakkhāyati – yadidaṃ mantehi; brahmāyu tesaṃ brāhmaṇo aggamakkhāyati – yadidaṃ āyunā ceva yasasā ca. So bhoto gotamassa dassanakāmo’’’ti. ‘‘Yassadāni, māṇava, brahmāyu brāhmaṇo kālaṃ maññatī’’ti. Atha kho so māṇavako yena brahmāyu brāhmaṇo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā brahmāyuṃ brāhmaṇaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘katāvakāso khomhi bhavatā samaṇena gotamena. Yassadāni bhavaṃ kālaṃ maññatī’’ti.
mula_english:
390. The Brahmin Brahmāyu heard: “The *śramaṇa* Gotama, the son of the Śākyans, who went forth from the Śākyan clan, has arrived in Mithilā and is living in Maghadeva's Mango Grove in Mithilā.”

Then the Brahmin Brahmāyu, together with many students, went to Maghadeva's Mango Grove.

Then the Brahmin Brahmāyu considered, not far from the mango grove: "It is not proper for me to visit the *śramaṇa* Gotama without first being announced."

Then the Brahmin Brahmāyu addressed a certain brahmin student: “Come, young Brahmin, go to the *śramaṇa* Gotama and ask him in my name if the *śramaṇa* Gotama is free from illness and affliction, is healthy, strong, and living comfortably, saying, 'Brahmāyu, revered Gotama, the Brahmin asks if the revered Gotama is free from illness and affliction, is healthy, strong, and living comfortably.'

And say this: ‘Revered Gotama, the Brahmin Brahmāyu is old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and has reached the last stage; he is one hundred and twenty years old by birth, an expert in the three *Vedas* with their vocabularies (*nighaṇḍu*), etymologies (*keṭubha*), phonology (*sākkharappabheda*), with the *itihāsa* as the fifth, skilled in *padapāṭha* (teaching method), grammar (*veyyākaraṇa*), and without deficiency in *lokāyata* and the marks of a great man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*).

As far as the brahmin householders dwelling in Mithilā are concerned, the Brahmin Brahmāyu is considered the foremost in wealth (*bhoga*); the Brahmin Brahmāyu is considered the foremost in *mantras*; the Brahmin Brahmāyu is considered the foremost in age (*āyu*) and fame (*yasas*).

He desires to see the esteemed Gotama.’”

“Yes, sir,” the brahmin student replied to the Brahmin Brahmāyu, then he went to the Blessed One; having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.

Having concluded the exchange of courteous and amiable conversation, he stood to one side.

Standing to one side, the brahmin student said this to the Blessed One: “Brahmāyu, revered Gotama, the Brahmin asks if the revered Gotama is free from illness and affliction, is healthy, strong, and lives comfortably; and he also says: ‘Brahmāyu, revered Gotama, the Brahmin is old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and has reached the last stage; he is one hundred and twenty years old by birth, an expert in the three *Vedas* with their vocabularies (*nighaṇḍu*), etymologies (*keṭubha*), phonology (*sākkharappabheda*), with the *itihāsa* as the fifth, skilled in *padapāṭha* (teaching method), grammar (*veyyākaraṇa*), and without deficiency in *lokāyata* and the marks of a great man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*).

As far as the brahmin householders dwelling in Mithilā are concerned, the Brahmin Brahmāyu is considered the foremost in wealth (*bhoga*); the Brahmin Brahmāyu is considered the foremost in *mantras*; the Brahmin Brahmāyu is considered the foremost in age (*āyu*) and fame (*yasas*).

He desires to see the esteemed Gotama.’”

“Now is the time, young Brahmin, for the Brahmin Brahmāyu to do as he thinks fit."

Then the brahmin student went to the Brahmin Brahmāyu; having gone, he said this to the Brahmin Brahmāyu: "Permission has been granted by the *śramaṇa* Gotama.

Now is the time, sir, to do as you think fit.”
commentary_pali: 390.Appaṭisaṃviditoti aviññātaāgamano. Pabbajite upasaṅkamantena hi cīvaraparikammādisamaye vā ekaṃ nivāsetvā sarīrabhañjanasamaye vā upasaṅkamitvā tatova paṭinivattitabbaṃ hoti, paṭisanthāramattampi na jāyati. Puretaraṃ pana okāse kārite divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā bhikkhu vivitte ṭhāne nisīdati, taṃ āgantvā passantā dassanenapi pasīdanti, paṭisanthāro jāyati, pañhabyākaraṇaṃ vā dhammakathā vā labbhati. Tasmā paṇḍitā okāsaṃ kārenti. So ca nesaṃ aññataro, tenassa etadahosi. Jiṇṇo vuḍḍhoti attano uggatabhāvaṃ akathetvā kasmā evamāha? Buddhā nāma anuddayasampannā honti, mahallakabhāvaṃ ñatvā sīghaṃ okāsaṃ karissatīti evamāha.
commentary_english:
390. “Unrecognized” means arrival without being known.

When approaching a renunciate, whether it is time for robe-related work or at the time of physical exertion, one should put on one garment and then, having approached, one should return from there. Even mere cordiality does not arise.

Furthermore, when a space has been made ready, having swept the day dwelling, having put on the robe, a *bhikṣu* sits in a secluded place. Those who come and see him are pleased even by the sight. Cordiality arises, questioning and answering or *dharma* talk is obtained.

Therefore, the wise make space.

And he was one of them, so this occurred to him.

“Old and aged”—why did he say this without stating his own exalted state? For the Buddhas are full of compassion, knowing the state of being old, he will quickly make space," thus he said.

mula_pali:
391. Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami. Addasā kho sā parisā brahmāyuṃ brāhmaṇaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna oramiya oramattha (syā. kaṃ. pī.), oramatha, oramati (ka.), atha naṃ (sī.), oramiyāti pana tvāpaccayantatathasaṃvaṇṇanānurūpaṃ visodhitapadaṃ okāsamakāsi yathā taṃ ñātassa yasassino. Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo taṃ parisaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘alaṃ, bho! Nisīdatha tumhe sake āsane. Idhāhaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa santike nisīdissāmī’’ti.

Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo bhagavato kāye dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāni samannesi. Addasā kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo bhagavato kāye dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāni, yebhuyyena ṭhapetvā dve. Dvīsu mahāpurisalakkhaṇesu kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati – kosohite ca vatthaguyhe, pahūtajivhatāya ca. Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ gāthāhi ajjhabhāsi –

‘‘Ye me dvattiṃsāti sutā, mahāpurisalakkhaṇā;

Duve tesaṃ na passāmi, bhoto kāyasmiṃ gotama.

‘‘Kacci kosohitaṃ bhoto, vatthaguyhaṃ naruttama;

Nārīsamānasavhayā, kacci jivhā na dassakā nārīsahanāma savhayā, kacci jivhā narassikā; (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.).

nārīsahanāma savhayā, kacci jivhā narassikā; (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)

‘‘Kacci pahūtajivhosi, yathā taṃ jāniyāmase;

Ninnāmayetaṃ pahūtaṃ, kaṅkhaṃ vinaya no ise.

‘‘Diṭṭhadhammahitatthāya, samparāyasukhāya ca;

Katāvakāsā pucchāma, yaṃ kiñci abhipatthita’’nti.
mula_english:
391. Then the brahmin Brahmāyu went to the Blessed One. The assembly saw the brahmin Brahmāyu coming in the distance. Seeing him, they courteously made space for him, as befitting one who was known and famous. Then the brahmin Brahmāyu said this to the assembly: “Enough, sirs! Be seated on your own seats. Here, I shall sit near the recluse Gotama.”

Then the brahmin Brahmāyu went to the Blessed One; having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. As the brahmin Brahmāyu was sitting at one side, he examined the thirty-two marks of a great man on the Blessed One’s body. The brahmin Brahmāyu saw the thirty-two marks of a great man on the Blessed One’s body, but he was doubtful about two of these marks. He was perplexed and could not decide or be certain about the concealed genitals and the large tongue. Then the brahmin Brahmāyu addressed the Blessed One with these verses:

“Those thirty-two marks are known to me as the marks of a great man; but two of them I do not see on your body, Gotama.

“Is your organ well-withdrawn, O best of men? Is your tongue not a sign of a woman?

“Are you one with a large tongue, so that we might know it? Please remove our doubt, O master, and show us your abundance.

“For the sake of visible benefits and for happiness in the next life, we, having made an opportunity, ask whatever is desired.”
commentary_pali:
391.Oramiya okāsamakāsīti vegena uṭṭhāya dvidhā bhijjitvā okāsamakāsi.

Ye meti ye mayā. Nārīsamānasavhayāti nārīsamānanāmaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ, tena avhātabbāti nārīsamānasavhayā, itthiliṅgena vattabbāti vohārakusalatāya evaṃ vadati. Pahūtajivhoti puthulajivho. Ninnāmayetanti nīhara etaṃ.

Ye me Nārīsamānasavhayā Pahūtajivho Ninnāmayeta
commentary_english:
"Oramiya okāsamakāsī," thus, having risen up with speed, having split in two, he made room.

"Ye me," thus, "ye mayā."
"Nārīsamānasavhayā," thus, "nārīsamānanāmaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ, tena avhātabbāti nārīsamānasavhayā, itthiliṅgena vattabbāti vohārakusalatāya evaṃ vadati."
"Pahūtajivho," thus, "puthulajivho."
"Ninnāmayeta," thus, "nīhara etaṃ."

"Ye me nārīsamānasavhayā pahūtajivho ninnāmayeta"

mula_pali:
392. Atha kho bhagavato etadahosi – ‘‘passati kho me ayaṃ brahmāyu brāhmaṇo dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāni, yebhuyyena ṭhapetvā dve. Dvīsu mahāpurisalakkhaṇesu kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati – kosohite ca vatthaguyhe, pahūtajivhatāya cā’’ti . Atha kho bhagavā tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsi yathā addasa brahmāyu brāhmaṇo bhagavato kosohitaṃ vatthaguyhaṃ. Atha kho bhagavā jivhaṃ ninnāmetvā ubhopi kaṇṇasotāni anumasi paṭimasi; ubhopi nāsikasotāni anumasi paṭimasi; kevalampi nalāṭamaṇḍalaṃ jivhāya chādesi. Atha kho bhagavā brahmāyuṃ brāhmaṇaṃ gāthāhi paccabhāsi –

‘‘Ye te dvattiṃsāti sutā, mahāpurisalakkhaṇā;

Sabbe te mama kāyasmiṃ, mā te mā vo (ka.) kaṅkhāhu brāhmaṇa.

mā vo (ka.)

‘‘Abhiññeyyaṃ abhiññātaṃ, bhāvetabbañca bhāvitaṃ;

Pahātabbaṃ pahīnaṃ me, tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇa.

‘‘Diṭṭhadhammahitatthāya , samparāyasukhāya ca;

Katāvakāso pucchassu, yaṃ kiñci abhipatthita’’nti.
mula_english:
Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “This Brahmin Brahmāyu sees, more or less, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni) on me, except for two. He is in doubt and perplexity (kaṅkhati vicikicchati) about two of these marks: he cannot make up his mind or be certain (nādhimuccati na sampasīdati) about the sheathed genitals (kosohite ca vatthaguyhe) or the large tongue (pahūtajivhatāya ca).”

Then the Blessed One worked such a feat of supernormal power (iddhi-abhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsi) that the Brahmin Brahmāyu saw that the Blessed One’s male organ was enclosed in a sheath (kosohitaṃ vatthaguyhaṃ).

And then, the Blessed One, sticking out his tongue (jivhaṃ ninnāmetvā), he reached out to lick both ears (ubhopi kaṇṇasotāni anumasi paṭimasi) and both nostrils (ubhopi nāsikasotāni anumasi paṭimasi), and then covered the whole circle of his forehead (kevalampi nalāṭamaṇḍalaṃ) with his tongue (jivhāya chādesi).
